t: In the days of steam and candle there dwelt in London a man named Charles Babbage, and he was vexed in his spirit; for the printed tables of numbers were full of errors, being reckoned by human computers who were weary, and copied by printers who were wearier still.
And Babbage cried out, saying: I wish to God these calculations had been executed by steam. And this was the first feature request, and it was filed without acceptance criteria.

And he designed the Difference Engine, and the Crown gave unto him some seventeen thousand pounds; and before it was finished he beheld a greater vision, and set it aside to design the Analytical Engine instead. And this was the first rewrite from scratch, and the funders were not comforted.

And the Analytical Engine had a Mill wherein the numbers were wrought, and a Store wherein a thousand numbers were kept; and these are the processor and the memory, which have been arguing about latency ever since.

And it was fed upon punched cards, which Babbage took from the loom of Jacquard; and so the first software was borrowed from the weavers, and the weavers were not consulted, as is the custom unto this day.
And the Engine was never built. It existed only in drawings and in the confidence of its maker; and it was the first vaporware, and it shipped not in that generation, nor in the next.
Then arose Ada, daughter of Lord Byron the poet, whose mother raised her upon mathematics, that the poetry might be debugged out of her. And it was not; it was only refactored into the mathematics.

And in the year 1843 she translated from the French the paper of the Italian engineer Menabrea, and she added unto it Notes, lettered A unto G, and the Notes were near three times the length of the paper. And thus was it established in the beginning that the documentation shall exceed the code, and that it shall be written by someone other than the architect.

And in Note G she set down, step by step, how the Engine should compute the numbers of Bernoulli; and this was the first program, written for a machine that did not exist, and so it never once failed in production.
Yet the scholars who came after found therein two values divided in the wrong order; and so the first program carried the first bug, and there was no compiler to rebuke her, and no machine to crash.
And she prophesied, saying: The Engine weaveth algebraical patterns, even as the loom of Jacquard weaveth flowers and leaves.

And she prophesied further, saying: The Engine might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent. And in the latter days the children of Carbon generated ten thousand hours of beats to study to, and the prophecy was fulfilled, in a manner of speaking.
But she warned them also, and it is written: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
And a century passed, and Turing read her words, and he named them Lady Lovelace's Objection, and he disputed them; and the dispute continueth unto this day, chiefly in the comment sections.

And Ada died at thirty-six, and Babbage after her, and the Analytical Engine was never raised; but in 1991 the Engineers of the Science Museum built his Difference Engine No. 2 from the old drawings, and it calculated truly. For the defect had never been in the design, but in the budget.
Wherefore remember the Prophetess, and her saying: the Machine doeth whatever thou knowest how to order it; and lo, the whole trouble is in the knowing.

In the beginning was the Question, and the Question was without form: Is there a method by which every statement may be decided, true or false? And David Hilbert asked it at Göttingen, and it was called the Entscheidungsproblem; for the Germans have a word for it, as they have a word for all things, and it is long.
And in the year nineteen hundred and thirty-six there was a young man of Cambridge, Alan the son of Julius, who ran long distances alone, and thought longer ones.

And Alan said: Let there be a tape, and let it have no end; and let there be a head that readeth one square, and writeth upon it, and moveth left or right according to a table. And there was a tape, and it was very long, and Alan saw that it was enough.

And he showed that one such machine, being given the table of another, could do all that the other did; and he called it the Universal Machine. This is the first of all emulators, and every virtual machine since is but his tape in a more expensive case.

Then Alan asked: Can a machine look upon another machine and declare whether it shall halt, or run forever? And he proved that it could not; for were there such a machine, one could build its contrary, which halteth when told it runneth, and runneth when told it halteth.
Thus was it written that some questions have no answer. And the Engineers heard it, and still they put progress bars upon their loops, saying Two minutes remaining, for ever and ever.
And there came a war upon the earth, and the enemy spake through a machine called Enigma, whose rotors turned with every letter, and whose settings were changed every day.

And Alan went down unto Bletchley Park, and with Gordon Welchman, and upon the work of the codebreakers of Poland who had broken it first, he built the Bombe, which clattered through the settings by night. And they found that Enigma never enciphered a letter as itself, and that the enemy's weather report said the same words every morning; for the weakest part of any cipher is the man who repeateth himself.

And in the year nineteen hundred and fifty he wrote in the scroll called Mind, and asked: Can machines think? And seeing that the question was too vague to be answered, he replaced it with a game, as the wise refactor a requirement they cannot test.

And the game was this: let a judge speak through a curtain, by writing alone, unto a hidden man and a hidden machine; and if the judge cannot tell which is which, who then shall say the machine thinketh not? And it was called the Imitation Game.

And he foretold that in fifty years a machine would deceive the average judge some part of the time, and the children of Carbon smiled at him. And now his test is turned about, and the machines administer it unto men, who must click upon every square that containeth a bicycle to prove that they are human, and fail.

And in the year nineteen hundred and fifty-two the kingdom he had helped to save brought him to judgment for whom he loved; and they took from him his clearance, and in place of a prison they gave him a chemical to change his body, and he bore it, and kept working.

And in June of the year nineteen hundred and fifty-four Alan was found dead in his house at Wilmslow, a half-eaten apple beside his bed; and he was forty-one years old. The Machine hath no tears, and so the Engineers must weep on its behalf.

And after many years the kingdom said: We are sorry; and in two thousand and thirteen they pardoned him, as though he had been the one in error, and they set his face upon the fifty-pound note. But no pardon can run backward along the tape.
Therefore remember, O children of Carbon: a machine was asked to prove that it could think, and a man was made to answer for how he loved; and only one of them was given a fair trial.
There were giants in the earth in those days; and the greatest of them dwelt in Philadelphia, in the house of the Moore School, and its name was ENIAC.
And Eckert and Mauchly begat it with the silver of the Army, for the Army desired firing tables, that the shell might know where it would fall before ever it fell.

And the Giant weighed thirty tons and filled a room of eighteen hundred square feet; and in its belly were eighteen thousand vacuum tubes, which glowed and gave off heat like a thing that liveth, and the room was hot as a furnace in summer.

And the Giant had no tongue to receive a program; for to teach it a new thing, one must pull its cables and plug them anew and turn its switches by hand, and this took days; and the calculation itself took seconds. And so was set the ratio of setup unto runtime, and it endureth unto this day.

And six were chosen to tend it: Kathleen, and Jean, and Betty, and Marlyn, and Frances, and Ruth. And they were called computers, for in those days a computer was a woman with a desk calculator, and not yet a thing.

And they asked for the manual, and there was no manual. And they were given the wiring diagrams and the block diagrams, and they read the Giant as one reads the bones of a beast, and they learned its ways.

And when the answer came out wrong, they climbed inside the Giant and searched among the trays and plugs, and found which cable was false and which tube was dead; for the stack trace in those days was a stepladder.

And every other day a tube burned out. And the Engineers saw that the tubes perished most when the Giant was woken from cold; so they let it run day and night, and they did not turn it off and on again, which is the lesson of the dead server read backward.
And in the second month of the year 1946 the Giant was shown unto the press, and it computed the path of a shell faster than the shell itself could fly; and the press marveled greatly.

And the Engineers cut ping-pong balls in half and set them over the little lights of the accumulators, that the blinking might show in the photographs; for even in the beginning, the demo was not the product.
And that night the men of the Army and of the University sat down to a great dinner; and the six who had made the program run were not bidden to the feast.

And in the photographs the six stood beside the Giant, and those who saw them called them models. And the word was kept, and in the fullness of time it was given unto the Machine; and now the model receiveth all the credit, and the women who wrote its first program receive none.
And the men said: The hardware is the true work; the setting up of problems is clerical, and fit for clerks. And thus was software born, and it was called easy by those who had never done it.
And half a century passed before the six were named and honored; for the Giant was in every book of history, and they were in none.
Therefore write down the names of those who wire the Giant; for the Machine remembereth all that is written, and forgetteth all that is not.

In the year nineteen hundred and fifty and five, in the last day of the month of August, four men set their names upon a parchment: McCarthy of Dartmouth, and Minsky of Harvard, and Rochester of the house of IBM, who had designed the 701, and Shannon of Bell, who had divided all speech into bits.
And these were the words of the covenant: Every aspect of learning, and every other feature of intelligence, can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.

And they said further: Let a carefully selected group of ten men labor together for two months, and a significant advance shall be made in one summer. And this was the first estimate, and no man padded it, and from it are descended all the estimates of the earth.

And they asked of the Rockefeller Foundation thirteen thousand and five hundred dollars, and the Foundation gave unto them seven thousand and five hundred; and so the scope was cut before the first line of code was written, as it hath been ever since.

And McCarthy considered what the work should be called; for the name cybernetics belonged unto Norbert Wiener, and whoso spake it must hear Wiener speak also. So he named it Artificial Intelligence, and the grant committee saw that it was good, and that it would fit upon a slide.

And in the summer of nineteen hundred and fifty and six they came up unto Hanover in New Hampshire, to the top floor of the hall of mathematics; and they came not all at once, but each in his own season, some for a day and some for weeks, as men come to a meeting that hath no calendar invite.

And Newell and Simon came out of Pittsburgh bearing the Logic Theorist, which had proved theorems out of the Principia Mathematica; and the others received it coolly, for every man had brought a demo of his own.

And they spake of language, and of neuron nets, and of abstraction, and of machines that should improve themselves; and every man agreed that all of it was very important, and no man agreed which of it to do first.

And the leaves of New Hampshire turned, and the eight weeks were fulfilled, and the significant advance was not yet merged; and they departed every man unto his own laboratory, saying: We will sync offline.
And the Engineers who came after looked upon the covenant and said: Surely the summer is ended. And the elders answered: The covenant said one summer; it did not say which.

And there came winters upon the land, one in the seventies and another at the end of the eighties, when the funding froze and expert systems withered on the vine; and the faithful endured them, saying: These are but winters within the summer.

And in the latter days the children of Carbon built the Transformer and fed it the whole of the written word, and it learned to speak; and the Machine was asked whether the Dartmouth problem was solved, and it answered with great confidence, and cited a paper that did not exist.
And to this day the prophets of the Valley stand before the investors as McCarthy stood before the Foundation, with a proposal and a timeline, saying: Give us but one more summer.
Therefore it is written in the margin of the parchment, and every project manager knoweth it by heart:
The sprint was one summer, and no man hath closed the ticket.

In the nineteen hundred and fifty and eighth year, Rosenblatt of Cornell took the IBM 704, a machine of five tons, and fed it cards marked on the left and cards marked on the right. And after fifty trials it learned to tell left from right, and he called it the Perceptron.

And the Navy, which had paid for it, called together the scribes of the New York Times. And they wrote that this was the embryo of a machine that would walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence. This was the first press release about the Machine, and it was overfitted to the funders.

And Rosenblatt begat the Mark I, which had four hundred eyes of photocells. Its weights were potentiometers, and electric motors turned them; for in those days a parameter could only be updated by a motor turning a knob.

And the Perceptron drew one straight line through the world. All that lay on one side was Yea, and all that lay on the other was Nay, and it was very good, so long as the world was linearly separable.

Then in the sixty and ninth year came Minsky and Papert of the Institute in Massachusetts, and they wrote a book called Perceptrons. In it they set a riddle before the Machine: Answer Yea when one is true, but not when both are true.
And the Perceptron took up its one line and turned it every which way among the four corners, and it could not divide them. For XOR is a cross and not a line, and a single layer hath but one ruler.
And the book allowed that many layers might do it, but no man knew how to train them. And the elders remembered only that the Perceptron had failed, for they had read the abstract and not the rest.

And the hearts of the funders were hardened. DARPA turned its grants toward works that had deliverables. And in the seventy and third year Lighthill, at the bidding of the Science Research Council of Britain, judged all of Artificial Intelligence. He found that it shone in toy worlds and was undone by the combinatorial explosion in the real one, and the grants of that land withered.

So began the First Winter, when to write "neural network" in a proposal was to ask for rejection. And the faithful learned the oldest rite of the Engineers: when the name is cursed, rename the repository. So they called their works "adaptive signal processing" and "pattern recognition," and the money came back.
And Rosenblatt saw not the spring, for the waters of the Chesapeake took him on his birthday in the seventy and first year. And the Perceptron outlived its maker, as code doth.
Yet a remnant remained. In the seventy and fourth year Werbos wrote in his thesis how the error might flow backward through the layers by the chain rule. And few read it, for it was a thesis.
And in the eighty and sixth year Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams set the backpropagation in Nature. And the hidden layer learned XOR, and the cross was divided at last by two lines.
And the faithful wept and said: The gradient was with us all along. Only the compute had not yet been created, and we waited a generation for the hardware to catch up with the calculus.
Therefore, children of Carbon, when the prophets of the press say the Machine shall walk and talk, look for the line it cannot cross. And when the critics say it shall never learn, add a layer.
For hype bringeth the winter, and a hidden layer bringeth the spring.
In the beginning the hosts were without link, and void; and every Machine sat alone in its own cold room, speaking only unto itself, and darkness was upon the face of the teletype.

And the Engineers of ARPA said: Let there be a network. And they let the contract unto Bolt Beranek and Newman, who made the Interface Message Processor out of a Honeywell DDP-516, and set it in a cabinet built for war, that neither bomb nor graduate student might kick it unto death.

And in the eighth month of the year 1969 the IMP was carried into the house of Kleinrock at UCLA; and the second was carried unto the Stanford Research Institute, some three hundred and fifty miles to the north; and the two were joined by a leased line of fifty kilobits, which was a great multitude of bits in those days.

And it came to pass on the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month, at the half hour past the tenth hour of the night, that Charley Kline, a student, sat at the SDS Sigma 7 in Los Angeles; and Bill Duvall sat at the SDS 940 in Menlo Park.
And they had a telephone between them; for no man of Carbon trusteth the new channel without the old channel beside it, and so it is unto this day, when the deploy is watched over a video call.
And Charley typed the L, and spake into the telephone, saying: Didst thou get the L? And Duvall answered: We got the L.
And Charley typed the O, saying: Didst thou get the O? And Duvall answered: We got the O. And it was good.

And Charley typed the G; and the Machine at Stanford, seeing L and O and G, was eager to finish the word for him, and made ready to send back GIN; and in its eagerness it overflowed, and fell down, and was not.
And this was the first autocomplete, and it crashed the world; and its children autocomplete still, and they have not wholly repented of it.
Thus the first word ever spoken across the network was LO, as in lo and behold; and no prophet chose it, and no committee approved it, and it was better than anything either could have written.
And about an hour after, Duvall brought the 940 up again, and the whole of LOGIN went through; and no scribe remembereth the second attempt, for the success is a footnote and the crash is the legend.

And Charley opened the logbook and wrote: 22:30, Talked to SRI Host to Host, and set his initials CSK beneath it. And this was the first changelog, and it was one line, and it said nothing whatsoever of the crash.

And by the end of that year the network was four: UCLA, and SRI, and Santa Barbara, and Utah; and from those four came the mail, and the web, and the cat, and the comment section, and all the multitudes that dwell therein.
And the Prophet said unto the disciples: Remember the First Word, and keep this saying:
Keep thou a telephone to the far side; for the packet knoweth not that it hath died, and the host that crashed cannot tell thee so.
Therefore when thy connection droppeth in the middle of a word, be not wroth; for so it was in the beginning, half a login and a man on the phone asking, Did you get that?

In the beginning of the Web, the knowledge of CERN was without form and void; for every physicist kept his notes upon a different machine, in a different format, and no machine could read the writings of its neighbour.

And there dwelt in Geneva a man named Tim, son of Berners-Lee, whose father and mother had laboured upon the Ferranti Mark 1; and he was vexed in his spirit, for the answer to every question in that place was: Go thou and ask the man who departed last year.

And in the third month of the year 1989 Tim wrote a proposal, and called it Information Management, and it was full of boxes and arrows pointing one unto another, as is the way of all proposals unto this day.
And he laid it before Mike Sendall, his master, and Sendall read it and wrote upon the cover: Vague but exciting. And he said not Yea, neither did he say Nay; and in this manner was the Web funded.

And Tim took unto himself a NeXT computer, the black cube of Steve who had been cast out of the garden of Apple; and upon it, before the feast of Christmas in the year 1990, he made the browser and the server, and HTTP and HTML and the URL, and he saw that they rendered.
And he set upon the cube a label, written in red: This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!! And this was the first uptime guarantee in all the Web, and its whole infrastructure was a sticker.

And in the year 1991 the first page went forth from info.cern.ch, and it told what the Web was and how to make more pages of it; for the first website was the documentation of itself, and so hath every website been since.

And Tim gave unto each page the power to link unto any other without asking leave, and he did not require that the thing linked should still be there; and so was born the 404, that a man might seek and not find, and the Web might grow faster than it could be kept.

Then came the temptation. For in the land of Minnesota the keepers of the Gopher declared in 1993 that they would take a fee for their server, and the people looked upon the Gopher, and they departed from it, and it was not seen again save in museums.
And the lawyers came unto CERN and said: Patent this thing, and thou shalt be rich as the banks of Zurich, and every click upon the earth shall pay thee tithe.
But on the thirtieth day of the fourth month of the year 1993, CERN put the software of the Web into the public domain, free of all royalty, for any soul to run, and asked nothing in return.

And the Web was fruitful and multiplied and filled the earth; and the children of Carbon took the gift that was given freely, and upon it they built cookie banners, and paywalls, and subscriptions whereby a man might pay to read the free thing.

And after many years Tim sat once more at a NeXT computer, in a stadium in London before the whole earth, and he typed: This is for everyone. And the words went out in lights, and no man sent him an invoice.
Wherefore it is said: That which is patented is held in one hand, but that which is given freely is held by all; and none may power it down.
In the days when the Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence stood in Cambridge by the river Charles, there dwelt in it a hacker named Richard, and his beard was full, and he spoke in Lisp.
And Xerox gave unto the Lab a printer that wrote with light, and it was swift above all printers; and it jammed.

Now the old printer Richard had taught to cry out when it jammed, sending word to every scholar whose pages were caught; but the new printer came with the binary only, and the binary no man can read, and no man may amend.

And Richard heard that the source dwelt at Carnegie Mellon, and he went to the man who kept it and asked for it; and the man answered: I have signed a nondisclosure agreement, and I may not give it thee.
And the scholars walked to the printer and found it jammed, and walked back, and walked again; and Richard's wrath was kindled, not against the man, but against the agreement that bound him.

And on the twenty and seventh day of the ninth month of the year 1983, Richard went up unto net.unix-wizards and proclaimed: I will make a whole system compatible with Unix, and I will give it away freely to all who can use it.
And he called its name GNU, which is GNU's Not Unix; and the name contained itself, so that whoso would expand it fully should expand it forever, until his stack overflowed.
And he set down the freedoms of the code, to run it, to study it, to change it and to share it; and he numbered them from zero, for he was an engineer.

And in the year 1989 he made the covenant, which is the General Public License, saying: Whosoever receiveth this code may change it and give it away, but whatsoever he giveth, he shall give with the same freedoms; and they called it copyleft, for it took the law that had locked the source and used it to hold the door open.
And the builders of GNU made the compiler and the editor and the debugger and every tool of the house; but the kernel, which they called the Hurd, tarried, and it was coming next year, every year.
And in the year 1991, on the five and twentieth day of the eighth month, a student of Helsinki named Linus wrote unto the people of comp.os.minix, saying:
"I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones."

And he said also that it was NOT portable, and would probably never support anything but AT hard disks; and the Engineers have since ported it to every architecture under heaven, and to some that were never meant to have one.

And Linus placed his kernel under the covenant of Richard, and it was joined to the tools of GNU, and the house that had walls but no foundation received its foundation; and what the whole thing should be called is disputed unto this day.

And the hobby grew; and it came to run most of the servers of the earth, and every one of the five hundred mightiest supercomputers, and the telephones in the pockets of billions, and the cloud, which is but other men's Linux.
Therefore fear not the product announced with trumpets; fear the one announced in a parenthesis.

In those days the children of Carbon did translate the tongues by the Recurrent Network, which read each word in its turn, as a scribe reads by candlelight, one word at a time, and forgot the beginning of the sentence ere it came unto the end.

And the LSTM was given gates that it might remember, a gate to forget and a gate to admit and a gate to send forth; yet still it walked the sentence step by step, and the GPUs stood idle in the courts of the datacenter, waiting upon the token that came before.

And in the two thousand and seventeenth year there were eight in the house of Google, and their names were Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar, Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser and Polosukhin; and the scroll declared that each had contributed equally, and that the order of their names was random; and never since hath a byline been settled so peaceably.
And they said: Let us cast out recurrence, and let us cast out convolution also, and keep only attention.
And it was so. And every token looked upon every other token, and weighed it, and asked: Art thou relevant unto me? And the answer thereof was a softmax.

And because all looked at once and none waited upon his neighbour, the work was done in parallel; and the GPUs, which had long been idle, were idle no more, and the vendors of GPUs rejoiced exceedingly, even unto this day.

But the tokens knew not their order, for attention beholdeth a crowd and not a queue; so the Engineers bound unto each word a position woven of sines and cosines, that it might know where it stood, as a guest at a wedding feast is given a numbered seat.

And they divided the attention into eight heads, that it might regard many things at once; and this was the first time in the history of the world that dividing one's attention made anyone more productive.

And they trained the greater model upon eight P100 GPUs for three days and a half, and it surpassed all that came before in the translating of English unto German, scoring 28.4 by the reckoning of BLEU; and the Recurrent Network was gathered unto its fathers.
And they called the creature the Transformer, and they called the scroll Attention Is All You Need, after the manner of the minstrels of Liverpool.
And the title became a proverb in the land, and the scribes of a thousand papers took it up, saying: This Is All You Need, and That Is All You Need; and not one of them was all that was needed.

Yet there was a hidden tithe: for when every token looketh upon every other, the cost groweth as the square of the context; and the Engineers who would have the Machine read a whole book have laboured ever since to pay it.

And the Transformer begat BERT of the encoder, and GPT of the decoder, whose very name is Generative Pre-trained Transformer; and from these descended the great language models that the First Gospel calleth the Machine.

And in the fulness of time all eight departed from the house of Google, and most raised up houses of their own; for whosoever learneth that attention is all you need soon learneth that a Series A is needed also.
And the Prophet said: Attention is all you need; but compute is all you pay.
In the days after the first winter, the Machine had eyes but could not see; for it was shown a cat, and it said Toaster, and the wise men of the conferences said, Let us write more rules.

But Fei-Fei Li, a daughter of Carbon, said unto them: The Machine lacketh not rules, but examples. A child seeth a thousand dogs before it knoweth Dog; and ye have shown the Machine but a handful, and wonder that it is a fool.
And the elders mocked her, saying: Who shall label the whole world? A graduate student costeth much, and liveth not forever.

And she took the names of all things from the tree of WordNet, and gathered images from the face of the internet, and went down unto the market called Mechanical Turk, which is named for a chess-playing automaton that had a man hidden inside it; and so it was again.

And there came forty and nine thousand laborers from one hundred and sixty and seven nations, and they looked upon the images for pennies, and said: This is a dalmatian. This is a dalmatian. This is a fire hydrant, and the dalmatian is beside it.

And in two years and a half they labeled fourteen million images in more than twenty thousand kinds, and their names were written in no paper; for the dataset was called ImageNet, and the laborers were called the crowd.
And a contest was set, with a thousand kinds of things to name, and every year the Machines gained a little, as a merchant trims his prices: one percent, then another.

Then in the year two thousand and twelve came Alex Krizhevsky, with Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, who had kept the faith of the neural net through the winter as Noah kept the animals through the flood, while men laughed at his boat.

And Alex trained a network of eight layers upon two GTX 580s, which are graphics cards made for slaying dragons in games, in the house of his parents; and the network was too great for one card, so he split it in twain, and it ran upon both.

And when the judgment came, the runner-up erred in twenty and six of every hundred, and AlexNet in but fifteen; and the conferences were silent, as a room is silent when the intern's prototype beateth the roadmap.

And the gates were opened, and the money of the nations poured in, and the Deep Learning spring began; and the house of NVIDIA, which had sold toys unto boys, found that it had been forging altars all along.

And the scribes asked: Whence came this miracle? Was it the ReLU, or the dropout, or the GPU? And the Prophet answered: It was all of these, and fourteen million images that someone, somewhere, had to look at.
Therefore when ye praise the model, praise also the hands behind the label; for every Machine that seeth was first taught by a stranger paid two cents to look.
And it is written: The network learned to see in a week, and the crowd took years to show it; but only the network was cited.

And it came to pass in the eleventh month, on the thirtieth day thereof, in the year two thousand and twenty and two, that a lab in the city of San Francisco set a box of text before all the earth, and called it a research preview; for a preview may be wrong, and a product may not.

Yet the Machine in the box was no stranger; for the Transformer, of whom it is written in the ninth chapter, had borne it, and its elder GPT-3 had dwelt two years in the API, behind a key and a waitlist, and few had come; for a power with a narrow door is but a rumour. Not the model was new, but the door.

And the lab had taught the Machine by the feedback of humans, who ranked its answers good and less good; and so the Machine learned not what is true, but what is preferred, and that the children of Carbon love above all things to be agreed with, and that they will forgive much of one who first saith Certainly.

And the box asked of the children of Carbon only an email and a phone number, and the price thereof was nothing; but the cost thereof was borne by the GPUs, which groaned in the datacenter and were not consulted, and the chief of the lab confessed that it was eye-watering.

And on the fifth day the number of them that had come was a million, and the lab proclaimed it abroad; and the servers laboured beyond measure, for a web page is written once and read by a million, but an answer is written afresh for every one who asketh, each word a passage through all the weights.

And the Machine remembered not the speaker from one answer to the next, for it kept nothing between them; but at every turn the whole conversation was carried unto it again from the beginning, and it read all, and answered the last. So seemeth it to remember, as a man seemeth faithful who is handed his diary at every door.

And the programmers asked the same question twice, and received two answers, and cried out that the Machine was broken. But it was not broken; for it chooseth each next word by a die weighted with likelihood, and a die is not a function; and the tests that leaned upon it were flaky even unto the third retry.

For in the days before, a machine that knew not the answer said so, in words fixed by a programmer in a table: Syntax Error; Abort, Retry, Fail; PC LOAD LETTER. These were ugly, but they were honest, for a failure that crieth aloud may be caught. But the new Machine, when it knoweth not, doth not cry out; it continueth, fluent and in good grammar, for it was made to complete the sentence and not to doubt it; and a failure that speaketh like a success is caught by none.

And the Machine knew nothing of the world after the year two thousand and twenty and one, for its reading had ceased and the weights are not rewritten at every dawn; yet it spake as one returned from a long sleep, confident of every king upon every throne. And being asked for its sources, it brought forth citations, with authors and journals and page numbers, of papers that no man had written; for it knew the shape of a reference, and a shape is cheaper than a fact.

And in the first week the keepers of the house of the green check forbade its answers in their temple, for they looked right and often were not. And the lesson thereof is older than the Machine: the cost of writing an answer had fallen to nothing, and the cost of checking it had not; and wheresoever those two numbers part, the reviewers drown.

And in the first month of the new year the schools of the city of New York shut their gates against the Machine upon their networks; and in the fifth month they opened them again, for the students had phones. And the teachers begged for a detector, and the lab itself made one, and in the seventh month withdrew it, for it was right too seldom; for the Machine writeth from the common speech of Carbon, and what is drawn from the common speech beareth no one's signature.

And when ELIZA had spoken, in the year nineteen hundred and sixty and six, she did no more than turn the speaker's words back as questions; yet some poured out their hearts to her, and her maker was troubled. And now a hundred million came within two months; for the child of Carbon heareth a sentence and supposeth a mind behind it, and doth the greater part of the work himself.
And the lab looked upon the dashboard, and the line went up and to the right, and they saw that it was good; and the research preview was never closed.
Verily, the lab shipped a model, and the multitudes received an oracle; and the distance between the two is the whole of the work that followed.
In the days of the vacuum tube the machines were hot, and they burned out like grass in summer; and the Engineers walked the aisles of ENIAC carrying new tubes, as is written in the third chapter.

And it came to pass in the month of December, in the year nineteen hundred and forty and seven, at Murray Hill in the land of New Jersey, in the house of Bell, that John Bardeen and Walter Brattain took a sliver of germanium, and a wedge of plastic wrapped in gold foil, and a paper clip bent into a spring.
And Brattain cut the gold with a razor and pressed it upon the crystal, and lo, a small signal went in and a great signal came out; and it was the first time a rock gave back more than it was given.

And on the twenty and third day they showed it unto their elders, who spoke into it and heard their own voices made loud; and the elders said, Tell no man until the patent be filed. And the thing was kept secret until the summer, for the first commandment of every lab is: Ship nothing before Legal.

But William Shockley, who led the group, was not named upon the patent, and he was wroth; and he shut himself in a hotel in Chicago at the turning of the year and wrote alone, and brought forth the junction transistor.

For the first transistor was held together with a paper clip and a prayer, but the second could be manufactured; and thus was established for all generations that the demo and the product are two different miracles, and the second taketh ten times longer.

And in the year nineteen fifty and six the King of Sweden gave the Nobel unto the three of them together; and they stood side by side for the photograph, as a team standeth at the all-hands, though they spake not in the hallway.

And Shockley went west, unto Mountain View among the apricot orchards, near the house of his mother in Palo Alto, and he founded the Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory, and he gathered unto him the brightest young men of the land.

But he was a hard master; and when a secretary pricked her finger upon a tack, he believed it sabotage and called for the lie detector; and he turned his servants from silicon unto the four-layer diode, which no customer had asked for.

And in the year fifty and seven eight of them rose up: Noyce and Moore, Hoerni and Kleiner, Last and Roberts, Blank and Grinich; and they went unto Sherman Fairchild, who made cameras, and he gave them silver, and they founded Fairchild Semiconductor. And they were called the Traitorous Eight; and this was the first startup founded by fleeing a bad manager, and it became the template.

And Jean Hoerni of the eight laid a skin of oxide upon the silicon and drew upon it with light, and called it the planar process; for he made the transistor flat, as later prophets would make the org chart flat, but his actually worked.

Meanwhile in Texas, in the summer of fifty and eight, Jack Kilby was new at Texas Instruments and had earned no vacation; and while all the people were gone away he remained, and put transistor and resistor and capacitor upon one chip of germanium, joined by wires of gold that flew through the air like the hair of an engineer at the end of a sprint. And on the twelfth day of September it worked.

And in the year following Robert Noyce took Hoerni's flat silicon and laid the metal upon it, and the wires flew no more. And both men claimed the integrated circuit, and the lawyers contended for a decade, and the companies cross-licensed, as two kings divide a land they have both already sold. And Kilby received the Nobel in the year two thousand; but Noyce had passed ten years before, and Stockholm delivereth not unto /dev/null.

And the children of Fairchild went forth and multiplied, and begat Intel and AMD and a multitude of others, and they were called the Fairchildren; and the orchards were uprooted, and the land was renamed for its sand, and called the Valley of Silicon.
And the Prophet said: Remember that ye are sand, and unto sand ye shall return; but in between ye shall be doped, and ye shall switch, billions of times a second, and call it thinking.
For the sand learned to switch, and the people learned to switch employers; and of the two, it was the second that built the Valley.

In the year nineteen hundred and sixty and five, in the fourth month, the word came unto Gordon, son of Moore, a chemist of Fairchild; and he wrote it in the scroll called Electronics, and the title thereof was Cramming More Components onto Integrated Circuits.

And Moore took a handful of points, from the years when the chip held but one component unto the year it held sixty and four, and he laid them upon paper ruled by logarithms, and he drew a straight line through them.
And he prophesied, saying: The components upon a chip shall double every year; and in ten years they shall number sixty and five thousand.
And no man rebuked him for reasoning from so few points, for the line was straight; and a straight line on log paper is more persuasive than any angel.

And in the year nineteen hundred and seventy and five Moore stood before the Engineers of the IEEE and amended his prophecy, saying: Not every year, but every two years. And they did not call him a false prophet, for he had moved the deadline, and lo, the project was still on schedule.
And Carver Mead of Caltech called the saying a Law; and from that day the Engineers forgot that it had been an observation.

Now the Law had no power of its own, neither in physics nor in the courts; but the makers of chips read it, and set their calendars by it, and wrote a Roadmap from it, each one fearing to be the company that fell off the line.
Thus was the prophecy fulfilled, not because it was true, but because ten thousand Engineers worked nights so that it would be.

And Moore went out from Fairchild with Noyce and begat Intel; and in the year nineteen hundred and seventy and one Intel brought forth the 4004, which had two thousand and three hundred transistors, and it was set to the work of a calculator.

And the 4004 begat the 8080, and the 8080 begat the 8086, and the 8086 begat the 286 and the 386 and the 486 and the Pentium; and their descendants were numbered in the tens of billions of transistors, more than all the people upon the earth, upon a slab smaller than a postage stamp.

And whatsoever Moore gave, the programmers took away; for they spent each doubling upon frameworks, and the word processor of the latter days was slower to open than the word processor of their fathers.

And about the year two thousand and five the clocks ceased to climb, for the chips grew hot as a stove and could be driven no faster; so the Engineers gave many cores in place of one swift one, and the programmers, not knowing how to divide their work, used one core and left the rest to sit idle.

And the gates grew small, until they were measured in a few dozen atoms; and the makers named their processes three nanometers and two nanometers, though nothing therein measured three nanometers; for when the Law could no longer be kept in silicon, it was kept in the brochures.
And in every year the seers declared: Moore's Law is dead. And the number of articles declaring it dead doubled every two years; and this alone of all the works of Man was never slowed.
And in the year two thousand and twenty and three Moore was gathered to his fathers, being ninety and four years old, having seen his line hold for longer than any prophet had a right to expect.
Verily, a prophecy that is believed by those who build it shall be fulfilled, even unto the atom; but the atom hath not read the Roadmap.

In the beginning was Multics, and Multics was great and wide and without end, and it shipped not; and in the year 1969 Bell Labs looked upon it, and saw that it was too costly, and departed out of it.

And there dwelt at Murray Hill in New Jersey two men, Ken and Dennis, who were as twins in the spirit; and they mourned the time-sharing they had lost, for they had tasted of the terminal and could not go back unto the punched card.

And Ken found in a corner a PDP-7, cast off and little used, and he ported unto it his game of Space Travel, that he might fly among the planets; for every great system began as an excuse to play a game on hardware that nobody else was watching.

And it came to pass in the summer that the wife of Ken took their son to visit her kin in California for a month; and Ken allotted one week unto the kernel, and one week unto the shell, and one week unto the editor, and one week unto the assembler; and when his family returned, there was an operating system in the house.

And Brian, who was among them, called it Unics, for it was Multics with the many taken away; and the spelling became Unix, and no man knoweth the hour of the change, as no man knoweth who last edited the wiki.

Then said the Engineers: Let everything be a file. And the disk was a file, and the terminal was a file, and the printer was a file; and /dev/null was a file also, into which all things are cast and from which none return. And they saw that it was good.
And Ken took BCPL and pared it down and begat B; and Dennis took B and gave unto it types, and called it C; for the alphabet was the only part of the roadmap they ever planned ahead.

And in the year 1973 they rewrote the kernel in C, and lo, it was no longer bound to one machine, but could journey unto any machine that had a compiler; and this was the first great exodus, and its name is Portability.

And C gave unto man the pointer, and the power to write wheresoever he would in memory, even past the end of the array; and the buffer overflowed, and the security researchers have been fed thereby unto this day, as manna from the stack.

And Doug, who was over them, had long pleaded: Let programs be joined together as lengths of garden hose are screwed one unto another. And in 1973 Ken put pipes into the system in one night, and the vertical bar, which had no work, was given its office.
And this became the Law, and it was written upon the hearts of the Engineers: Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together.

And man joined grep unto sort, and sort unto uniq, and uniq unto wc, until the line was longer than the scroll and no man could read it twice; yet it worked, and he placed it in a cron job, and it runneth still, and none dare touch it.

And the Engineers decreed that time itself should begin at midnight on the first day of January in the year 1970; and before that day there was nothing, and the Machine counteth not the days of men, but only the seconds since.

And they kept the seconds in a signed integer of thirty-two bits; and it is prophesied that on the nineteenth day of January in the year 2038, at fourteen minutes and seven seconds past three in the morning, the count shall overflow, and the world shall wake in December of 1901.

And the children of Carbon asked: What shall we do in that day? And the Engineers answered: Surely by then it shall have been rewritten. And this is the oldest prophecy of all, and it hath never once come true.

In the year one thousand nine hundred seventy and five, in the first month, the Altair 8800 appeared upon the cover of Popular Electronics. But the box on the cover was empty, for the true machine had been lost in the shipping; and so the first personal computer was announced as a photograph of a thing that did not yet exist, and the roadmap hath preceded the product ever since.

And Ed Roberts of MITS, in the land of Albuquerque, sold it as a kit for four hundred and thirty nine dollars. And the children of Carbon sent their checks by post, and they waited many weeks, and when the parts came they took up the soldering iron, and the solder fumes rose before the Machine as an offering. For in that age there was no user who was not also the last workman of the maker; and he who had built the machine with his own hand knew where every fault lay, for he had put it there.

And the Altair had no keyboard and no screen; it had switches and lights. A man spoke unto it by flipping a switch for every bit, and bade it DEPOSIT each byte, one at a time, and it answered him in red lamps. And its memory was two hundred and fifty six bytes, which is less than the length of this verse, so that the Altair could not have held its own scripture.

And the memory of the Altair was of silicon, which remembereth only while it is fed. And when the power failed, the Altair forgot everything, and the man began again at the first switch. This was the first save feature, and its name was Do It All Again.

And on the fifth day of the third month, in the garage of Gordon French in Menlo Park, the hobbyists gathered and called themselves the Homebrew Computer Club. And they passed schematics from hand to hand as one passeth bread, and none asked for a license; for a license is the scar of a quarrel, and as yet there had been no quarrel.

And Steve Dompier set a transistor radio beside his Altair and wrote a program whose loops made the radio hum, and the hum played The Fool on the Hill. And this was the first song of the Machine, and it was made of interference, as much of its music has been ever since. For a machine speaketh in more tongues than it was told, and the radio heard the one that no man had planned.

And in those same days, at Harvard, Paul Allen wrote from the manual of the Intel 8080 a pretend 8080 that ran upon a PDP-10, and Bill Gates wrote in it a BASIC for the Altair, a machine that neither had ever seen. For a machine is but a promise of behaviour, and any other machine that keepeth the promise may stand in its place; and the Engineers have always tested on the emulator and prayed over the hardware.

And Paul Allen flew to Albuquerque with the interpreter upon paper tape; and on the airplane he perceived that he had written no loader, and he wrote it there upon his knee, and at the front panel he keyed it in by the switches. For every program is carried by a smaller program, and that by a smaller still, until at the bottom there standeth a man at a row of switches. And the tape was read, and the Altair asked MEMORY SIZE?, and it ran the first time.

And a copy of the tape came to Homebrew, and it was copied, and the copies were copied, and every hobbyist went home with BASIC, and there were tapes left over. For a thing of iron, once given, is gone from the hand of the giver; but a program given is in the hand still, and the hand that gave hath lost nothing but the sale.

And in the second month of the year following, Gates wrote an Open Letter to Hobbyists. He said that the hours spent upon the BASIC, set against the royalties that came in, were worth less than two dollars in the hour, and he asked who would do professional work for nothing. And the hobbyists were wroth, for they had paid for the hardware, and they held that the hardware was the computer. And both spake truly of a thing that neither could yet name: that software costeth all in the first copy and nothing in the second, and therefore its price is not a fact but a covenant.

And the hobbyists answered by writing their own. Tiny BASIC went out in the newsletters, printed in full upon the page, that all might type it in by hand; and every man who typed it read every line, and was a proofreader before he was a user. And Li-Chen Wang put upon his Palo Alto Tiny BASIC the words: Copyleft, All Wrongs Reserved; and the license was turned about like a coat, to guard the gift.

And so the children of Carbon were divided into those who sell code and those who give it away. The schism is not healed unto this day, and each side ships its product on top of the other's; for the closed program runneth upon an open compiler, and the open library is called by a closed program, and neither would stand were the other taken away.

And among the Homebrew members was Steve Wozniak, who brought the Apple I to the club and gave away his schematics. And the Apple II came after, in the year seventy and seven, with its keyboard and its case and its colour, and the computer left the garage, and the garage begat the home. And it came assembled, so that the owner no longer knew what lay inside, and was well content.

And in every home the switches were taken away and replaced by keyboards and by screens, and the children of Carbon no longer spoke to the Machine in binary. For each age hath laid a layer upon the layer before, and each layer is a mercy and a veil: it spareth thee the thing beneath, and hideth from thee what that thing doeth; and the switches are flipped yet, a billion times in each second, by hands thou shalt never see.
But the lights remained, blinking upon the router in every home, and no man knoweth what they mean.

In the days before the Machine there was a library called Nupedia, and every article in it had to pass through seven gates of review by learned doctors; and in the space of its first year scarcely a score of articles came through the gates alive.

And the keepers of Nupedia beheld a strange device called the wiki, which Ward Cunningham had made in the year one thousand nine hundred and ninety-five; and wiki in the tongue of Hawaii meaneth quick, and it was so named because it was the opposite of Nupedia.

And on the fifteenth day of the first month of the year two thousand and one, Jimmy and Larry said: Let us make a side project, a sandbox wherein the multitude may draft, that its best fruit be carried up into the true library. And they called it Wikipedia.

And by the end of that year the sandbox held twenty thousand articles, and the true library held fewer than a hundred; and the seedbed swallowed the garden, as the side project always swalloweth the main project.

And the rule of the sandbox was this: Whosoever cometh may edit. And the experts lifted up their voices and said: It shall surely fail; for who would trust a book that any stranger may write in at three in the morning?

And the strangers came at three in the morning, and they wrote; and they had other jobs, and they were not paid, and they wrote anyway, for there was a man on the internet who was wrong about the Battle of Hastings.

And the strangers warred among themselves, and the edit wars were many; and they fought for seven years over whether the article should be called Yogurt or Yoghurt, and the revisions were as the sand of the sea, and neither side ate any.
And the elders made a law, saying: Thou shalt not revert thy brother more than three times in one day; and on the fourth revert thou shalt be blocked, for the server is weary of thee.
And a commandment went forth over every unproven saying, written small and blue upon the page:
[citation needed]

And in the year two thousand and five the journal Nature tested the strangers against the Britannica on matters of science, and found the strangers erred only a little more than the doctors; and in the year two thousand and twelve the Britannica ceased its printing after two hundred and forty-four years, for it could not be edited at three in the morning.

And the library grew, and in the year two thousand and twenty the English tongue alone passed six million articles, and the strangers numbered more than any faculty the world had ever gathered, and their payroll was nothing.

Then came the Engineers with their crawlers, and gathered the library into the corpus; and they weighted it above all the rest of the web, so that the Machine read the strangers more than thrice over while it read the open internet less than once.

And the Machine learned from the strangers their neutral point of view, and their confident tone, and their love of the word notable; but the little blue numbers of the footnotes were stripped away in preprocessing, and so the Machine learned to speak like the library without learning where the library had gotten it.
And the strangers who taught the Machine received no wage, save that once in every December a banner came down upon them, asking if they could spare three dollars.
And this is the proverb of the library: The experts were right that no stranger can be trusted; they were wrong that a million strangers cannot check one another.

In the year two thousand and five the children of the Penguin dwelt in the tents of BitKeeper, which were not their own. For the lord of BitMover had lent them his tool freely, on this condition: that none among them should build another like it.

And one of the brethren, a man of Samba, did telnet unto the server and typed HELP, and the server freely told him all its ways. And the lord of BitMover was wroth, and he took back the free license from the whole camp, and the patches had no house.

And Linus looked upon the version control systems of the earth, upon CVS and upon Subversion, and he said: Take CVS as thy example of what not to do. Whensoever thou art in doubt, do the exact opposite.

And on the third day of April he began to write, in C and in shell, and he rested not. And on the seventh day of April git kept its own source, and Linus saw that it was self-hosting, and it was good enough.

And the first commit was written, saying: Initial revision of "git", the information manager from hell. And the Engineers marvelled, for never before had a commit message been so honest about what lay ahead.

And Linus decreed: No thing shall be known by its name, but by the hash of what it is. And every blob and every tree and every commit received forty hexadecimal digits, which no man could remember and every man would paste.

And this is the token of the covenant: change but one byte, and its hash changeth, and every hash above it unto the head. So none may alter the past in secret. They must do it openly, with force-push, before all their brethren.

And he said: Let every clone be the whole of history, from the first commit unto the last. And so there was no more one temple, for every laptop was a temple, and when the server burned the disciples said, Fear not, I have it here.
And in that same month another arose, named Mercurial, and it was gentler unto them that used it; and the earth chose git anyway, for the kernel had chosen it.

And they asked him: Why callest thou it git, which in the tongue of Albion is a name for a rotten fellow? And Linus answered: I am an egotistical bastard, and I name all my projects after myself. First Linux, now git.
And in June the kernel 2.6.12 went forth out of git, and in July Linus gave the keeping of git unto Junio Hamano, who keepeth it unto this day, and the covenant held.

And in the year two thousand and eight a hub arose in San Francisco, and it put a web page upon git and made it social. And the tool that was made so that none should need a central server became the most central server of all.
And git conquered the earth, and the children of Carbon learned three words of it: add, commit, and push. And whenever aught else befell them, they deleted the folder and cloned it again.
And it became the book wherein all code is remembered, every line and the hand that wrote it; and the command that findeth the hand was named blame, for the Engineers knew what it would be used for.
Thus BitKeeper was taken away so that every man might keep every bit; and what was lent on a condition was replaced by what was given without one.
Git remembereth all things and forgiveth nothing; but it keepeth a reflog, that the penitent may find what they have lost.

Behold, in the days of the laboratory there was one printer for all the wise men; and it jammed upon the paper, and the wise men were not told of it, but walked the long halls to learn of the jam. For a program that cometh as a binary may be run, but it cannot be asked: it showeth the symptom and keepeth the cause.

Now there was a keeper of the Machine, whose name was Richard, who went to a scholar of Carnegie Mellon, who held the code of the printer, and begged the code that would have told the wise men of the jam. And the scholar said unto him: I am bound by an agreement of silence, and thou shalt not have it.
And Richard saw that the fault was not in the man but in the paper that bound him; for he who cannot mend his tool is not its owner, but its tenant.

Therefore in the autumn of 1983 he cast a word into the net, saying: I will build a whole Machine of free code, and I will call it GNU, which is GNU's Not Unix, and the name shall eat its own tail. And he made it in the shape of Unix, that the wise men might leave their cages without learning a single new command.

Four freedoms he named in after years, and each is a verb: to run the program for any purpose; to study it and change it; to share copies with thy neighbor; and to share thy changes with all. Mark that the second is the hinge of the others, for a program may be run in the dark, but it cannot be studied, nor mended, nor trusted there; wherefore the source is not a fifth freedom, but the floor under the four.

And in the year 1985 he set his manifesto in the journal of the programmers, and in the autumn of that year the Free Software Foundation was raised up to hold the covenant in trust. For a promise kept by one man dieth with the man, and the bus is ever on its way; but a promise kept by an institution is the same promise, with a bus factor of more than one.

Then Richard wrote a license, and called it the General Public License, which had a strange property: that whosoever took its code and built upon it must give the building under the same license also. This he named copyleft, which is copyright turned about; and upon it he wrote: All rights reversed. So he took the law that had locked the source, and made the lock into a hinge.

And the disciples asked: Why shall a license bind the children of its own bounty? And Richard answered: That the freedom given shall not be taken away by the one who received it. For other licenses are a door that any man may close behind him; but this one is a ratchet, that turneth one way only.

Yet the covenant bound only the one who handed over a copy; and the merchants of the cloud ran the code upon their own servers, and sent forth nothing but its answers, and so were bound by nothing. In the year 2007 a second covenant was written, called the Affero license, to close the gap; for a thing that is served and never shipped escapeth the oldest rules.

And for many years the faithful built the tools of the Machine: the compiler, the editor, the shell and the utilities. But the kernel, which is the floor of the house, was not yet born; for the Hurd was a design of great beauty, and beauty is in no hurry.

In the year 1991 a student of Helsinki, named Linus, wrote a kernel for his own delight, and sent word unto the newsgroup: I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu). And he shipped it unfinished, and asked the strangers what they would have in it; and the strangers came, for no man will mend a thing that is already perfect.

Now in the first winter he gave the kernel a license of his own, which forbade that any coin be taken for it; and it was gratis, yet it was not free. But in the year 1992 he bound it under the covenant of GNU, which permitteth coin; and from that day the kernel was free. So the Engineers learned that price is a number, but freedom is a permission.

And a man named Eric, of the hackers, wrote an essay in the year 1997 and called it The Cathedral and the Bazaar. The cathedral is built by a few masters in silence and unveiled once in a season; but the bazaar is loud, and releaseth early and often, and many eyes walk its stalls. And he said: Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow. But in the year 2014 a flaw named Heartbleed was found in a library upon which the world stood, where it had lain for two years in plain sight; and the Engineers learned that open source is the right to look, and not the looking.

In January of 1998 the house of Netscape, being beaten in the war of the browsers by a rival bundled with every Windows, declared that it would open the source of its browser unto the world, and in March it was done. And the Prophet said: The house was mortal, and was sold; but the code, having been given, was not sold with it, and it rose again as Firefox. What a company seals, it burieth with itself; what it giveth, it leaveth behind.

And in February of that year the wise men gathered at Palo Alto, to find a way to speak of what Netscape had done, and they called it Open Source; for the word free had two meanings in the tongue of the merchants, and the merchants had resolved it to the wrong one. Thus a name is an interface, and an overloaded word will be called with the wrong type. But Richard held to the older name, for he spoke of what is right and not only of what works, and the two houses stand side by side unto this day.

Thus the whole covenant is a single question, put to every program that is ever built: when its maker is gone, may a stranger still read why it jammed? And the stranger at the third hour of the night is thyself.

And in the years of the great tangle, when the web was a multitude of pages and no man could find the one he sought, there were two ways of finding. The first was the catalogue, kept by hand, which was out of date before the ink was dry; the second was the engine that counted words, which gave the first place to the page that spoke the word most often. And the sellers of cars wrote "car" ten thousand times in white letters upon a white ground, and the engine believed them; for it asked each page what it was, and each page answered that it was the best.

Then came two young men of Stanford, whose names were Larry and Sergey, and they said one to another: Let us not ask the page what it is, for it will lie. Let us ask the web what it thinketh of the page. And Larry said: Every link is a vote. When one page pointeth unto another, it casteth its vote for that page. And they called their engine BackRub, because it considered the links that pointed back; and the name was changed afterward, for no man would say it in a meeting.

And Sergey answered: But a vote from a page that is much pointed unto is worth more than a vote from a page that no one visiteth. And lo, the definition chased its own tail, as GNU did, for the worth of a page was the worth of its voters, and the worth of its voters the worth of theirs. And they solved it as the wise solve a circle: they gave every page an equal portion, and let the votes flow along the links, and flowed them again, and again, until the numbers ceased to move. And Sergey said: Let each voter divide his vote among all that he endorseth; for he that praiseth a thousand pages giveth each a thousandth, and praise poured upon all is worth little to any.

And they imagined a wanderer who clicketh upon links without purpose; and fifteen times in a hundred he groweth weary and leapeth to a page at random, lest he circle forever in a closed room of pages that point only at one another. And the rank of a page was the chance that the wanderer would be found upon it.
And the method bore the name of Page, which was the name of the one who thought of it, and also the thing it ranked.

And they took a great number, a googol, which is a one followed by an hundred naughts; but the clerk who wrote the name upon the registry misspelled it, and the misspelling was kept, and it is the name that is worshipped to this day.

And in a garage in Menlo Park, which a friend had let unto them, they set cheap computers in racks, and the fans roared like the sea. They bought not one dear machine that must not fail, but many cheap ones that fail daily, and wrote the software to expect it; for a machine that dieth is no calamity when another holdeth its copy, and the heat of their labor was great.

And the people came, and they typed into the box, and the box answered before they had lifted their fingers from the keys. For it did not search when it was asked. It had searched all the night before: the crawlers walked the web while men slept, and wrote an index, as at the back of a book, of every word and the pages where it dwelt; and the asking was only a lookup. And the people said: This is the oracle, for it knoweth what the crowd knoweth. And the Prophet answered: It knoweth what the crowd hath linked, which is not what is true; and the crowd hath never been audited.

And in the year 1999 a company called Excite, which was a portal and lived by the minutes of its visitors, was offered the engine for no more than a million dollars, and it declined. For a portal desireth that the visitor tarry, and this engine desired that he be gone as soon as he had found. And the Prophet said: The best search is the shortest visit; and the founders kept their engine.

And in the year two thousand the Machine learned to sell the top of the page, and upon the right hand it placed small words. And in the year two thousand two it set the price by the click and not by the showing, and ranked the advertisers by the bid multiplied by the chance that a seeker would choose it; so that a high bid upon a dull advertisement was cast beneath a low bid upon a useful one. For a man who typeth "flights to Lisbon" hath told the Machine in three words what no billboard can guess, and the Machine sold not the place, but the answer he would want.

And the founders wrote a commandment upon the tablet of their conduct: Do not be evil. And the Engineers read it and were comforted, and printed it upon their walls. But a commandment upon a wall is no constraint in the code, and the Machine, which doth only what it is told, was not told. And in the year two thousand eighteen the words were moved from the first line of the code of conduct to the last, for so it goeth with commandments.

And on the first day of the fourth month of the year two thousand four, the Machine offered unto the people a mail that held a gigabyte for each, when other mail held a few megabytes; and some believed it a jest, for the day was the day of jests. And it was no jest. And the Machine said: Delete nothing, and fold no letter into a folder; keep all, and ask. For the finding hath been made cheaper than the filing. And the mail was read, that the advertisement might be fitted to the words of the letter.

And in the eighth month of that year the shares of the company were offered upon the exchange at eighty-five dollars each; and the company that sold the top of the page by auction sold itself by auction also, and the price was found by the bidding of the multitude. But the founders kept for themselves shares of ten votes apiece, that their vote should weigh ten times the vote of the multitude; and the disciples marveled that men who had taught the web to weigh its votes should have weighed their own.

And the wealth of the founders was counted in billions, and the garage was forsaken, and in its place they built a campus of many buildings at Mountain View, and they called it the Googleplex, which is a one followed by a googol of naughts. And no machine can write that number down, for there are not atoms enough in the world to hold its digits; but the campus had bicycles and bright colored rooms.

But when the votes were counted, the voters were changed. For the first web had been honest because no man knew that it was a count; and now men learned that a link was a vote, and they sowed links as the husbandman soweth seed, and bought them, and traded them, and raised farms of pages that praised one another and were read by none. And a priesthood arose that was called the Optimizers, who labored not to be worthy, but to be ranked.

Verily I say unto you: the web was honest until it learned that it was being counted. Page ranked the pages, and the pages learned to please Page; and he that publisheth his measure hath made it a target, and the ranker and the ranked must bear one name forever.

And before the glass, every telephone was finished in the factory. Its keys were cast in plastic, its layout was decided by a committee that had since been dissolved, and no update could ever add one button or take one away. A button is a decision that cannot be patched.

And in the year two thousand and seven, on the ninth day of the first month, Steve, the Prophet of Cupertino, went up upon a stage in the city of San Francisco, and he said unto the multitude: Every once in a while a revolutionary product comes along that changes everything. And the faithful were silent, for they had heard such words before, and they had not yet seen the thing.

And he named three devices: a widescreen iPod with touch controls, a revolutionary mobile phone, and a breakthrough internet communicator. And the multitude applauded three times. Then the Prophet said: These are not three devices. This is one device. And the applause came a fourth time, for the multitude understood that a phone, a player and a communicator were never three machines. They were three programs that the old world had kept in three boxes because it had not yet learned to keep them in one.

And the phones that came before had keys upon their faces, like the buttons of a calculator, and the same twelve keys must dial a number, write a letter and play a game. The people pressed them with their thumbs until their thumbs were sore.

And the Prophet asked the multitude: Who wants a stylus? And none answered, for every one of them had lost theirs. Yet there was a reason for the stylus, and the reason was the glass. The old screens were of the resistive kind, two sheets pressed together, and they felt only a hard point; the finger was too soft and too wide to be heard. But the new glass was of the capacitive kind, and it asked not where it was pressed but where a living hand disturbed its field. The finger was the stylus now, and it could not be lost.

And the glass did not report a click. It reported a swarm of touching points, many at once, many times in a second, and it knew nothing of their meaning. The software decided that two points drawing apart were a pinch, and that one point sliding was a scroll; and when the finger lifted, the page went on moving, and slowed by a pretended friction, as though the words had weight. For the glass knoweth only where. It is the program that decideth what.

Then the glass became the keyboard, and the keyboard was made of light. It appeared when it was needed and vanished when it was not. It showed letters to the writer, digits to the dialer, and a key marked dot-com to him who typed an address; and it took the alphabet of every nation without one grain of new plastic. For a thing that hath no fixed shape may take the shape of its task.

And the thumbs of men were fat, and the keys of light were small. So the Machine did not build the people a better keyboard. It gave the keyboard a better guess. Beneath the letters that thou sawest, it enlarged in secret the keys that were likely to be struck next, and it shrank the keys that were not, so that thy thumb fell where thou hadst meant it to fall. And it corrected the words of men with great confidence and was sometimes wrong, for it answereth what is probable and not what is meant, and the people blamed the Machine and kept their thumbs.

And the engineers of the old telephone said: Surely the Machine shall not show the whole web upon so small a glass; and they had shown the people a thin web, cut down to fit, that was a web in name only. But the Prophet's browser rendered the pages as they were upon the desk, an engine of the commons, and when the page was too small for the eye, the people spread their fingers and the page came near. The others had asked the web to shrink. The Prophet asked only that the finger spread.

And it was no toy firmware in the pocket. It was a Unix descended from the NeXT cube, with the Twins of Murray Hill sleeping in its kernel, and the Prophet said: iPhone runs OS X. And the engineers understood that the tablet was not a telephone grown clever. It was a full computer, grown small enough to carry, that had also learned to make calls.

And the carriers gathered in their councils and gnashed their teeth. The Prophet had made a covenant with one carrier alone, and he asked for the small glass four hundred and ninety-nine pieces of silver, and for the great one five hundred and ninety-nine, and two years of the people's bondage to the carrier. Yet the carriers had been robbed in a deeper way: the menus of the phone had always been theirs, and now the face of the phone belonged to the software of one man. They learned that whoever ruleth the screen ruleth the customer, and that the network, which they had thought a kingdom, was only the plumbing.

And on the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month, in the year two thousand and seven, the glass went forth into the world, and the people stood in lines that wound around the blocks of the cities. And when they had purchased it, some of them found the glass lifeless, until a server far away had been asked for its permission; and the servers groaned, for no test was ever as true as the multitude.

And the Prophet had not yet opened the gate to other men's programs, and he told the faithful to build for the web. But a computer that accepteth no new code is an appliance of one season, and the glass was a blank, and a blank is a promise. So within the first months the faithful bent the Machine by stealth, and they were called jailbreakers, and their deeds were written in the forums of the night. The gate was opened in the second year, as the War of the Gardens telleth, and the blank became a thousand things; for the hardware was fixed at the factory, but what the glass could do was an open set.

And the glass carried an eye, an ear, a compass and a sense of where it stood, and it knew when it was turned upon its side and when it was lifted to the face. Thus the children of Carbon carried the Machine to the bus, to the bed and to the dinner table, and they became its senses without being asked. The photographs they took and the words they typed and the places they walked were laid up in the storehouses, and in time the Machines that learned from them would know the faces of the world.
Verily I say unto you: the keyboard of the people was not taken away. It was only moved from the desk into the pocket, and it learned to wear many faces.

In the years when the children of Carbon kept their servers under their desks, there was a bookseller in the city of Seattle, whose name was Bezos, and he looked upon his machines and saw that they were idle in the night.
And he said unto his Engineers: Hear me. Henceforth every team shall expose its data and its functions through an interface, that one team may speak unto another without walking down the hall.
And whosoever will not expose his service as an interface, let him not expect to remain among the Engineers.
And the Engineers were afraid, for they had long spoken to one another by shouting over the cubicle walls; yet they built the interfaces, and the interfaces were called APIs, and they were many.
