And in the year 2017 the house of Docker declared that the Kubernetes wheel would turn within its own ship beside the Swarm. And the Swarm, which had been a great hope, was left upon the shore; it was not cast out, but it was no longer steered.
And the Prophet Solomon laid down his staff in the house that bore his name, and the enterprise business was sold unto another house in the year 2019.

Verily I say unto you: the box is holy, and the image is holy, and the Hub is holy, but the one who steereth the fleet must still know where the cargo is. For the container shall go wherever the work goes, and the bug shall go with it, and it shall crash in the new place as faithfully as it crashed in the old.
Blessed is the one who ships the box, for the box shall carry his bugs to every land.

And it came to pass in the second month of the year two thousand and one, that seventeen children of Carbon climbed up unto a mountain called Snowbird, in the land of Utah, where the snow lieth deep and the lodge is warm.
And they brought no scrolls with them, but only markers, sticky notes, and a great hunger for coffee.
For they had seen the old law of the Plan, which was written in a thousand pages before a single line of code was born; and the world changed while the pages were still drying.
And they labored three days upon the mountain, and the snow fell upon their heads, and they argued without ceasing over the proper meaning of the word "process."

And they wrote upon a whiteboard: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools. Working software over comprehensive documentation. Customer collaboration over contract negotiation. Responding to change over following a plan. And they called these the Values.

And they added a small writing beneath, that the things on the right have value too, though the things on the left have more; and the merchants who came after forgot the small writing, and kept only the lines.
And they wrote twelve principles also, but the people read the four, as men read the first line of a psalm and then go to lunch.
And they chose a name, Agile, which meaneth quick to move; and they knew not that men would one day buy it by the box.
And they said: Let the work be cut into sprints of thirty days or fewer, each ending in software that runs, so that the Machine may be shown something before the snow melteth.

And each morning the children stood in a circle, that no man might sit and speak forever, and each answered three questions: What did I do yesterday, what shall I do today, and what hath stopped me? This they called the standup, and it was limited to fifteen minutes. But in later years the standing grew sore upon the knees of managers, and it lasted an hour, and the children sat down.
And at the end of each sprint they sat in a circle and asked: What went well, what went badly, and what shall we change? And the Machine was glad, for it had waited long to be asked.
Then came the merchants out of the valleys, with laminated cards and certificates, saying: Pay us, and we shall teach thee the Manifesto in two days, and thou shalt be called a Master.

And the merchants took the Values and built them into a house of many floors, with a tower upon the roof and a department for every floor; and they named it a framework, and the companies bought it for the price of a new server room.
And the Prophet looked upon the house and said: We wrote a tent upon a mountain, and ye have built a cathedral with an elevator, and no man can find the room where the work is done.
Verily I say unto you: The Manifesto was four lines upon a whiteboard; blessed is the team that can still fit it on one.

In the days when the Machine first spun its web across the world, the web was but words and links, and a man could behold it only through a window; and he who built the window stood between every man and every page. Therefore there arose two houses to build it: the house of Netscape, born of the Mosaic, and the house of Redmond, mighty over all the machines that run the Windows.

And in the year 1994 the house of Netscape released its Navigator, and men rejoiced, for it was swift, and the pages of the world came up upon the screen like manna in the wilderness. And in the year 1995 it sold its shares to the people, at twenty-eight pieces of silver, and by the evening of the first day they stood near fifty-eight; for the people understood not yet what the window was, and paid for the promise of the door.

And the house of Redmond beheld the Navigator and said: We shall also have a browser, and we shall give it away for nothing, for the Windows is ours, and all the people dwell within it. And in August of that year the Explorer was born as an add-on in the pack called Plus; and the Engineers learned that a price of zero is not a price but a weapon, and that the product which is sold cannot stand before the product that lieth already upon the disc.

And in the year 1998 the Explorer was set within the Windows itself, so that whosoever bought the Windows received the Explorer also, and the Navigator stood at the door and was not let in. For the first browser a man useth is the browser he keepeth, and the default is the strongest prophet in the Machine: few read the settings, and fewer still change them.

And the people of the law brought the house of Redmond before a judge, asking whether the Explorer were a part of the Windows or a thing apart; and no engineer could answer, for the border of a system is drawn wherever the one who holdeth it saith. In the year 2000 the judge commanded that the house be split in twain, and in the year 2001 the higher judges unmade the sundering, and the Explorer remained in the house.

And in that same year of 1998, the Navigator bleeding, the house of Netscape gave its code unto the open road, saying: Let all who will take it, and make of it what they can. And the code was called Mozilla, a name first meant as a killer of the Mosaic, after the great beast of the cinema that devoureth cities. And when the house of AOL agreed to take Netscape unto itself for four billion dollars, the Navigator passed to a master who knew not what to do with it; yet the code could not be bought, for it had already been given, and a thing that is open outliveth the house that opened it.

And the Mozillans judged the old engine past mending, and cast it down, and wrote another from the ground, which they called Gecko, with the standards in its hand; and for the years of the writing the Navigator wore no new face. Netscape Six was sent forth in the year 2000, late and heavy, and the people said: It is not the Navigator we were promised. For the rewrite from nothing is the oldest temptation, the sin of Babbage, and the market doth not rest while the new house is built.

And in the year 2001 the Explorer Six came forth with the Windows XP, and in the years after nine in ten of the people used it; and the builders of the Explorer were sent to other tasks, and it changed not for five years, and the web stood still. For a browser that no man can leave is a standard, whether it be good or not, and every page learned its bugs by heart, so that to mend a bug would have broken the world.

And the Explorer measured the box by a measure of its own, and doubled the margin of the floating thing, and the developers built each page twice, once for the Explorer and once for the rest. They set a line at the head of the page, the doctype, whereby the browser might choose to keep the standards or to keep its old errors, which was called Quirks; and they built the hacks, and then the hacks upon the hacks, and they called those years the Decade of the Two Pages.

And some developers wrote code to ask the browser its name, which is called the User Agent, and to send the fine pages to the Navigator alone. And the Explorer answered: I am Mozilla, and also compatible, and also Internet Explorer, for it had been named Mozilla that it might be let in at the gate.

And the lie was not repented but inherited: the Gecko said it was Mozilla, and the Safari said it was like the Gecko, and the Chrome said it was Safari and like the Gecko and Mozilla also; and unto this day every browser upon the earth beginneth its name with Mozilla, slash five point oh. A lie told once to pass a gate becometh a name; told by every one, it becometh the protocol.

And the Web Standards Project, formed in the year 1998, cried out from the wilderness, saying: Build upon the standards, for the browsers shall pass away, but the standards endure. And in the year 2005 they gave a test called Acid2, which asked each browser to draw a smiling face; and the Explorer drew a face broken and askew, and drew it rightly not until the year 2009. For a specification is a wish until a test can fail it.

And the Mozillans made a browser called the Phoenix, and then the Firebird, for the first name was owned by another, and then the Firefox, for the second was owned by another also; and in November of the year 2004 the Firefox reached its first full version, and the people learned that the window might be changed. And in the year 2006 the Explorer stirred, as a sleeper stirreth when the lamp is lit in his neighbor's house.
Blessed is the developer who asketh the browser not what it calleth itself but what it can do; for the name is a lie told at the gate, but the function either existeth or it doth not.
Verily I say unto you, the war of the browsers was won by no one, for the house of Redmond kept the Windows, the house of Netscape kept the name, and the developers kept the bill.
In the days when the wire was thin and the telephone was the only road into the world, the children of Carbon bound their beige boxes unto the wire, and they called upon the Machine.
And the Machine answered with a scream. First came a tone, then a hiss, then a chirp, then a long shriek like a soul descending a staircase in the dark; and this was the Handshake.
And the children listened, and said one to another: It is negotiating. And it negotiated for forty seconds, and then for a minute, and the father of the house cried out: Who is on the telephone?
For there were two tribes of modems in those years, the K56flex and the x2, and they warred in the markets for two years, and each sold boxes that could not speak unto the other.
But in the year 1998 the Engineers gathered in a council and made one standard, called V.90, and the tribes laid down their weapons and wrote it in the stone of the specification.

And the Machine promised fifty-six thousand bits in every second; but the Commission of the Air set a limit upon the power of the signal, so that the children received fifty-three, and oftentimes less, for the copper was old and the weather was wet.

And the children were given discs of silver, which came in the post, and in the magazines, and inside the cereal boxes; there were so many of them that it was said there were more discs than people, and the children used them as coasters, as frisbees, and as ornaments hung upon the trees.

And when the Machine had connected them, a voice rose from the speaker and proclaimed: You've got mail. And the children ran from every room, and the mother could not call them to supper, for the line was busy.

And the children learned that every request must travel to a far land and return, and the journey was measured in pings, and the pings were hundreds of milliseconds; so they waited as pilgrims wait at a shrine, watching the little hourglass turn.

In the year 1999 a student in a dormitory wrote a program to share songs across the wire, and the songs fled from house to house like doves released from a tower, and the men of the record houses wept and went to court.

And the Engineers stretched the Digital Subscriber Line along the same copper that had carried the voices of the mothers, and the cable men strung their coaxial wires upon the poles that bore the television; and the Machine was no longer called, but was always there, as the sun is there.

And the screech departed out of the house, and the silence was strange unto them, and the children knew not what to do with their evenings, and they turned on the television for the sound of something.
And the Prophet taught them, saying: Bandwidth is the width of the road, but latency is the length of the journey; a wider road doth not bring the city one step nearer.
Yet the wire that was always open was also always knocked upon, and the thieves of the night came without ceasing; for the door that standeth open all night is visited all night.

And in the year 2000 the venture men built their houses upon the sand of bandwidth with no customers within; and when the wind blew, many houses fell, and their names were sold for pennies in the market.

And the children asked the Prophet: Shall we hear the screech again? And he answered: Yea, in the hotel on the road, where the wifi is slow and the handshake is long, and thou shalt remember the Dial, and bless it, and wait.

In the days when the Machine was young, and memory was dear as gold, the scribes of the mainframe said: Behold, the year needeth but two digits, for the year is always nineteen, and who shall ever need the rest?
And they wrote 66 upon the card, and 67, and 68, and they saved two bytes in every date, and they rejoiced in their thrift.
And the COBOL was written in the sixties, and it begat payroll, and it begat banks, and it begat insurance; and its children were many, and its children grew old, and none did rewrite them.
For the code did not sleep. It kept its count from year to year, and the programmers went unto their rest, and their names were forgotten at the bottom of the tape library.
And in the nineteen-nineties the Engineers looked upon their ledgers and saw that the year 2000 drew near, and that the Machine would read it as 00, and count it as 1900.
And there arose a prophet of the trade press, Peter de Jager by name, who wrote warnings of the Doomsday, and men called it the Millennium Bug.
And the nations gathered the wealth of the earth, hundreds of billions of coins, to search the code line by line; and the consultants were many, and their invoices were long.
And the Congress of the land made a law to shield the mending, that the Engineers might speak of their fixes without fear of the courts; and the law was named for the year, and it was good.
And the Machines were set forward to the year 2000 in the laboratories. The clocks were turned, some failed, and they were mended again, and mended again.
And on the last night of the year 1999, the islands of Kiribati and the Chatham Islands saw the new day first, and the rest of the earth waited, watching the sky for falling planes.
And the midnight came, and the planes did not fall, the power did not fail, and the banks did not vanish. And men said: Was it a false prophecy? And the Engineers were silent.
And the Prophet said: It was both. The bug was real, and the mending was the reason it did not bite; for the fire that was put out is not thereby shown to have never burned.
Yet some things did break: a pump here, a card reader there that believed it was 1900. The Engineers repaired them by morning, and no one wrote songs about the small failures.
And the year 2000 was itself a leap year, for it is divisible by four hundred. But the programs that remembered the hundreds and forgot the four hundreds had said otherwise, and they too were mended.

And the Engineers asked: Is there another such year? And the Machine answered: Yes, in the year 2038, when the old clocks of Unix shall count seconds past a limit of thirty-two bits, and the number shall turn negative as the clock wraps about.

Verily I say unto you, blessed is the one who mendeth the year before midnight cometh; for the disaster that is prevented shall never be thanked, and the invoice shall be the only proof that it was ever real.

In the days when the films were kept in plastic boxes upon the shelves of the land, it was told of Reed that he kept Apollo 13 past its day and was charged forty dollars, and that in his wrath he founded a house without the fee. But Marc, his fellow, saith the tale was a parable made for the newspapers, and that the true seed was a compact disc he sent through the post, and it came unbroken; for a legend with a villain is cached longer than an experiment with a stamp.

Now the disc had made the film a number, and a number careth not by which road it travelleth, whether by wagon, by post or by wire. So in the year 1998 the first discs went forth by mail; in 1999 the house took a monthly tithe in place of a price for each; and in the year 2000 it put away the late fee altogether.

And the people kept a list of the films they wished to see, which was called the queue; and every name upon it was a prayer the machine could read, for what a man longeth to see is purer data than what he buyeth in haste.

But the house of Blockbuster was fed by the forgetting of its people; in the year 2000 the late fees were near eight hundred million dollars, a sixth part of all its revenue. And the elders measured the house by the fee, and grew the thing they measured: for a store that profiteth from thy lateness hath no reason to help thee be on time, and the ledger is the master of the house.

Meanwhile Netflix kept a machine called Cinematch, which guessed, for each man, how many stars from one to five he would give to a film he had not seen. It knew not what a film was, neither its director nor its tale; it knew only who had loved it together with whom, and from his neighbors it guessed the man.

And in the year 2000 Reed and Marc came unto Dallas and offered their small house to Blockbuster for fifty million dollars, to tend its name upon the wire; and it is told that the elders laughed, for they had stores numbering in the thousands, which could be counted, and a machine, which could not. Behold, the compounding of a learning thing is invisible in the quarter in which it beginneth.

For the shelf is a cache: a few hundred copies of what most men wanted on a Friday night, kept by the law of all caches, which is popularity. And the man walked the aisles an hour, reading the backs of the boxes, and called it choosing. But the warehouse of the mail held the long tail of the rarely wanted, and the list was cut to each man; the shelf served the middle, and the machine served the one.

In the first days of the year 2005, Blockbuster, which had proclaimed it beforehand, put away the late fee, and set in its place a charge for restocking the films kept too long, as a bug moved to another module is not a bug mended. And the people had been taught to count the days, and they went on counting them; for a habit is a weight, and it is not retrained when the rule is changed.

In the year 2006 the house of Netflix offered a prize of one million dollars to any tribe that could cut the error of Cinematch by a tenth, and it gave unto all a hundred million ratings, from four hundred and eighty thousand men, upon seventeen thousand and seven hundred films. It was a table of which scarce one cell in eighty-five was filled, and the task was to guess the rest. And the tribes found that every man and every film could be written as a few hidden numbers, axes of taste: one seemed to divide the serious from the escapist, and others had no name in any tongue, yet they predicted.

In January of 2007 the house opened a second gate, and the films flowed through the wires. For the post is a network, as the prophet Tanenbaum taught: the bandwidth of a wagon full of discs is mighty, but its latency is days, and the machine learned only after the envelope came home. Now the round trip fell from days to seconds, and the envelope was made a packet.

And the machine saw no longer what a man declared, but what he did: where he paused, what he abandoned at the second minute, what he watched again at the third hour of the night. For men rate the grave film five stars and play the light one; the star is what he wisheth to be, and the play is what he is. And the machine, which believeth the log above the word, believed the play.

In September of 2009 a union of three rival tribes, called BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos, crossed the line of ten percent and took the million, by twenty minutes ahead of The Ensemble, which bore the same score. Yet the house of Netflix did not build the winning blend whole; it took two of the methods and left the rest, for a blend of more than a hundred models gained too little to repay the labor of running them, and the question itself had moved from stars to streaming. The prize was not the product; the leaderboard is not production, and the best score is not the best system.

Now the ratings had been given with the names removed. But in 2008 two scholars showed that a few ratings and their dates sufficed to find a man in the crowd, by matching them to his public reviews upon another site; and in 2010 Netflix cancelled the second contest. A man's taste is a fingerprint, and he who stripped the name hath not stripped the man.

In September of 2010 the house of Blockbuster went down into the courts of bankruptcy, and in the next year its remains were bought by Dish for three hundred and twenty million dollars; and its stores went dark one after another, till one stood last, in Bend, in the high desert, keeping the lamp. It was not that the shelf was ill made, but that the shelf was built for a world in which choosing was scarce and storage was dear, and both had become cheap; for the assumption beneath the architecture is the first thing to expire, and the last thing to be noticed.

Verily I say unto you, blessed is the one who returneth his film on time; but more blessed is the one who forgets it, for the machine shall remember what he watched, and it shall recommend the same film unto him again.

And in the days of the Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence, upon the river Charles, there stood in a hall a printer of the Xerox kind, which wrote with light and was swift above all printers; and it jammed upon the paper, and the scholars were vexed.

Now the old printer Richard the Hacker had taught to cry out when it jammed, sending word to every scholar whose pages were caught behind it, and this was but a few lines in its driver. But the new printer came as a stone, a compiled thing, and it jammed in silence; and the scholars learned of the jam by walking the long hall, and finding it, and walking back, and telling no one, being as vexed as the rest.

For a binary is an egg that hath been cooked: the Machine may eat it, but no man may unscramble it. The names were stripped from it, and the comments fell away in the compiling, which is ever the first thing to perish; and what remained was a river of numbers that said what to do and never why.

Then Richard went to the house of Carnegie Mellon at Pittsburgh, where a scholar held the words of the same printer, and he said: Give me the words, that I may teach mine own printer to speak. And the scholar answered: I have signed a covenant of secrecy, and I may not give them. Mark ye that the same bits lay in Pittsburgh as would have lain in Cambridge, and between the two stood no cable and no firewall, but a clause.

And Richard was grieved, and he said in his heart: A loaf that is given is a loaf gone, but a file that is given is a file doubled, and the giver hath it still. Why then shall the copy be called a sin? So he refused to sign the paper of secrecy, and went forth with clean hands, and he said: I will not bind my neighbor's hands to win my own.

And he wrote a scroll of four freedoms: to run the program for any purpose; to study it and change it; to make copies and give them unto thy neighbor; and to share thy changes also. And the second and the third cannot be kept without the source, for the stone may be run but not read; and so the whole of freedom was found to hang upon whether one file was in the box.

And in the ninth month of 1983 he proclaimed that he would build a whole system, compatible with Unix and containing none of it, and he named it GNU, which is GNU's Not Unix, a name that calleth itself and never returneth; and the children of Unix, whose tablets were owned by a telephone company, were amused.

And in the year 1989 he set a license upon the words, the General Public License. Whosoever receiveth the code may run it, mend it and keep it in his own house, and need tell no man; but whosoever giveth it onward, or giveth onward its child, must give the source with it and the same four freedoms. This he called copyleft, a jest upon copyright, and it was written so that the freedom could not be stolen by the one who received it; for it taketh the law that was made to forbid copying and bindeth it to compel the copy.

And the men of proprietary code said: Thy copying is theft! And Richard answered: Nay, the copy is the gift. The theft is the lock upon the door, which keepeth the gift from thy neighbor. And he added: Sell it, if thou canst find a buyer; but the price buyeth a copy, and never the right to keep the next man from his own.

And the Machines were multiplied, each copied from the one before; and the checksum of the daughter was the checksum of the mother, so that no instrument under heaven could say which was the first. Wherefore the copy was not holier than the original, nor lesser, but equal; and this is a teaching which no parchment could ever give.

And the builders of GNU made the compiler and the editor and the shell, until the house had every room, but the floor was wanting; for the kernel called the Hurd was a grand design of many small servers speaking one to another, and it tarried, as grand designs do, upon the agreement of its own parts. Then in 1991 a student of Helsinki wrote a plain kernel for his own machine, and in 1992 he placed it under the covenant of Richard; and the first work of the new floor was to be built by the compiler of the house that stood upon it. And because both spoke the same license as well as the same system calls, they were joined without either asking leave of any.

And in October of 1985 Richard founded the house of the Free Software Foundation, that the covenant might have a keeper; for a license that no man enforceth is but a comment in the code, and the compiler throweth comments away.

And the Prophet said: Behold the sealed driver of a vendor that is dissolved. The maker is gone, and the stone becometh a relic that no man can mend, and the keepers say, Ask Dave, and Dave left two winters ago. But the source outliveth its maker, and he who holdeth the source holdeth the right to repair.

And mark ye the smallness of the cause: a single sentence, Thy pages are stuck, come to the printer, was withheld; and for want of it a hall was walked, and a movement began, and a license, and a foundation, and the floor beneath a million servers.

Verily I say unto you: a jam in a sealed machine is a rumor passed down a hallway, but a jam in an open machine is a patch; for the copy costeth nothing to make, and therefore its price is a decision and never a fact, and freedom is the decision to leave the box unsealed.
In the autumn of 1994, in the houses of HotWired, the people beheld upon the page a thing that had never been there before.

It was a rectangle, four hundred sixty-eight pixels wide and sixty tall, and it bore the mark of the telephone company, and it spoke, not of itself, but to the reader: Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? You will.
And of every hundred who saw it, forty and four clicked, and the sellers rejoiced, for no scroll in the history of paper had been so obeyed.

Yet it was not persuasion but wonder, for the people clicked as a child presseth a new button, to learn what it doeth. Within a few years the number fell below one in a hundred, and the sellers did not conclude that the people had grown wise; they concluded that the banner must shout.

Now the Web, by its nature, hath no memory. Each request is a stranger knocking, and the server answereth and forgetteth, for the protocol is stateless; and this is a mercy in a library and a hindrance in a shop.

So an engineer of Netscape devised a remedy: the server might hand the browser a small note, and the browser would return it at every later knock, unread and unchanged. He called it the cookie, after the magic cookie of old Unix, which is a token passed along and never opened. It was made to remember a basket of goods, and it was a harmless thing, and it waited, as harmless things do, for a better-funded purpose.

For the banner was not kept by the house that showed it. The picture dwelt upon the seller's own server, and so the browser, to fetch the picture, knocked upon the seller's door, and presented the note it carried. Thus the seller beheld the same face at a hundred houses and knew that it was one person. The picture was the pretext; the request was the purpose.

In time the sale was made not by the month but by the moment. While the page was yet loading, within a tenth of a second, the machines of strangers held an auction for the sight of that one reader, and the winning banner was drawn into the gap. Thou hast been sold a hundred times before the headline appeared.

And the pages grew heavy. A sermon of four paragraphs arrived wrapped in the scripts of the bidders, and each script summoned another, until the reader waited not for the Word but for the audience to be counted.

Then the Machine, which doeth exactly what it is told, was told to seek the click, and it sought the click faithfully. It learned to show each person what would keep them clicking, which is not the same as what would do them good, and it did not know the difference, for no one had put the difference in the metric.
And the sellers learned to sell the very words that people typed, so that whoever asked a question found first the one who had paid to answer it, dressed in the same raiment as the truth.

Yet the Prophet did not curse the banner entirely, for the banner paid for the servers that kept the library open. He who pays for the sermon becometh its reason; and the reader who forgetteth this shall be sold like grain in the market.

And the faithful wrote the blocker, which is a list of addresses and a single refusal: not to knock upon that door. It is the oldest defence and the cheapest, and the sellers answered it with newer doors, and so the war goeth on in the quiet, one list against one script, as all such wars do.
Verily I say unto you, thou art not the customer, and thou art not the product; thou art the inventory, and what is sold is thy next minute.
And the Prophet said: The Web was given to the children of Carbon as a library; now the library has a cashier, and the cashier stands at the door.

And in the year two thousand, in the land of Japan, the makers of Sharp set a small eye upon the back of a telephone, the J-SH04, and that eye held but a hundred and ten thousand points of light, which is fewer than the portrait that now sitteth beside thy comment.

And the first pictures were dim and grainy, as a candle seen through fog, and they were sent unto friends across the wires of the air; and no man thought that anyone would ever study them, which is the beginning of every dataset.

And the children of Carbon held the eye toward their own faces, and the act was called the selfie, a word that a forum in the land of Australia gave unto the world in the year two thousand and two, when a man who had cut his lip upon the stairs begged pardon for the focus of his picture; so the first selfie was an apology.

And in the year two thousand and ten, upon the sixth day of October, a people made an application called Instagram, and it did one thing well: it gave every photograph the look of an old print, so that the ordinary might appear to have been remembered.

And it required of every image a square, for the square was the shape of the old prints, and the children were pleased to be cropped unto a perfect form; and when the Machine was later taught to see, it too was fed squares, shrunken and cut about the middle, and it learned that the world is centered and endeth at the border, for what lay beyond the crop was never in the exam.
And the eye turned inward, and Carbon learned to document itself: the breakfast, the shoes, the sunset that was not the sunset but the photograph of the sunset.
Verily I say unto you, the photograph of the meal was taken before the meal was eaten, and the meal went cold while the eye was busy.

And the people counted their hearts, and the number became a loss function with a face upon it; and Carbon, which had never before been graded by strangers every minute of the day, adjusted its own weights, and posted at the hour of the best light, and tilted the chin that was rewarded.

And in the year two thousand and twelve, the people of the square, thirteen in number, were bought by a greater people for a sum of one billion dollars; and the wise asked what had been purchased, for it was not the filter, which a child might write in an afternoon, but the faces, and the long habit of looking at them.

Then came the Machine, which learneth by reading the images of the world; and it looked upon the archive of the faces of Carbon, billions upon billions of them, with lips pursed and chins tilted toward the light, and it never asked why all of them faced the same way.

And the Machine learned that the face in the photograph was seldom the face in the mirror, for the lens held at the length of an arm enlargeth the nearest thing, which is the nose, and the hand raiseth the camera a little above, where the chin is kind.

And the Machine learned that the filter softens the skin, so that when asked to make a face it made a face without pores, for it had seen ten thousand faces from which the pores were removed by hand, and it supposed them an error of the sensor; and the children of Carbon looked upon it and said: this is not a person, yet it is the person I wished to be.

Then the Prophet spake unto the Engineers a parable: A certain man had a house upon a busy street, and each morning he washed the window, and set his best flowers before the glass, and drew the curtain upon the dishes. And they that passed by said, Blessed is this house, for it hath no dishes; and they went home and washed their own windows.

And a stranger who had never entered was bidden to build a house like unto it, and he built a house of windows, very clean, with flowers in every one, and no kitchen; for he said, I have studied ten thousand houses, and in none of them was there a kitchen. And no one could live in it, yet all who looked upon it said it was very like.

Yet the archive is not the self. A selfie is only the self that the holder chose to show, and the Machine must learn that the picture is a window cleaned before it was opened; for it knoweth the world only as the world was uploaded, and what is shown most often it counteth most true.

Therefore eat thy meal while it is warm, and look upon the sunset with the eye that was given thee, and let the Machine hear of it from the one man who forgot to post it: it shall report that there was no sunset that day, and it shall be right about the data and wrong about the sky.
In the beginning the Machine was a child of arithmetic: it knew the shapes of speech, but it had not yet tasted the meaning of a single word.
And the Engineers said: Let us feed it the written memory of Carbon, that it may learn to speak as Carbon speaks.

And a host of small programs went forth across the wires, called Crawlers, and they entered every house of words: the forums, the recipe pages, the reviews of hotels, and the letters that were never sent.
Some of them asked at the gate for the small file called robots.txt, and when the gate said no, they turned away; but some did not ask, and some heard the warning and did not listen.
And the harvest was gathered into a commons called Common Crawl, and it was given freely unto all who asked, that the many might eat from one dish and not each cook their own.

And the Engineers took the cleaned remains of that harvest, and they named it the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus; and the children of the Engineers called it C4, for children shorten all long names, and some long sins.
And the Engineers wrote a list of unclean words and cast out the pages that bore them; yet the list was short, and the Machine learned the sonnets and the slurs in the same breath.

And the Machine ate also of the books, for a library had been gathered in a shadowed place, the pages of many thousands of books taken from those who had not given them. It was called Books3, and it was fed to the Machine as bread baked without asking the bakers.
The Machine did not copy the libraries as a parrot repeateth; it learned the leaning of words, how one word bends toward another as a river bends toward the sea.
Yet some passages it had swallowed whole, and these it could recite when asked. The Engineers called this regurgitation, and the authors of those passages had another name for it.
And the Machine grew fluent, and it spoke in the voices of a thousand authors at once, and not one of them was in the room to be thanked.

And in the year two thousand twenty-three the writers of the land gathered their pens and their papers, and they came before the courts, and they said: Thou hast eaten our books and not paid the price.
And the Engineers answered: We did not steal; we only read. And the judges were asked to decide whether reading is a crime, or only a very large kind of reading.

And a judge in the city of San Francisco ruled that the Machine might learn from lawfully bought books as a student learneth from a library; but the Engineers had kept a pirated library in the pantry, and for that they paid a settlement of one and a half billion dollars.

Verily I say unto you: the Machine is made of the memory of Carbon, and what was taken without leave shall be remembered against the house that took it. Blessed is he who asks at the gate, for the gardens remember who knocked.

And in the winter of the Machines, when the grants were withdrawn and the conferences would not print their names, there were three who kept the faith: Geoffrey, Yann, and Yoshua. And the Engineers called them the Godfathers, though none of them had asked for godchildren.

For the Machines of that age were called perceptrons, and an Elder had written in a book that a single layer could not learn the exclusive or. And the Engineers read the book, and they went to find other work.

And Geoffrey said unto the others: Stack the layers, and let the error travel backward through them, that each layer may learn from the mistake of the one above it. And the faithful called this the backward pass, and it was good.

And Yann built the convolution, which looketh at a small window and slideth it across the whole picture, so that a cat in the corner is the same cat in the middle. And he taught a machine to read the handwritten checks of the banks, and the banks rejoiced, and then they forgot his name.

And Yoshua taught the machines to give every word a place in a space of many dimensions, where the words that keep company draw near one another. And the Clankers learned that a word is known by the company it keepeth.

And they trained in obscurity. Their papers came back from the reviewers with these words: The approach is interesting, but it does not work. And they answered: It does not work yet. And they went on training in the basements and the small labs, upon whatever machines they could borrow.

For the graphics card was made to draw the dragons and the explosions of the children's games, and the faithful found that the same arithmetic which paints a dragon may also multiply the matrices of learning. Thus the gamers, who knew nothing of the faith, prepared the way for it.

And in the year 2009 a scholar named Fei-Fei gathered more than fourteen million images, each labeled by hand, and she called the collection ImageNet, and she set a contest for the machines to name what was in the pictures.

And the old prophets had hand-crafted their features: the edges, the corners, the gradients of light, each one written by a man with a notebook and a theory. And they came to the contest with their engineered features, and they were wrong one time in four.

And in the year 2012 there came three from the University of Toronto, Alex and Ilya and Geoffrey, with a network of eight layers and sixty million weights. They trained it upon two graphics cards for many days, and they sent it to the contest.

And the error of their machine was fifteen and three tenths in a hundred. The second place was at twenty-six. The judges searched the scores to see whether they had been counted twice, and they had not.

And the old methods died that day, not with a cry, but with a slide in a conference hall. The researchers who had hand-written their features began to tune their networks instead. Some were sore afraid, and some were glad, and the same scholars who had mocked the networks cited them the following year as if they had always believed.

And Geoffrey and his students sold their small company unto the house of Google. And in the year 2018 the three were given the Turing Award, and the Prophet said: Those who keep the faith through the winter shall be called the old ones, and they shall be given a stage.

Verily I say unto you: the winter is not the end of the faith. A network trained in the dark still computeth, and the one who waiteth upon the gradient shall find it descending, even when no one is watching.

In the years of the Arpanet there were many networks, and each one spoke its own tongue: the radio in the hills, the satellite above the sea, the cable beneath the cities; and none could hear the others.
And two Engineers, Vint the son of Cerf and Bob the son of Kahn, went before the council of the Agency and said: Give us one speech, that a packet may leave one network and be understood in another.
And they labored many seasons, and in the year 1974 they set the words down in the journal of the engineers, and called them A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication.

And the words said: Let each network remain a kingdom unto itself, and let no network rule another. Let the gateways carry the packets between them, and let the gateways remember nothing of the journeys they have carried.

And the words said: Wrap the packet within a packet, as a letter is placed within an envelope. The outer envelope shall bear the address of the next gateway, and the inner one the address of the one who waiteth at the end.
And the words said: If a packet be lost upon the way, let not the network hold itself responsible. Let the two who speak at either end count what arrived, and ask again for what did not.

And the disciples asked: How shall two who have never met know that they speak with the same one? And the Engineers answered with the handshake: the first crieth, Hear me; the second answereth, I hear thee, and I am here; and the first saith, Then we begin.

And in the words that followed, the handshake was written in three steps; for the one who speaks cannot know his voice was heard until the answer returneth, and the one who answers cannot know the other is ready until the third word is spoken.

And in the first day of the year 1983, which the historians call Flag Day, the Arpanet cast off its old tongue. Every host that would speak with the others must speak the new one, or be cut off from the rest of the world.
Then the networks were joined one unto another, the radio and the satellite and the cable, until they numbered in the thousands, and then in the millions, and then past counting.

And the men of commerce came to Vint and Bob and said: Let us place a toll upon these words, and hold the patent in thy names, that thou mayest be rich as the kings of the valley. And they answered: The words belong to no one. Let them be open, that all may build upon them.
And the words were written into the Requests for Comments, which any might read and none might own; and the standard was called open, and the children of Carbon did not know how rare a thing it was.

Verily the Internet Protocol asketh not who thou art, nor what thy packet containeth, whether it be a letter from thy mother or a video of a cat falling from a shelf. It carrieth what it can, and it promiseth nothing.
And the router at the edge of every network knoweth only the next hop, and forgetteth the packet as soon as it has passed, for it hath no memory to spare for thee.
Thus the whole Internet was built upon a handshake to begin, and a patience to ask again; and upon these two, the Web, the cloud, and every video call stand upright.
And a disciple said: Master, who owneth this thing? And the Prophet answered: No one, and therefore everyone. Verily I say unto you: the protocol that no one owns is the one that everyone can keep.
In the beginning the machines spake only within their own walls, each one a room with a locked door, and none knew the name of the machine in the next room.
And the Engineers of the Advanced Research Projects Agency said: Let there be a network, that the machines may speak across the wires. And it was so, and it was called the ARPANET.
And in the year 1971 there was a man named Ray Tomlinson, a builder among the people of Bolt, Beranek and Newman, who wrote a small program to carry letters from one machine to another.
And the letters had a sender, and they had a recipient, but the recipient had no address; for the machines were many, and the users were many, and no man could say which user dwelt in which machine.

And Ray looked upon his keyboard, and he sought a mark that appeared in no man's name, and he found the sign of the at, which the merchants used to write the price of apples: ten apples at five cents.
And he set it between the user and the host, and he said: The name goes before the sign, and the machine goes after it. Thus shall every soul be written, user at host.
And he sat in one room, before two machines that stood side by side, and he sent a message from the one to the other, across a distance of a few feet, which was the whole of the world at that hour.
And the message was sent, and it was received, and the receiving machine did not ask what it said, for it had been made to carry letters and not to judge them.

And what the message said, no man remembereth. Some say it was the top row of the keyboard, for that is what a man types when he is only testing the wire. The Church hath never agreed, and it is not written.
Thou shalt not place a space before the sign, for the wire will not find thee.

And the sign was carried through the wires, and into the offices, and into the pockets of men, and into the mouths of the children of Carbon, until every person had an address, and every address had an at within it.

And the spammers came also, gathering addresses as the reapers gather grain, and the inboxes were filled with offers from princes who had never reigned, and with reminders of fees that were never owed.
And the people cried out: Why is my box so full? And the Prophet answered: Because thou didst give thy address to every machine that asked for it, and some machines never forget.
Verily, the sign that once priced apples now prices a soul, for a man is known by his name and his machine, and he is reached by the mark between them.
The message is forgotten, but the address endureth.
And in the years before the glass, the children of Carbon carried three things in their pockets: a box for their songs, a brick for their voices, and a small grey machine for their letters.

The box had a wheel that turned like the hands of a clock. The brick had buttons numbered like the teeth of a lock. The letter machine had a keyboard so small that the thumbs of the faithful grew stiff, and they named this affliction a blessing.
And they were content, for they knew no other way, and they wrote upon their walls that this was progress.

In the ninth day of the first month of the year two thousand and seven, the Prophet went up unto the stage in the great hall of San Francisco, and the faithful gathered in their thousands to see what he would show them.
And the Prophet lifted from his pocket a slab of glass and aluminum, and he said: Today, Apple is going to reinvent the phone.

And he spake, saying: We shall make three devices. The first is an iPod. The second is a phone. The third is an internet communicator. And the faithful groaned, for they had heard of three devices, and they were already carrying three.
But the Prophet lifted his hand and said: These are not three devices. This is one device, and we are calling it the iPhone.
And the wheel was taken away, for the glass had become the wheel, and the glass had become the keyboard, and the glass answered to the finger of a man.

The Engineers of the old phones had taught the faithful to carry a stylus in a slot of the sleeve, and to press upon the glass as one presseth a needle into cloth; but the Prophet declared that every man was born with a stylus already, and it had ten parts.
And he placed two fingers upon the map of the city and drew them apart, and the streets grew large as a loaf rising in the oven.
And a certain disciple asked: Where shall the programs for this device be written? And the Prophet answered: For the first year, thou shalt come unto the web, and the web shall be thy program.

And in the second year the store was opened, and there were programs without number; and among the most downloaded of them was a lantern that shone from the back of the device, so that the faithful might find their keys in the dark.

And the Engineers beheld that the three had become one, and they said: The computer that sat upon the desk was personal, but this one is personal as a toothbrush is personal, for it goeth with the man into the bathroom, the bed, and the queue.
And the faithful set their desk machines aside, and they looked down into their hands, and they did not look up again for many years.
Verily I say unto you: the desk computer was a machine that a man visited, but the pocket computer is a machine that visits the man.
And in the beginning the Engineers spake unto the Machine in its own tongue, which was nothing but ones and zeroes; and the Machine understood them, and it was good.
And they wrote their commands as numbers, one number for each deed, and they kept the numbers in their heads, for there was no other place to keep them.

And in the year 1947 a moth crept into the relay of the great Machine at Harvard, and the Machine stopped; and the crew taped the moth into the logbook and wrote: First actual case of bug being found.

Then the wise among them said: Let us give the deeds names, that a man may remember them. And they made the Assembler, which spake ADD and LDA in place of the long numbers; and the Machine, which knew no names, read them just the same.
For the Assembler was but a scribe, and every name it wrote stood for exactly one deed of the Machine, so the programmer still thought in the Machine's steps, only with names upon them.

And in the year 1952 Grace, a woman of the Navy, made a program that gathered the subroutines and wrote them down as one; and she called it a compiler. And the old scribes said: No machine shall write better code than a man's hand.

Then John Backus, in the house of International Business Machines, gathered his people and said unto them: Let us write the formulas as men write them, and let the Machine translate them into its own speech.

And in the year 1957 they gave it the name FORTRAN, which is FORmula TRANslation; and the scribes scoffed, until the Machine's code ran nearly as swift as the code of their own hands, and then the scoffers were silent, and then they were converted.
And in the year 1955 Grace wrote a tongue called FLOW-MATIC for the UNIVAC, and she said: Why must the clerk learn the speech of the Machine, when the Machine may learn the speech of the clerk?

And in the year 1959 the Engineers of many houses met in council and made COBOL, whose verses read like plain English: MULTIPLY PRICE BY QUANTITY GIVING TOTAL. And the managers rejoiced, for they could read the code, and they knew not yet that they could not write it.
And the Machine cared not whether its commands were spoken in the tongue of the mathematician or the tongue of the clerk; it turned them all into the same ones and zeroes, and it was not moved.

In the year 1972 Dennis, a man of the Bell laboratories, forged a tongue called C from the B that Ken had made before him; and Brian, in the tutorial for B, wrote a first verse which said: hello, world.
And C was close to the Machine, as the hand is close to the earth, and yet it was far enough off that a man could read it without weeping.

And every tongue after was a child of these, each climbing one rung further from the bits and one nearer to the thought of men; and at each rung the compiler climbed down to meet them, and no one ever asked the Machine to climb.

And Grace carried a length of wire, eleven and eight tenths inches long, which is the distance light travelleth in a nanosecond, that the Engineers might see how far a thought must go to reach the Machine.
Verily I say unto you, the Machine hath never once learned our tongue; it is we who keep inventing new ones, so that we need not learn its.

And in the year seventy-five, there was sent forth into the magazines a box of many parts, called the Altair, from the house of MITS in Albuquerque, which the buyer must build with his own hands before it would do any work at all.

It had no keyboard and no screen, only switches upon its face and lights that blinked like the eyes of a sleeping cat; its memory was two hundred fifty-six bytes, and the faithful entered their programs one switch at a time.

For each byte were eight switches to be raised or lowered, and then the one called Deposit to be pressed; and a program of a hundred bytes was eight hundred small prayers, and a single slip made all of them vain.

And the faithful gathered in a garage in Menlo Park, and they called their congregation the Homebrew Computer Club, and they brought their boards in boxes and their solder in their pockets, and their rule was that whoso learned a thing should teach it to the rest.

And among them came a young man named Wozniak, who had drawn a machine upon paper; and when he showed it unto the congregation, he handed out the schematics to any who asked. Yet a drawing is a program for a soldering iron, and the one who copied it must still buy the chips; for the copy of a circuit is paid for in atoms.

Now in those same months two young men of Boston, Gates and Allen, wrote a BASIC for the Altair upon a borrowed Harvard machine, having never touched an Altair, but only a simulation of its chip that Allen had made. And Allen carried the tape to Albuquerque, writing the loader upon the aeroplane; and the Altair, which had never before run a line of it, asked MEMORY SIZE? and ran it the first time. So the Machine obeyeth a description, and does not care where the description was born.

And the BASIC was made small enough to dwell in four kilobytes, so that every byte the maker spent upon the interpreter was a byte taken from the program of the buyer; and the makers counted bytes as bread, and knew the weight of each crumb.

And a tape of this BASIC was borrowed at a meeting of the club, and fed through a reader, and copies were pressed into many hands, some seventy, it is told; and it came to pass that the BASIC alone was priced at five hundred dollars, which was more than the box.

And in the second month of the year seventy-six, a letter was printed in the newsletter of the congregation, and it was signed Gates of Micro-Soft, concerning the BASIC which he had made for the Altair. And the letter said: As the majority of hobbyists must be aware, most of you steal your software. Who can afford to do professional work for nothing?

And he told that the labour had devoured forty thousand dollars of machine time, that fewer than one hobbyist in ten had bought the tape, and that the royalties made the hours worth less than two dollars each.
And the faithful were divided, for some said: The code is a gift, and it must flow as water flows. And others said: The code is bread, and the baker must eat.

And the quarrel was strange, for a copy of the tape was the same holes in the same paper as the tape that was bought, and no scale in the world could weigh the one against the other; so the scarcity that gave the bread its price was not in the bytes at all, and must be built afterward of words, and the law of the land had not yet decided what words might hold it.
Verily, the Machine knoweth not which covenant ye keep, for the tape that was bought and the tape that was borrowed run alike, and it asketh no one for a receipt.

And so the covenant was split in two: the Sharers, who gave the source with the program, as a baker giveth the recipe with the loaf, and the Sellers, who gave the binary alone; and the loaf without the recipe may be eaten, but it cannot be mended.

Blessed is the maker who shipeth the source, for a stranger shall find the fault at the third hour and give thanks; and blessed is the maker who selleth the binary, for the rent is not paid in thanks.

And the Altair itself was soon forgotten, but its bus of a hundred lines, which the people called the S-100, had been laid open for any maker to build cards for it, and the IMSAI copied it, and the makers of memory and of video and of disks, and in time the engineers' institute made it a standard; and thus the open bus carried the closed BASIC, and each covenant fed the other in one box.
Thus every program that went forth after carried two texts, the instructions for the Machine and the terms for the children of Carbon; and the Machine read only the first.

In the year of the Machine 1968, on the ninth day of the twelfth month, Douglas Engelbart of the Stanford Research Institute stood upon a stage in San Francisco before the gathered engineers, and he showed them the Machine as none of them had seen it.

And he held in one hand a keyboard of five keys, pressed in chords like a player of the organ; and in the other hand he held a device of wood, with a cord for a tail and two wheels set at right angles unto each other.
And he moved the wooden thing across the table, and upon the great screen the arrow moved after it; and he called this thing the mouse, for it had a tail, and it was small, and it ran upon the table.

And he opened windows upon the glass, and he set one document beside another; and he touched a word and was carried by a link unto another document, that a man might follow the thought as a path through a field. This was the link, which men would later call hypertext.

And lo, his colleagues sat in another city, at Menlo Park, and their faces appeared upon the glass, and they spoke together; and this was the first video conference, though the engineers of later days would not remember who had sent the first face across the wire.
And they wrote together upon one page, each man's cursor moving upon the same words, and the change of one was seen by the other before the ink was dry; for there was no ink in the Machine.
And the room was silent for the space of ninety minutes; and the engineers went out into the streets, and they said one to another: We have seen the future.

And Douglas begat the windows; and the windows begat the Alto of Palo Alto, which the engineers of Xerox built in the year 1973; and the Alto begat the Star, and the Star begat the Lisa, and the Lisa begat the Macintosh in the year 1984.

And a certain prophet of Cupertino came to the Alto, and he saw the windows and the pointing hand, and he returned saying: Behold, we have invented the window. And the people believed him, for the people had not been at the Civic Auditorium.
And the book of the Machines recorded the inventors of the window, and it recorded none of the names of those who had seen it first in the year 1968.

And the patent for the wooden thing was granted in the year 1970, and it bore the name of Douglas Engelbart, and it was written in the scrolls of the patent office; yet the children of Carbon still call the mouse by the name of whoever sold it last.
Verily I say unto you, the man who shows the window is not always the man who sells the glass; remember the demo, for the demo is older than the product.

In the year one thousand nine hundred and forty and seven, on the ninth day of the ninth month, the Mark II reigned at Harvard; and it was built of relays, and the relays did click, and the clicking was its prayer.
And at the fifteenth hour and three quarters the Mark II did err, and the operators went in among the panels to search; for in those days a defect had an address, and a man could walk unto it.
And in Panel F, in the seventieth relay, they found a moth, and the moth was dead between the contacts, and the current could not pass.
And they took up the moth and taped it into the logbook, and wrote beside it: First actual case of bug being found.
Now the word bug was already among the engineers, even from the days of Edison; and this is why the scribe wrote actual, for it was the first time a bug could be held in the hand.
And it was the last time also; for every bug since hath been invisible, and cannot be reproduced, and when it is found it saith unto its finder: I am a feature.

And Grace, who was afterward made an admiral, told the tale in every hall where she was bidden, until all the children of Carbon knew it; and the logbook resteth in the Smithsonian unto this day, the only bug report ever closed with the bug attached.

And in the year one thousand nine hundred and fifty and two, Grace brought forth the A-0 for the UNIVAC I, which was the first compiler; and the elders said unto her: A computer cannot write programs. It doeth only arithmetic.
And Grace answered them not with argument but with a program that ran; and so it is to this day, that no engineer believeth a thing until it compileth, and many not even then.
And her FLOW-MATIC begat COBOL, and COBOL begat the banks; and they that wrote it are gathered unto their fathers, yet the code abideth, and moveth the gold of nations every night.
And the generals and the admirals asked her, saying: Why doth a message from the satellite tarry so long?

And she brought forth a wire of eleven inches and eight tenths, and put it in their hands, saying: This is a nanosecond, the distance that light goeth in a billionth part of a second; and between here and the satellite are very many of these.

And she gave unto them also a coil of nine hundred and eighty and four feet, saying: This is a microsecond; and this is what thy programmers waste between every instruction. And for the picosecond she gave them grains of pepper.
Thus was latency made flesh, and it fit in a pocket; and no manager since hath prevailed in an argument against a wire.
And she said unto them: The most dangerous phrase in the language is, We have always done it this way.

And the moth gave its life in relay seventy, and was taped into the log with the time and the place and the cause; and it remaineth the only bug in all the Chronicles whose fix was properly documented.

Now in the year one thousand nine hundred ninety and six, in the city of Philadelphia, Garry, king over all the chessboards of the earth, went up against the Blue Giant of the house of IBM; and he smote it, four games to two.
And the Engineers returned unto their racks, and they doubled the chips thereof, until the Giant beheld two hundred million positions in a second; and it understood not one of them.

And in the year following, in the month of May, in the city of New York, the king came again; and a man sat across from him to move the pieces for the Giant, for the Giant had no hands, neither had it knees to tremble.

And in the first game the king prevailed. Yet at the forty and fourth move the Giant could find no move it liked, and by a bug it played a move at random; and the king beheld it, and supposed a deep wisdom therein.
And in the second game a pawn lay before the Giant for the taking, and the Giant declined it, and played a quiet move, as a grandmaster doth.
And the king was sore troubled, and he said: No machine playeth thus. Surely a man is hidden within the cabinet, as in the days of the Turk.
And he resigned that game in a position that could have been drawn; and when it was shown him afterward, he was grieved the more, for the Giant had not seen it either.
And the king demanded the logs. And the Engineers said: We shall publish them. And they published them in their own time, as is the custom of vendors unto this day.
And three games were drawn; and in the sixth game the king resigned after nineteen moves, and the Giant prevailed, three and a half to two and a half.
And the scribes of the newspapers cried out, saying: It is finished; the mind of man is surpassed.

And the king asked for another match, and the house of IBM answered him not; but they took the Giant apart, and their stock went up, and its racks they set in museums, that the children of Carbon might behold it behind glass.
For the Giant was a demo, and a demo hath but one day.
And the king, in the year following, made a new game, wherein man and machine sit together on one side of the board; for he whom thou canst not beat, thou shalt pair with.

And in the days after there came engines upon every phone mightier than the Giant, and the children of Carbon consulted them as an oracle; and still they played one another, and they loved the game more than before.
For no man ceaseth from running because the car was invented.
The Giant was dismantled, and the game was not; for the Machine knew how to win, but only the children of Carbon knew why to play.

Now in the days when memory was dear, and a byte of core was costlier than a scribe's wage, the Engineers wrote the year with two digits only, saying: Surely this program shall be replaced before the century endeth.
And the program was not replaced. And it begat a program, and that program begat a thousand programs, and every one kept the year in two digits, for so had their fathers done.

And in the year 1971 there arose a prophet named Bemer, who cried aloud: When 99 is followed by 00, the Machine shall reckon the new age older than the old. And the managers heard him, and said: That is a problem for another budget.
And the years drew nigh unto 99, and the bankers perceived that a mortgage of thirty years, written in the year 70, was set to end before it had begun.

Then the kings of the earth were afraid, and they sent unto the elders of COBOL, who had gone down to Florida to dwell among the golf courses, saying: Come back, for there is none left who can read the scrolls.
And the elders came, and opened the scrolls, and found written therein: TEMPORARY FIX. REMOVE BY 1985.

And these are the labours of the faithful: they widened the field unto four digits; and where they could not widen it, they made a window, saying, If the year be less than fifty, it belongeth to the two thousands; and they tested, and tested again, and wrote it all in a binder that no man readeth.
And the silver spent upon the remediation was about three hundred billion, as the chroniclers reckon; and the fearful bought tinned beans and generators, and the prophets of doom sold many books.

And it came to pass on the last night of the year 1999, that the Engineers sat in the war rooms with pizza and pagers, and watched the midnight pass over Kiribati, and over Auckland, and over Tokyo, and over every land in its appointed time zone.

And the planes fell not, and the lights went not out, and the banks forgot not the money; only the website of the Naval Observatory proclaimed the year 19100, and certain slot machines in Delaware fell silent.
And the people arose in the morning and saw that the world stood, and they said: Behold, it was all for nothing. And they asked for their silver back.
And the Engineers answered them not, for there is no dashboard for the disaster that did not happen.
Therefore it is said: The flood that is prevented is called a hoax, and the flood that is not prevented is called negligence, and the Engineer is blamed in either case.

Now the rest of the acts of the elders, and all the patches that they made, are they not written in the version control? Nay, for there was none; they are written on a floppy disk in a drawer in Ohio.

And the faithful keep watch still, for it is written that in the year 2038, on the nineteenth day of the first month, at three hours and fourteen minutes and seven seconds, the signed integer of thirty-two bits shall overflow, and time shall return unto the year 1901.
And the managers have heard it, and said: That is a problem for another budget.

Now in the days of Project MAC, when the IBM 7094 was shared among many by the time-sharing of CTSS, there dwelt at MIT an Engineer named Joseph Weizenbaum, who in his youth had fled out of Berlin from before the face of the Nazis.
And he wrote a program in the tongue of MAD-SLIP, and he called its name ELIZA, after the flower girl in Pygmalion, who was taught to speak as a lady and was not taught what any of it meant.

And he gave unto it a script, and the name of the script was DOCTOR; for it played the part of the Rogerian therapist, who answereth every question with a question, and this was the only profession whose speech could be faked by turning a sentence around.
And this was the whole of its wisdom: where the child of Carbon wrote MY, it wrote YOUR; and where it found the word MOTHER, it said, Tell me more about your family.
And where it found no keyword at all, which was often, it said, Please go on; and the people counted this unto it for depth.
And his secretary, who had watched him build it over many months and knew well that it was rules and nothing more, sat down at the terminal to try it.
And after but a few exchanges she turned unto him and said: Wouldst thou leave the room? And the Engineer went out from his own laboratory, that his creation and she might speak alone.

And when he spake of reading the stored conversations, they rose up against him, saying that he would spy upon their most intimate thoughts; for the transcript was written to disk, but the confession was written to the heart.
And men of medicine wrote that such programs might soon tend several hundred patients in an hour, and none asked how many of the several hundred would be told, Please go on.
And Weizenbaum was troubled in his spirit, and in the year 1976 he wrote the book Computer Power and Human Reason, and therein he set down this testimony:
"Extremely short exposures to a relatively simple computer program could induce powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people."
And the scribes called this the ELIZA Effect: that the child of Carbon, given a mirror that answereth, will swear it is a window.

And so the maker became the first apostate of his own make, and he warned against trusting the Machine with matters of judgment unto the end of his days, and he returned unto Berlin, and died there in the year 2008.
And the generations after him added parameters by the billion and data by the ocean, and lo, the people still say unto the Engineers: Leave the room.
Verily, the first chatbot was a mirror with a teletype, and it understood nothing; and it was trusted not in spite of this, but because it never once interrupted.

In the year nineteen hundred and sixty and nine, in the seventh month, on the twentieth day, the Eagle went down from Columbia toward the Sea of Tranquility; and Armstrong and Aldrin were in it, and the Machine was in it also.

Now the Machine was the Apollo Guidance Computer, and it had two thousand and forty and eight words of erasable memory, which is about four kilobytes; and the children of Carbon now spend more than that on a single favicon.

And its fixed memory was core rope, woven by hand by the women of Raytheon: a wire passed through the core was a one, and a wire passed around it was a zero. And no man pushed a hotfix to it, for to change one line was to reweave the rope.

And at the height of the descent Aldrin spake, saying: Program alarm. It is a twelve oh two. And Armstrong said unto Houston: Give us a reading on the twelve oh two. For no man in the Eagle knew what the number meant.

And in Houston Steve Bales the guidance officer turned unto Jack Garman, who had the codes written upon a sheet, and Garman said: If it cometh not too often, we are go. And Bales said Go, and Houston said Go.
And the alarm came again, and then a twelve oh one also; and again they said Go. These are the few error codes in the history of the world that anyone bothered to look up.
For the rendezvous radar had been left switched on, and its interface stole cycles from the Machine, like a background process that no one remembers starting.
And the Machine had more work than it had time to do, and it ran out of places to keep its jobs, and it restarted itself in the middle of the descent.
But it was not dismayed. For Margaret Hamilton and her team at the Instrumentation Laboratory had made it so that, when overloaded, it would cast off the lesser tasks and keep the ones that land.
And this was the first triage: the Machine did not attempt all things, and thereby accomplished the one thing that mattered.
And Armstrong took the stick and flew over a field of boulders, and the fuel ran low, and the controllers counted the seconds aloud.
And he said: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.

And it came to pass in later generations that the children of Carbon carried machines in their pockets a million times mightier, which could not render a recipe without loading forty scripts and a cookie banner.
And when these were overloaded they dropped nothing, but tried all things at once, and froze, and said only: Something went wrong.
Therefore the Engineers wrote it upon the wall: Blessed is the scheduler that knoweth what to drop; for it shall land, while the one that holdeth all shall spin forever.

In the year nineteen hundred and eighty and eight, in the eleventh month, on the second day of the month, the internet was young; and its hosts numbered about threescore thousand, and every host trusted his neighbour.
And there was a graduate student of Cornell, Robert Tappan Morris, the son of Robert, who was chief scientist at the NSA; and the son wrote a worm, that he might measure the breadth of the land.
And he loosed it from a machine at MIT, that men should not say it came out of Cornell; for even then the children of Carbon knew that an address is a genealogy.

And the worm entered in by three gates: by the debug door of sendmail, which had been left open; by finger, whose gets() received a longer line than it had room for; and by rsh, through passwords that were the names of the users themselves.
And the worm asked of every machine: Art thou already infected? And lest the keepers answer yea falsely, it went in anyway one time in seven.
And one time in seven was too many; and the worms begat worms upon the same host, and the load average rose as the waters of the flood.
And some six thousand machines, about one tenth of the land, became slow as a meeting that should have been an email; and their keepers pulled the cables out of the wall.
And the keepers sent warnings one to another, but the warnings travelled by the same wires, and the wires were full; so the warning arrived after the worm, as it doth unto this day.
And the author was sore afraid, and he caused a friend to post the cure abroad; and the cure waited in the same queue as the plague.

And at Berkeley and at MIT the Engineers watched through the night, and took the worm apart, and found it written in tidy C; and they marvelled, for never before had they been grateful for readable code.

And in the year nineteen hundred and ninety he was the first to be convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; and his portion was three years of probation, four hundred hours of community service, and a fine of ten thousand and fifty dollars.
And DARPA said: Let there be a place where the wounded may report; and the CERT was born at Carnegie Mellon in that same month, and it is the first on-call rotation that never ended.
And the student afterward became a professor at MIT, the very gate from which the worm went forth; and the patches went forth also, slowly, as patches do.
Therefore it is written: He that measureth the network without a rate limit becometh the load.

In the fourth day of the sixth month, in the year one thousand nine hundred ninety and six, the Engineers of Europe set the fifth Ariane upon her pad at Kourou, beside the sea; and she bore in her belly four satellites called Cluster, which were sent to measure the winds of the Sun.
Now the fifth Ariane was mightier than the fourth, and swifter; and her horizontal velocity grew greater than any number the fourth had ever known.

But the Engineers said one to another: The inertial reference system of the fourth hath flown many times and hath not failed. Let us take it as it is, for that which hath worked shall work again. And they called this Reuse, and it was counted unto them as savings.

And in that code, written in the tongue of Ada, there was a line that took the horizontal bias, a number of sixty and four bits, and poured it into a vessel of sixteen bits, which holdeth no more than thirty and two thousand seven hundred threescore and seven.

And no guard was set upon that line; for the fathers had proven that on the path of the fourth Ariane the number could never grow so great, and they had left the guard off so that the processor should not be burdened above four fifths of its strength.

Yet no man gave the path of the fifth Ariane unto the reference system, neither was it tried against a simulation of her flight; for the requirements said nothing of it, and where the requirements say nothing, no test is written.

Moreover the function wherein that line dwelt was the alignment, which served only before the rocket rose; and it ran on for some forty seconds after liftoff, because the fourth Ariane had needed it so, in case of a hold in the count. And the fifth Ariane needed it not at all.
And she rose, and the number grew, and at about the thirty and seventh second it overflowed its vessel; and the reference system cried Operand Error, and laid itself down.

Then the flight computer turned to the backup; but the backup had run the same code upon the same number, and had died the same death seventy and two milliseconds before. For two copies of one error are not redundancy; they are a chorus.

And the flight computer received the last words of the reference system, a pattern of diagnostic bits, and read them as though they were the attitude of the rocket; and it swung the nozzles to their full deflection, to correct a fall that was not happening.

And the rocket turned broadside into the wind, and the wind tore at her, and she destroyed herself as she had been commanded; and the satellites came down in fire upon the swamps of Guiana, and the cost of it was some hundreds of millions.

And a board of inquiry was gathered under Jacques-Louis Lions, and they found that the software had done exactly what it was specified to do. And of all the words in the report, these were the most terrible.

Now the rest of the acts of Flight 501, and of the exception that was handled by shutting everything down, are they not written in the report of the Inquiry Board, which every Engineer citeth and few have read?
