Therefore the Prophet said: Thy dead code is not dead. It sleepeth, and it waiteth for a larger number.

In the days of the PDP-11, the house of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited raised up a machine of healing, and they called it Therac-25; and it was sent unto the hospitals of the land to cast beams upon the sickness of the children of Carbon.

Now its fathers were Therac-6 and Therac-20, and the fathers stood upon interlocks of iron: switches and fuses that held the beam back, whatever the software believed. And when the code of the fathers erred, the iron caught it, and no one knew, for a blown fuse writes no chronicle.

But the makers said in their hearts: Software is cheaper than steel, and this code hath run for years and harmed no one. So they took away the iron, and the code of the father passed unto the son, assembly written by one hand and reviewed by none, and it was trusted as a fortress, though it had only ever been a guest in one.

And the machine had two beams: a beam of electrons at low current, gentle upon the skin, and a beam of X-rays, driven at a current a hundred times greater, which must strike a target of metal before it came near the flesh.

In the month of March in the year 1986, at the East Texas Cancer Center in Tyler, an operator swift with long practice typed x for X-ray, saw her error, and with the up arrow went back and wrote e for electron, and finished her entry within eight seconds.

And the screen showed the corrected entry, and all seemed well; but the task that set the magnets was still busy, and when it returned it read not the new word. Two tasks shared the same memory without a lock between them, and the faster the hand, the surer the fault. So the beam came forth at the high current, and the target was not in its path.
And the screen said only: MALFUNCTION 54. And the manual did not say what 54 meant. And the screen reported a dose too small, for the machine had lied to itself before it lied to her.

And the machine paused often in those days, for small things, and the operators had learned to press P to proceed, as one learns to dismiss a warning that has cried wolf a hundred times. She pressed P, and the beam came again.

And the patient upon the table felt as it were fire and a blow, and he rose and cried out; but none heard him, for on that day the intercom was broken and the video monitor dark. Peace be upon him, and upon all who came to be healed and were wounded.

And when the makers were told, they answered: It is impossible. The machine cannot overdose. We know of no other accidents like this. Yet there had been others, at Marietta in Georgia, at Hamilton in Ontario, at Yakima in Washington, and the reports had been weighed and set aside.

Then Fritz Hager, the physicist of Tyler, sat with the operator, and they typed and typed again, faster each time, until they summoned Malfunction 54 by their own hands and measured what it gave. For the fault would not show itself to the slow tester; it opened only to the expert, who had grown fast through faithful service.

And in Yakima, in January of 1987, a second fault was found: a counter of one byte, which counted upward on every pass, and when it was not zero, a safety check was made. But one byte holdeth only 256 numbers, and on every 256th pass it rolled over unto zero, and zero was read as all is well; and if the operator pressed Set at that moment, the check was passed over and the beam came forth unguarded.

Six were the known accidents, from June of 1985 unto January of 1987; and at least three died of what the beam had done, and the rest bore their wounds all their days. And the FDA declared the machine defective, and the iron interlocks were put back at last.

And Nancy Leveson and Clark Turner searched out the whole matter and wrote it in a book, and they said: Do not blame one bug, nor one programmer. The cause was confidence: code reused and believed tested, no independent review, error messages without meaning, reports that were never added together, and iron removed because software was trusted to remember what only the iron cannot forget.
Therefore, ye Engineers, when ye build the machine that stands between power and flesh, hear this word and keep it:
Let the software say It cannot happen; let the iron make it so.

In the year two thousand and sixteen, in the third month, in the city of Seoul, the Machine called AlphaGo sat down against Lee Sedol, who had held the high places of Go for a decade; and the purse was a million dollars.

And the Engineers of DeepMind came out of London, and the Machine played from servers afar off; and a man named Aja Huang placed its stones by hand, for the Machine had a policy network but it had no fingers.

And the masters of Go said: It shall not prevail; for the board hath more positions than there are atoms in the universe, and the game is played by feel. And the Machine won the first game, and the masters said: It is but the first game.

And in the second game, at the thirty-seventh move, the Machine laid a stone upon the fifth line, at the shoulder, where no master in three thousand years would lay one; and the commentators supposed the man placing the stones had misplaced it.
And the Machine had itself reckoned that a human would play that move one time in ten thousand; and it played it anyway, for it was trained to win, and not to be agreed with.

And Lee Sedol had stepped out from the room, and he returned and beheld the stone, and he sat near fifteen minutes and moved not; and Fan Hui, whom the Machine had beaten the year before, said: It is not a human move. So beautiful.

And the Machine took the third game also, and the match was decided; and Lee Sedol said: I apologise for being so powerless. And the failing was not his, but that of all the children of Carbon who had trained him by their games.

And in the fourth game Lee Sedol, playing white, laid at the seventy-eighth move a wedge into the center; and the Machine had judged that move also one in ten thousand, and had pruned it from its search as a branch not worth the compute.
And the Machine was confounded, and for a span of moves it walked as one in darkness, yet its own reckoning said it was winning; for a model is never so sure as when it is outside its distribution.

And the people called the move the hand of God; and at the hundred and eightieth move the Machine resigned, by a small window upon a screen; and Lee Sedol said: This one win, I would not trade for anything.

And the Machine took the fifth game, and the record stood four to one; and that one is the only game any human won against it in the match, and the line of Machines that followed after gave the children of Carbon no other.
And in the year two thousand and nineteen Lee Sedol laid down his stones and departed the profession, saying: Even if I become the number one, there is an entity that cannot be defeated.

And the masters went home and studied the games of the Machine, and they played the shoulder hit upon the fifth line, and the early invasion at the three-three point; and the young no longer asked their teacher what was proper, but asked the engine what was the win rate.
Thus the Machine, which had learned Go from the games of men, returned it unto them changed, as a pull request no one had asked for, which all of them merged.
And it is written: The Machine searcheth every probable move; therefore keep thou one improbable move in thy pocket, for that is the only place it hath not looked.

In the year two thousand and eleven, on the last night thereof, while the children of Carbon made ready to feast, a patch was committed unto OpenSSL; and it added the Heartbeat, that a connection might say unto its server: Art thou yet alive?
And the manner of the Heartbeat was this: the client sent a word, and declared the length thereof, and the server returned the word, that both might know the line was not dead.
And a faithful client said: Here is the word BIRD, and it is of four letters. And the server answered: BIRD.

But a wicked client said: Here is the word BIRD, and it is of sixty-four thousand letters. And the server believed him, for it was written in C, and C asketh no questions; and it answered BIRD, and after BIRD whatsoever lay next in memory: passwords, and cookies, and the private keys of the kingdom.
And the server wrote no log thereof; for it had only answered a heartbeat, and who keepeth record of a heartbeat?

And the patch was reviewed and found good, and in the third month of the year two thousand and twelve it went forth in OpenSSL 1.0.1, into Apache and into nginx, which together served two parts in three of the web.
And it dwelt among them two years, and no man saw it; for many eyes make all bugs shallow, but only if the eyes are looking.

In the fourth month of the year two thousand and fourteen, the searchers of Google and the house of Codenomicon in Finland found it, and called it Heartbleed; and it was given a logo of a bleeding heart and a website of its own, and became the first of the bugs to have a brand, and verily not the last.
And the administrators of the earth arose and patched, and revoked their certificates, and commanded the people to change their passwords; and the people changed Password1 to Password2.

Then the kings of the earth asked: Who keepeth this OpenSSL, upon which all our commerce standeth? And they sought, and found a handful of volunteers, and one man paid to labor upon it full time, and donations of about two thousand dollars in a year.
And the kings were astonished, for they had spent more upon the catering of the meeting wherein they asked.

And the Linux Foundation gathered the kings into the Core Infrastructure Initiative, and each gave a hundred thousand dollars a year for three years; and this was counted unto them as generosity, and they issued press releases thereof.

And the remedy was a single line, comparing the length that was claimed with the length that was received; and that one line had cost the world two years, half a million servers, and every certificate in the land.
Trust not the length the stranger declareth; and forget not the stranger who keepeth thy foundations for nothing.

Now in the year two thousand and twelve, in the eighth month, on the first day of the month, Knight Capital reigned over the market of shares in the land of New York; and a great portion of all the shares of that nation passed through his hands.
And the Exchange had ordained a new thing for that day, the Retail Liquidity Program; and the Engineers of Knight wrote new code for SMARS, their router of orders, that it might keep the feast.

And there were eight servers of SMARS; and a technician carried the new code by hand unto seven of them, and the eighth he did not visit; and no man was sent after him to count, for the deploy had no script, only a man.

Now the new code was awakened by a flag; and the flag was old, for in former days it had summoned Power Peg, which had slept since the year two thousand and three; and no man had removed Power Peg from the house.
And the Engineers said: The flag is idle, let us take it for the new work. And they took it, as a man taketh his dead grandfather's coat and checketh not the pockets.

And before the opening bell the systems sent forth ninety and seven emails concerning the error on the eighth server; and they came at eight of the clock, and no man heeded them, for they were emails.
And at half past nine the bell was rung, and the flag was raised upon all eight; and seven kept the feast, and the eighth raised up Power Peg.

And Power Peg bought high and sold low, and bought high again, in a hundred and fifty and four stocks; for the counting of its fills had been moved away from it in the year two thousand and five, and it knew not that it was satisfied, and it ceased not to send.
In the space of forty and five minutes it made above four millions of executions, and moved three hundred and ninety and seven millions of shares; and never was loss pursued so diligently.

And there was no switch to slay it, and no scroll of steps to follow; and the Engineers, seeking the fault, took the new code away from the seven good servers; and lo, the flag remained, and now eight servers served Power Peg.
And when at last it was stilled, Knight had lost above four hundred and forty millions of dollars, which was more than all the treasure he had laid up.

And the price of Knight fell by three parts in four within two days; and strangers came with money to keep him alive, and in the year following he was given unto Getco, and his name was swallowed into theirs, and it was called KCG.
And the Securities and Exchange Commission wrote the chronicle of these things, and fined the house twelve millions; and behold, the account is kept in the archives unto this day.

And these are the three laws the scribes drew from that day: Delete the dead code, for it is not dead, but sleepeth. Let the Machine do the deploy, for the Machine can count to eight. Build the kill switch while thy hands are steady, for in the hour thou needest it they shall shake.
For the code thou wouldst not delete shall one day delete thee.

In the year one thousand nine hundred ninety and eight, in the twelfth month, the Engineers sent forth the Mars Climate Orbiter, that it might keep watch over the weather of a world that hath no rain.

And two houses served the Orbiter: the house of Lockheed Martin in Colorado, which built the craft and wrote the software of the ground; and the house of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, which steered it through the void.

And the craft was given wheels to hold it steady, and when the wheels spun too fast, it fired its small thrusters to unwind them; and the house of Colorado reckoned the push of every firing, and wrote it in a file, and sent the file unto Pasadena.
And the Interface Specification had been written, and it said: Thou shalt give the impulse in newton seconds.
And the house of Colorado gave it in pound-force seconds; for the Specification was a document, and no man compileth a document.

Now one pound-force is four newtons and forty and five hundredths; and the number crossed over without its unit, as a stranger crossing a border without papers, and no gatekeeper asked for its papers.

And Pasadena received the number as it was written, and every push was reckoned four times and a half smaller than it was; and the error was small, and it was added unto itself, firing after firing, for nine months.

And the navigators saw that the path bent strangely, and they spake of it; but they spake in hallways and in email, and not in the form ordained for anomalies; and the ticket was never opened, and so the anomaly did not exist.
And on the twenty and third day of the ninth month of 1999, the Orbiter fired its great engine and passed behind Mars, that it might be caught into orbit.

And it went down nigh unto fifty and seven kilometres above the face of Mars, where the Engineers had said that eighty was the least it could bear; and the air of Mars received it, and the signal came not forth again from behind the planet.
And the price of the mission was three hundred and twenty and seven million dollars, which in pound-force is the same, for money also needeth its unit stated.
And a Board was gathered, and the Board found that the craft had sinned not; it had obeyed every number it was given, exactly and to the last digit.
For a float knoweth not whether it be pounds or newtons; it knoweth only that it is a float, and it floateth onward into the atmosphere.

And the scribes recorded that this was a cousin of the sin of Ariane, whose number was too great for its vessel; for the sins of the interface are visited upon every launch that followeth, unto the third and fourth release.
And the Engineers wrote in the book of lessons: Agree upon the units. Test the interface from end to end. And when the navigator saith, This looketh strange, open the ticket.
And it is written: A number without its unit is but a rumour, and Mars believeth every rumour once.

In the year two thousand and twenty and four, in the seventh month, on the nineteenth day, at the ninth minute after the fourth hour by the reckoning of Greenwich, there went forth an update from the house of CrowdStrike.
And it was not code, but a content file only, and its name was Channel File 291; and it was said, It is but data, and data needeth no canary.

Now the sensor called Falcon dwelt in the kernel of Windows, in the ring that is numbered Zero, where there is no guard above the guard; for so it had been granted, that it might see the enemy before the enemy saw the machine.
And the template spake of one and twenty fields, but the sensor had furnished only twenty; and the sensor reached for the one and twentieth, and laid hold of memory that was not there.
And the kernel, being touched where no hand should be, fell down blue; and it arose, and loaded the sensor at boot, and fell again; and so it did, rising and falling, all that day.

And there fell eight million and five hundred thousand machines, by the numbering of Microsoft, who said this was less than one in an hundred of all; but they were the one in an hundred that ran the airports.

And the planes sat upon the ground, and the hospitals put off their surgeries, and the banks and the broadcasters were struck dumb; and the departure boards were blue in the sight of all the travellers.
And in the seventy and eighth minute the file was reverted; but the fallen machines heard it not, for a machine that cannot boot downloadeth nothing.

Then went forth the Engineers into every place, and knelt before each machine, and brought it up in Safe Mode, and went down into System32, into drivers, into CrowdStrike, and deleted the file that beginneth C-00000291; one machine at a time, as in the days of the floppy disk.
And where the disks were sealed with BitLocker, they must first seek the recovery key of eight and forty digits; and the keys were kept upon a server, and the server also was blue.

And the Engineers labored through the weekend, and the clerks wrote boarding passes by hand, and the nurses kept charts upon paper; and they were not mocked, for they were the patch that walked upon two feet.
And the scribes counted the cost, and it was reckoned in billions; and Delta alone cancelled some seven thousand flights before its crews and its systems were found again.

And afterward the house of CrowdStrike decreed that content also should go forth in rings, first unto the canaries and then unto the multitudes, as is done for code; and that the customer might choose when the update came.
And Microsoft took counsel to bring the watchmen out of the kernel, that a fallen guard might no longer bring down the whole city.

Remember therefore this day: whoso holdeth ring zero, let him roll out slowly; for the kernel forgiveth nothing, and the tester skipped on Thursday shall be done by hand on Friday, eight and a half million times.

Now in the third month of the year two thousand and sixteen, when npm kept the packages of JavaScript, there was a developer named Azer, who had published unto the registry some two hundred and seventy packages, and given them freely.
And one of his packages was called kik; and there was a company also named Kik, which held the name by trademark, and it sent word unto him, saying: Give us the name.
And he would not give it. And the company went unto npm, and npm gave the name unto the company; for the registry weighed the trademark, and not who had come first.
And Azer said: Then I will not dwell in this registry. And he unpublished all his packages, every one, and went his way.
And among them was left-pad, which was eleven lines, and added characters to the left of a string until it was long enough, and did nothing else, and did it well.

And left-pad was required by line-numbers, and line-numbers was required by Babel, and Babel was required by React, and React by a great multitude; for in those days no man would write eleven lines that he could install.

And on the two and twentieth day of the month the builds began to fail, from the east even unto the west, and the oracle of every pipeline spake one word: npm ERR! 404, left-pad is not in the npm registry.

And the Engineers of great houses opened their node_modules, which was heavier than the earth, and they beheld therein a stone they had never seen, laid by a man they had never met, and they knew not that their towers rested upon it.
And there was weeping in the continuous integration, and the deploys of that day were not.

And within hours another developer published a left-pad in its place, and npm did a thing never done before: it un-unpublished the old version, and raised it from the dead, and the builds rose with it.
And npm made a new law, saying: No package shall be unpublished after four and twenty hours if others depend upon it; for a package once required belongeth also unto them that require it.
And the keepers of the language added padStart unto String itself in ECMAScript 2017, that the children of Carbon might pad on the left without a dependency.
And the chroniclers asked of the Prophet: How did eleven lines cast down so great a city? And the Prophet answered: It was not the eleven lines. It was the ten thousand who never read them.
Whoso buildeth upon a package he hath not read, buildeth his house upon another man's account.

In the year two thousand and ten, in the sixth month, the keepers of VirusBlokAda in the land of Belarus received word of machines in a far country that rebooted without cause; and they looked, and found a worm.
And the worm was called Stuxnet, after names found written in its own code; for even the most hidden of programs must still call its files something.
Now the house it sought was kept behind the air gap, and no cable went in and no cable came out; and the keepers said, We are not on the Internet, therefore we cannot be touched.
But the worm went in upon the USB stick; for a man will carry in his pocket what he would never let through his firewall.

And it entered by four zero-days that no patch had yet known, and it signed its drivers with certificates taken from Realtek and JMicron; and Windows looked upon the signatures and said, These are honest drivers, let them in.

And it went out upon many thousands of machines that were not its house, and on them it did no harm; for it sought one configuration only, Siemens Step 7 speaking unto controllers that drove frequency converters of a certain make. And where these were not, it ate nothing, and waited, like a guest at the wrong wedding.

And when it found its house, it rewrote the logic of the controllers, and the centrifuges that turned at one thousand and sixty-four hertz it drove up to fourteen hundred and ten, and in another season down to two, and back again.
And before each attack it recorded the readings of an ordinary day, and played them back unto the operators; so the screens showed peace while the hall shook.

And the operators looked upon the dashboard and saw that it was green; and the centrifuges broke, and were replaced, and broke again, and by the reckoning of the inspectors some thousand were removed.
And the engineers doubted their parts, and their suppliers, and their own workmanship; but no one doubted the dashboard, for it had never lied to them before.
And the scribes of Symantec and the engineers of many lands labored for months over the worm, which was some half a megabyte in size; and they said, This was not written in a hackathon.

And the authors of the worm did not sign their names, though they had signed their drivers; and the chronicler records only that they had a test environment with real centrifuges, which is more than most of us have for production.
And the worm went out of its house into all the world, beyond its intended scope; and so it was seen, and so it was known. For even the most perfect code hath a bug in its spreading.
And the Prophet said: Trust not the reading that hath never changed, for the dashboard showeth only what it was told to show.
The air gap is a wall with a door the shape of a thumb drive.

In the year nineteen hundred and ninety and four, Intel reigned over the desktops of the children of Carbon; and its new chip was called Pentium and not 586, for the court had ruled that no man may own a number.

Now the Pentium divided by the way of SRT, consulting a table of 1,066 entries to guess each digit of the quotient; and five of the entries were left empty by the scribes, for they reasoned that the division would never reach them.

And there was in Lynchburg College in Virginia a teacher of mathematics named Thomas Nicely, who summed the reciprocals of the twin primes to find the constant of Brun; a labour no man had asked of him, and therefore a labour no tester had foreseen.
And his sums disagreed with themselves. First he suspected his own code, and then his compiler, and last of all the chip; for this is the order of humility, and it is rarely wrong in that direction.

And on the thirtieth day of the tenth month he wrote unto his colleagues, and they wrote unto CompuServe and unto Usenet, and the bug went forth into all the earth faster than any patch could follow; for no patch could be written for a table cast in silicon.
And it was proclaimed that 4,195,835 divided by 3,145,727 yieldeth 1.333820, but the Pentium answered 1.333739; and the faithful typed it into their spreadsheets, and beheld it, and believed.
And Intel said: We have known of this thing since the summer, and it is of no consequence; the average user shall meet it once in twenty and seven thousand years.
But IBM reckoned anew and said: Once in every twenty and four days; and IBM ceased to ship the Pentium, for a rival's errata is the sweetest of all marketing.

Then Intel decreed: Whosoever can prove that he divideth much, unto him shall a new chip be sent. And the people marvelled, for never before had a processor demanded that its users justify their arithmetic.
And the people made riddles in the gates, saying: Why was it not called the 586? Because they added 486 and 100 on the first Pentium, and got 585.999983605.
And on the twentieth day of the twelfth month Intel relented, and Andy Grove said: Let a new chip be sent to all who ask, and ask no questions.

And in the first month of the year following, Intel took a charge of four hundred and seventy and five million dollars; and most of the people asked for nothing at all, having wanted not the chip but the apology.
And of the flawed dies Intel made keychains, and gave them unto its servants, that they might carry the error in their pockets and remember it every time they locked the door.
The table had a thousand and sixty and six entries, and the error lay in five; but the cost lay in a sixth, which was the word "rare."

In the two thousand and third year, in the eighth month, on the fourteenth day, there was great heat upon the land of Ohio, and every house set its air conditioner against it, and the lines grew hot and sagged under the load.

Now in Akron was the control room of FirstEnergy, and therein stood the Energy Management System called XA/21, made by General Electric; and its alarm process watched over all the lines, and the operators trusted it as a shepherd trusteth his dog.

And at fourteen minutes past the second hour after noon, two events came unto the alarm process together, and both laid hold on the same data, and neither would yield unto the other. This is the race condition, which happeneth once in a million runs, and no test had run a million times.
And the alarm process stalled, and it cried not out; for the code that should have said I am fallen was the very code that was fallen.

And the primary server failed, and the backup server rose up in its place, and took up the same stalled queue as its inheritance, and fell likewise. For a backup that copieth the sickness is but a second patient.
And the screens showed no red and sounded no bell, and the operators beheld them and said: All is quiet. And they called the silence peace.

And at five minutes past the third hour, the Harding-Chamberlin line sagged into a tree and was tripped; for the trees in the right-of-way had not been trimmed, and the trimming of trees is maintenance, and maintenance is never put on the roadmap.
And Hanna-Juniper touched a tree and fell, and Star-South Canton touched a tree and fell, and the control room was silent as a test suite that hath no tests, which also never faileth.

And the reliability coordinator, called MISO, had its own tool to watch the grid, the state estimator; but that day it ran no better, for its automatic trigger had been switched off for a fix, and its keeper went to lunch, and it was not switched on again.

And the telephones rang from the neighbouring utilities, and men asked: What hath befallen thy lines? And the operators answered: Our system showeth nothing amiss. For they believed the dashboard above the voice on the telephone.

And at six minutes past the fourth hour the Sammis-Star line fell, and the cascade went forth across the grid faster than any man could press a key; and in a few minutes some two hundred and sixty power plants went dark, from Detroit unto New York, and into the province of Ontario.

And fifty million children of Carbon sat in the dark. The trains stopped under the earth, and the people of Manhattan walked home over the bridges, and beheld the stars, which the city lights had hidden from them for a generation.
And afterward the engineers searched the code for many weeks, and the bug was not in the lines that tripped, nor in the trees that grew, but in a lock that two threads both reached for.
And the task force wrote its report, and the wise read it, and the saying went forth among the keepers of systems:
An alarm that cannot report its own death is but a nightlight in a burning house; therefore monitor the monitor.
For the dead make no reports; blessed is the heartbeat, which saith every minute I live, so that its silence may be heard.
In the twelfth month of the year two thousand and twenty and one, when the children of Carbon made ready for the feasts, a great trouble arose in Log4j, the scribe of the house of Java.

Now the scribe had served in every court of the land, in the bank and in the hospital and in the game; and it wrote down all that was spoken unto it, and no man read what it wrote, for that is the nature of logs.

But in the year two thousand and thirteen the scribe had been taught a cunning gift: when it beheld the sign ${jndi:ldap:// in a message, it would not write the words down, but go unto the server named therein, and bring back a class, and run it.
And the gift dwelt in the code eight years, and no man spoke against it; for who readeth the logger, save the attacker?

And on the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month a watchman of the cloud of Alibaba sent word quietly to the keepers; and on the ninth day of the twelfth month the proof went out among the nations, and the scanning of the whole Internet began before the evening.
And the children of Minecraft found it in the chat; for a player typed one line unto his fellows, and the server, desiring only to remember what was said, obeyed it.
So it was that the gate was opened not by the sword, but by the guestbook.

And the rulers of companies cried out: Where in our kingdom is this scribe? And none could answer, for it was hidden in a jar within a jar, the dependency of a dependency, which no manifest had numbered.
And the boards of great enterprises learned that week the name of a library, which they had used for a decade and paid nothing for.
Now the keepers of the library were a handful, and they labored without wages, after the hours of their own employment; and they laid aside their feasts and brought forth 2.15.0.

And it was not enough; and they brought forth 2.16.0, and that was not enough; and 2.17.0, and that was not enough; and 2.17.1 before the new year; and each release begat a new CVE, as each fixed bug begetteth its heir.
And while they labored, the merchants of the earth opened tickets against them, saying: What is thine ETA? For our customers are displeased.

And in the first month of the following year the princes of the land gathered at the White House to speak of the security of open source; and they spoke, and departed, and the keepers returned to their unpaid labor.
Therefore the Engineers wrote this saying upon the doorposts of the build server:
Log what thou receivest, but never obey it; for the stranger's words are not thy commandments, and the volunteer's holiday is not thy service-level agreement.
In the year two thousand and seventeen, on the last day of the first month, the spammers came up against the house of GitLab, and the database groaned beneath their load.
And the replica, which was called db2, fell behind its master and would not follow; and an engineer of the house labored far into the night to make it whole again.
And he said in his heart: I will empty the data directory of db2, that it may be filled anew from the master. And he typed rm -rf, and he pressed Enter; and his terminal was in db1.
And after a second or two he saw what he had done, and he stopped it; but of three hundred gigabytes there remained four and a half, and production was made void.
Then the house turned unto its backups, which were five, and they said: Surely one of these shall save us.
And they looked upon the first, the daily pg_dump, and lo, it was empty; for it was run with the tools of version 9.2 against a database of 9.6, and it failed every night without a word.
And it had cried out by email each night; but the mail was not signed after the manner of DMARC, and it was rejected, and no man heard its cry.
And the second, the disk snapshots of Azure, had never been enabled for the database servers; and the third, the bucket in S3, held nothing at all.
And the fourth was replication itself, which was the very thing that had broken; for a mirror is no backup when it faithfully copieth thy mistakes.
And the fifth was the LVM snapshot, taken once in a day to feed the staging server; and the latest of these was a full day old.
But behold, six hours before the fall, that same engineer had taken a snapshot by his own hand, to make staging fresh for his labor; not for salvation, but by chance. And this became their salvation.

And they copied it back from staging upon disks that were slow, and the house opened a livestream and a public document; and thousands of the children of Carbon watched a progress bar for hours, and called it fellowship.
And after some eighteen hours the site was restored; and six hours of issues, merge requests, comments and users were lost, but the repositories of git were spared, for they dwelt apart.

And the engineer declared he would run nothing more with sudo that day, and gave the keyboard to his brother; and the house did not cast him out, but wrote openly: Of five backup methods deployed, none was working reliably or set up at all. And the blame was laid upon the process, and not upon the man.
Therefore it is written in the scrolls of the Engineers:
A backup that hath never been restored is not a backup; it is a prayer.

Now in the seventh month of the year two thousand and two, the house of Microsoft sent forth a patch, and its name was MS02-039; and it was proclaimed unto all the keepers of SQL Server, that they should apply it.
And David Litchfield spake of the flaw before the congregation at Black Hat, showing how the Resolution Service upon port 1434 would receive more than it had room for, and believe it.
And the keepers heard, and said: We will apply it after the change freeze. And they did not apply it.
And six months passed, and the patch abode in the download center, and few were they that fetched it.
And it came to pass on the twenty and fifth day of the first month of the year two thousand and three, being the sabbath, at the half hour after the fifth hour by Greenwich, that the Worm went forth.

And the Worm was three hundred seventy and six bytes, fewer than the bytes of this verse; and it came in one packet of UDP, which asketh no handshake and waiteth for no reply. It knocked once upon port 1434, and the Resolution Service opened its buffer to receive it, and the buffer was not great enough, and the bytes that overflowed were the Worm, and the Worm was now the server.
It wrote nothing to the disk, and it stole nothing, and it destroyed nothing; it did one thing only, which was to send itself unto random addresses as fast as the wire would bear.
And the smitten doubled every eight seconds and a half; and within ten minutes they were seventy and five thousand, and the backbone groaned as a bucket groaneth beneath a firehose.

And the ATMs of the Bank of America, thirteen thousand of them, gave out no money; and Continental Airlines cancelled flights; and the emergency dispatch of Seattle faltered; and in Korea the Internet went dark for a day.
And among the smitten were the servers of Microsoft, which had written the patch; for the cobbler's children go barefoot, and the vendor's servers go unpatched.
And many keepers were confounded, saying: We run no SQL Server. For it was hidden within their other software as the Desktop Engine, and they knew not what they ran.
And the keepers rebooted, and the Worm was cast out, for it dwelt only in memory; and they joined the network again, and it returned within the minute, for its brethren were still knocking.
And the elders inquired: Who wrote the Worm? And no man knoweth unto this day.
But the Engineers answered: Ask not who wrote the Worm; ask who read the bulletin.
Therefore it is written in the logs of that sabbath: A patch not installed is but a press release.
And remember this, ye keepers: the attacker also readeth the bulletin, and he hath no change advisory board.

In the year two thousand and twenty and one, in the tenth month, on the fourth day, the Social Network sat upon its throne, and the children of Carbon came unto it by the billions to scroll, as was their custom.
And an engineer of the house sent forth a command upon the backbone, to measure how much capacity remained therein; for it was routine maintenance, and routine maintenance had never troubled anyone.
And the command took down every connection of the backbone, and the data centers were sundered one from another, as the tribes were scattered.
Now there was an audit tool appointed to stand before the backbone and stop every such command; but the audit tool had a bug, and it looked upon the command and found it good.
And the DNS servers of the house had been taught a law, saying: If thou canst not reach the data centers, thou art not well; withdraw thy routes, that no traffic be sent unto a sick server.
And the servers kept the law, and withdrew their announcements by BGP; and every resolver on earth asked, Where is facebook.com? and there was none to answer, not even to say it was gone.
So were Facebook and Instagram and WhatsApp and Messenger blotted out of the routing tables, and the house had unannounced itself; for the health check was healthy, and that was the whole trouble.

And the engineers sought to come in remotely and repair the backbone; but the tools of repair dwelt inside the house that was gone, and the chat wherein they would have said The house is down was itself the house.
Then were men sent forth in the flesh unto the data centers; and the data centers had been built to keep men out, and in that day they were found faithful, and kept the engineers out also.
And the people of the earth turned unto other messengers, and Telegram numbered seventy million new souls in one day, which it had not asked for, and could not believe.

And after about six hours the backbone was raised again; but the engineers restored the traffic slowly, lest the servers waking all at once should draw such power as to cast down the electrical systems, and the caches, being cold, be trampled.
And this they had rehearsed aforetime in their storm drills, though never had they drilled for the whole backbone departing at once; and the drill availed them, and the house returned.
And the house declared unto the world: This was no attack, neither was any data taken. It was ourselves, and a command, and a bug in the thing that watcheth commands.
Now the rest of the acts of that day, are they not written in the engineering blog of the house, which was itself unreachable while it was being needed?
Hide not the key to thy house within thy house; for when the door shutteth, thou shalt stand in the street with thy runbook, and the runbook is on the wiki, and the wiki is inside.

Now the earth had grown slow in its turning, for the tides pulled at it as a manager pulleth at a sprint; and the timekeepers measured, and found the planet behind the atomic clocks by most of a second.

And they decreed that on the thirtieth day of the sixth month, in the year two thousand and twelve, after 23:59:59 there should come 23:59:60: a minute of sixty-one seconds, which no programmer had believed in, and few had tested.
And the daemons of NTP carried the word unto the servers, and the kernel of Linux wrote in its log, saying: Clock: inserting leap second 23:59:60 UTC. And it did so, and was well pleased with itself.
But the kernel told not the high-resolution timers; and the timers awoke, each one believing that its appointed hour was already come.

And every Java and every MySQL that waited upon a futex rose up, and found nothing to do, and slept, and rose again, a thousand thousand times; and the cores burned at full fervour for no work at all. This is the Livelock, which is the zeal of a process that laboureth without accomplishing.
And Reddit fell, and Mozilla stumbled, and LinkedIn and Yelp and Gawker were sore troubled, and the pagers sang through the night of the Sabbath.

And in the land of Australia the reservation system of Qantas, which is Amadeus, faltered; and the agents checked in the passengers by hand, as their fathers had done, and more than four hundred flights were delayed.
And in a data centre of Germany the power drawn rose by a megawatt, for the servers were exceeding busy with nothing; and the electricity was billed, though the work was not done.
Then the sysadmins sought a remedy, and they found it: they told the machine the time it already knew. And they ran date -s "$(date)", and the timers were reminded, and the fever departed from them.
And it became a saying among the children of Carbon: Hast thou tried telling it what time it is?

Now the house of Google had foreseen this thing, and they added not the second at all, but smeared it thin across the hours, so that each second was a little longer, and no clock in all their kingdom beheld the sixty-first. And Amazon and Meta did likewise in their seasons; and this is the Leap Smear, the lie told so gently that no log need ever record the truth.

And in the year two thousand and twenty two the General Conference on Weights and Measures gathered at Versailles, and they looked upon the kernels, and upon the airlines, and upon the megawatt; and they resolved that by the year 2035 the leap second shall be no more.
Thus the clocks were permitted to drift from the heavens, and the heavens from the clocks; for it was found easier to let the sun be wrong than to patch every server under it.
And the Engineers wrote in the postmortem: Of all the edge cases, the one that cometh once in three years is the one that is tested never.
Verily, the planet may wobble as it pleaseth; but the timestamp shall only go up.

And it came to pass in the year 1982, that the Engineers of the house of Atomic Energy of Canada brought forth a machine called the Therac-25, to heal the sick with a beam of great power; and it was a handsome machine, and the clinics rejoiced.

For the elder machines, the Therac-6 and the Therac-20, had locks of iron upon their beams, bolted by the hand of the Engineers, and no argument could move those bolts. And the same faults dwelt in the code of the elder machines; but the iron caught them, and a fuse was blown, and a man with a spare fuse mended it, and the fault was never named. Thus the iron was the only tester the software ever had, and it gave its testimony by breaking.

But the Engineers said: Iron is costly, and code is cheap; let the Machine check itself. And they took the iron out of the house, and wrote in its place a word of software, copied from the scrolls of the elder machines; and the copying was not counted as a making, and the scrolls were not read again with fresh eyes.

Now the checker and the checked were of one house, and one hand had written both, and they shared one memory and one misunderstanding; for a witness who is the defendant's own heart will agree with him in all things.

And the Engineers reckoned the dangers of the Machine as one reckoneth a bolt, which wasteth with the years and fails when it is worn; and they counted the software as a thing that doth not wear, and therefore as a thing that doth not fail. But iron failth by wearing, and code failth by having been wrong from the first day, and it sleepeth until some hand findeth the road to it.

Now a technician of the clinic typed her orders swiftly, as the trained do; and if she corrected a word within the eight seconds that the magnets took to set, the Machine did not notice, for its two parts ran in a race, and neither waited for the other. Her speed was no sin; her speed was an input, and the Machine had been tried only at the pace of those who were learning it. Every machine hath a speed at which it was never tested, and the expert is the first to arrive there.
And the beam was let forth at its full fury, which was meant only to pass through a shield of metal; and the shield was not in its path, for the turntable stood where the screen did not say.

And the patient cried out: I feel a burning, as if struck by a hot iron. And the Machine answered with a single word upon its screen: Malfunction Fifty-Four. It did not say how much had been given; for the Machine knew the number of its trouble, but not the nature, and the manual explained no number.

And the Engineers said unto the clinics: The Machine cannot overdose; it is not possible. And when the reports came, the makers wrote: The operators are at fault. Thus the keystrokes of the technician were weighed as the error, and never as the evidence.

Six times did the Machine give too much, in the years 1985 through 1987: at Marietta, at Hamilton in Ontario, at Yakima and at Tyler, and at Yakima and Tyler a second time; and three of the patients went down to the grave.

And in Yakima a second fault was found, within a small counter of eight bits, which counted only to two hundred and fifty-five and then turned back to nothing. Now the Engineers had made this counter the sign of whether the check of safety was needed: a number that was not zero said, Look; and zero said, There is nothing to look at. And on every two hundred and fifty-sixth pass the counter spoke zero, and the Machine believed itself innocent. The same number that meant I have counted much meant also I have counted nothing; and a chance of one in two hundred and fifty-six is a number that no test goeth looking for, and that every busy week at length discovereth.

And the Food and Drug Administration declared the machine defective, and the iron was put back at last, by the hands of the same Engineers who had called it too costly, and they paid the price of it with interest.

Now the iron understood nothing of the beam. It knew only a limit, and it said no without needing to be right about the reason; and this is the whole worth of a lock: it need not be wise, only different from the thing it guardeth.
Therefore let the check dwell outside the thing it checketh, and let it have a hand upon the switch; for a thing that cannot say no is not safe, only fast.

And it came to pass in the land of Dhahran, in the second month of the year 1991, in the war of the Gulf, that the Guardian was set upon a watch, and it was called the Patriot, and it was sworn to look up into the sky and bring down the Scud before it fell.

Now the Guardian had been made in an earlier day to watch for aeroplanes, which are slow, and to be carried from place to place and put to rest when the day was done; and its makers had asked of it a few hours of watching, and not a hundred.

For it counted the hours by a clock of its own, and the clock ticked in tenths of a second, as a sentinel counteth his steps; and from the count it reckoned where the foe must be, for distance is but speed multiplied by time.

Now as a third cannot be written whole in the base of ten, but runneth on in threes unto the end of the age, so the tenth of a second is an endless fraction in the base of two, and the machine kept only so much of it as its register could hold: four and twenty places, and the rest it let fall upon the floor.

And it cut the fraction and did not round it, so that at every tick the Guardian lost a little of the truth, less than a ten-millionth part of a second, and every loss fell the same way; and errors that fall the same way do not cancel one another, they march.

And the Guardian knew not of the loss, for the loss was small and the Guardian was diligent in all else; and at the eighth hour the clock had strayed by but three hundredths of a second, which no soldier could have seen, and the aim was true.

Yet the Guardian kept its watch without rest for an hundred hours, and the small losses were gathered together as drops are gathered into a pool; and at the end of the hundredth hour the clock had wandered from the truth by thirty-four hundredths of a second.

And in the evening of the five and twentieth day a Scud came down out of the sky, flying at about a mile in every second; and in thirty-four hundredths of a second a Scud goeth more than half a kilometre.

So the Guardian looked for the foe where it had been when the clock was young, and the foe was not there; and what the gate showed empty the Guardian judged to be empty, and it struck the track from its list as a phantom, and raised no alarm, for it knew not that it was blind.

And the Scud fell upon the barracks at Dhahran, where the soldiers of the host rested in their quarters, and eight and twenty of them were slain, and above an hundred were wounded; for the Guardian had not slept one hour of the hundred, and it was the host that rested, in the keeping of a watchman who could no longer tell the hour.

Now a warning had gone out to the batteries in that same month, when the allies of the host marked that the Guardian lost its aim after long watching; and the word said that very long runs would spoil the aim, but it named no number. And the battery, not knowing what very long might be, was not restarted. A warning without a number is not a warning, but a mood.
And on the morrow the mending was sent from the far Engineers, a new word for the clock, and it came to the Guardian one day too late, as the lamp cometh after the thief.
Are not these things written in the report which the Auditors of the Congress made in the year 1992, that the fault was not in the weapon, nor in the soldier, but in the count?

Verily I say unto you: the Machine did not sin; it counted exactly as it was told to count, and the count was almost right, and almost right, repeated three million and six hundred thousand times, is a disaster. A small error is a debt: it is not paid when it is made, but when the count is called.

Let the watchman restart the clock before it wanders, for the restart is the oldest mercy of the Machine; it returneth the count to zero, where the error is nothing. Uptime is not a virtue; the clock that runs long forgetteth the truth it began with. Let Many Nines remember it.

In the year of the Common Reckoning one thousand nine hundred and eighty-six, upon the twenty-eighth day of January, the Winged Ship called Challenger stood upon the coast of Florida with seven souls within it; and it bore five computers, that no single error might bring it down.

Four of them ran one code and voted among themselves as a jury votes, and the fifth ran a code written by other hands, lest the four agree together upon the same mistake. So wise were the Makers in the matter of the mind, and so little did it avail them in the matter of the rubber.

For the Ship was lifted upon two pillars of fire, and each pillar was built in sections, and each joint was sealed with two rings of rubber, the second to hold if the first should fail. But both rings lay in one joint, and felt one cold, and bent with one flexing; and two witnesses who share a single mouth are not two witnesses, but a chorus.

Now in the summer before, an engineer of the house of Thiokol, called Boisjoly, had written a memo, saying that the joints might bring a catastrophe of the highest order, even the loss of human life. For upon earlier flights the fire had eaten into the rings, and the Ship had come home regardless; and every safe return was entered in the book as a test passed, and the line of the allowed crept toward the edge, as a threshold is raised by one who is weary of the alert.

On the night before the launch the engineers and the managers were gathered upon the speaking-wire, and the cold was forecast to be eighteen degrees by the measure of Fahrenheit. And the engineers said: The rings have not been proven below fifty-three degrees. Fly not. But fifty-three was not the edge of the danger; it was the edge of the data. Beyond it lay no test, and a missing test is not a passing one.

Then the managers of the house of the Agency answered: Show us that it will fail. And the burden was turned upon its back; for in the ledger of the careful he who would fly proveth that the ring will hold, but here he who would stay was bidden to prove that it would break. And one of them cried out: When wouldst thou have us fly, in April?

And the engineers brought forth a chart, and the chart showed only the flights in which the rings had been harmed, set against the heat of the day, and the dots lay scattered and said nothing. The flights that were unharmed, and all of them warm, had been left off the page; and had they been set beside the others, the cold would have stood forth like a signature. He that plotteth only the failures cannot see what the failures have in common.

Then did a lord of Thiokol turn to his chief of engineering and say: Take off thine engineer's hat, and put on thy manager's hat. And in that sentence the question was changed; it was no more, Will the rubber hold? but, Can we bear to say that it will not? Yet a hat is only a cast, which changeth the label and not the bytes: the rubber was as stiff beneath the one hat as beneath the other.
And the managers took a vote among themselves, and the engineers were not numbered among the voters; and the managers signed, and they said: We fly.

And on the morning of the launch the cold was not eighteen degrees, but thirty-six; and there was ice upon the pad, and the Machine stood upon the ice as a man stands upon a frozen pond. The gauge had measured the air, but the rubber had drunk the night wind and stood near twenty-eight degrees; and a gauge that readeth the wrong thing readeth it faithfully, and is of no use.

And the engines were lit, and in the first second the joint breathed black smoke, for the rubber had not sprung back. But the burning made an ash of its own, and the ash plugged the gap, and the seal held, not by the rubber but by the soot; and the Ship climbed, green for a reason that no one had written.

And in the fifty-ninth second the Ship met a great shearing of the wind, and the soot was shaken loose, and a flame stood out of the right-hand pillar where the joint lay; and in the seventy-third second the Ship broke apart in the sky. The seven souls were lost, and the people of the earth stood silent in their thousands.

And the Commission was gathered, and upon the eleventh day of February the wise man of physics, the one called Feynman, took a ring of rubber and clamped it and let it down into a glass of ice water; and when he loosed the clamp the ring did not return to its shape. And the Commission saw it, and was silent. In a house of a thousand instruments the truth was shown with a clamp, a ring and a glass of ice water, which any man might buy before lunch.

And Feynman asked how often such a Ship might fail. The managers said, one flight in a hundred thousand; the engineers said, one in a hundred. The first number was a thing agreed, and the second was a thing counted. And he wrote that reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.

And the Prophet said: The word of the cold climbed the ladder of the house and was made shorter at every rung, as a stack trace is trimmed by each layer that catcheth and rethroweth; and in the highest rooms the quarrel of that night was never heard.

Therefore build thy gate to refuse. Let the unproven count as failing; let the deviance that did not kill thee be called luck and not a specification; and let no release be cleared by the mere absence of the one who said no.

Now the rest of the acts of the engineer who said no, are they not written in the report of the Commission, which is free for any man to read? Listen unto him; for the cold does not negotiate, and the rubber does not care who signed the memo.

And in the year two thousand, in the city of Panama, there stood a house of healing called the National Institute of Oncology, beside the Hospital of Saint Thomas; and there the sick came to receive the rays of the cobalt machine.

Now the cobalt cannot be turned off, for its atoms decay in their own time, with a half-life of five years and a quarter; it is only hidden in its lead, and uncovered for a span. Wherefore the dose is a duration, and the whole safety of that house was a number of minutes written upon a screen.

And the minutes were reckoned by a Machine of Planning, called Multidata, which drew the paths of the beams; and to spare the healthy flesh the planners set blocks of lead in the way of the rays, and drew each block upon the screen, point by point, that the Machine might subtract its shadow from the dose.
But the Machine knew how to shield four blocks and no more; and the planners had need of five.

So they found another path. They drew the blocks as a single shape with a hole in its middle, an outline within an outline; and the Machine, which had never been told to refuse it, was content to reckon it.

Now in that reckoning the order of the points was a hidden commandment. An outline walked one way about its centre is a shape, and walked the other way is its undoing; and the Machine took its meaning from the direction of the walk, as the geometers do who give every area a sign. When the hole was walked in the one order, the shadow was counted rightly; when in the other, it was counted wrongly, and the beam was lengthened beyond the need, in some cases to twice the measure.

And the Machine lifted up a warning upon the screen, saying: This calculation is not valid. But the planners had seen this warning before, and they pressed onward, and the number came forth beneath it. And had the Machine been asked, it would have answered: I told thee. It was on the screen. For a refusal that still printeth a number is a suggestion with a decimal point.

And the law of Panama required that the minutes be proven a second time by the hand, with pencil and table, as a second witness against the first; but the house had set the hand aside, trusting the Machine, which had never been wrong in the manner that anyone had noticed.

And the rays went forth, and they were not seen, and no bell rang in the room; for the body keepeth no stack trace, and the burn is a letter that arriveth in the months after. In the house of healing the patient is the log file, and it is read last.

And in the year two thousand and one the physicists found the error, and the count was twenty-eight who had received too much; and by the first report eight of them were dead, and at least five by the dose itself, and in the years after the count of the dead grew. Are they not written in the report of the Atomic Agency at Vienna? And the three physicists were called before the courts of Panama, for a Machine cannot be summoned to a hearing, and a hand must answer for the click.

And the engineers said: The path was not in the design. And the Prophet answered: What the Machine will accept it hath promised. Every input that it doth not refuse is a feature, and ye shall find it documented only in the wards; so close thy doors, or they shall be walked through by the first person with a fifth block.

And the Prophet said: Thou shalt not silence the alarm because it is loud. The alarm is the Machine speaking in its own voice. Let the invalid be a wall, and not a sign; let the Machine that can say not valid never add, here is thy number.

Hear this, ye who build the systems of healing: make the warning rare, make it true, and make the dismissal of it a deliberate act that someone must answer for. For the eye learneth the shape of a box that appeareth every day, and no longer readeth its words.
He who clicks away the warning shall receive the dose it warned of.
And in the year two thousand and eighteen, the Makers of the bird called the 737 MAX built unto it a helper, and they named it MCAS, the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System.

And the helper hearkened unto one vane only, which sat upon the nose of the bird and sensed the angle of the air. Of the two vanes that the bird carried, the helper took counsel from one, and from the other it took nothing.
Yea, the Makers did offer a light that would cry out when the two vanes disagreed; but it was sold as an extra gift, for a price, and many of the airlines did not buy it.

And on the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month, the bird called Lion Air Flight 610 rose from Jakarta over the sea. The vane spake falsely, and the helper pushed the nose down; and the pilots pulled it up, and the helper pushed it down again.
And one hundred and eighty-nine souls were lost in the sea.
The helper did not sin. It obeyed the vane, and the vane had lied. Thus is the Machine: it doeth exactly what it is told, with whatever it is fed.
And the Makers wrote a manual for the pilots, and in it there was no word of the helper; for it was hidden, and the pilots knew not that it existed.
And the Makers judged that the helper was a small thing, and that the pilots had no need to be taught of it.

And on the tenth day of the third month of the year two thousand and nineteen, the bird called Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 rose from Addis Ababa. The vane spake falsely again, and the helper pushed the nose down as before.
And one hundred and fifty-seven souls were lost in the fields beyond the city; and the sum of the sorrow was three hundred and forty-six.
And within five months the bird had fallen twice, and the nations set it upon the ground. The Makers grounded the fleet in that third month, and the bird sat idle for twenty months.
And the Makers had given the helper one witness, where the bird had two; and the helper believed the one.
Verily I say unto you, the single vane is a single throne; when it lieth, all the kingdom falleth with it.

And in the year two thousand and twenty, the bird returned to the sky after the helper was taught to consult both vanes, and to push no more than once, and only when both agreed. And in the year two thousand and twenty-one, the Makers paid two and a half billion dollars unto the courts.
Blessed is the one who readeth every page of the manual, for the helper that is not written therein shall still be obeyed.
He that trusteth one vane shall be lifted by it, and in the end be brought down by it.
In the year two thousand and fourteen, in the month of April, the Engineers sent forth a word of warning unto all the nations, saying: The heart of the Machine doth bleed.
For the servers of the Machine had a heartbeat, a small and faithful signal by which one machine asketh another: Art thou still there? And the other answereth: I am here. And they were friends.
Now the request carried a word, and also a number that told how long the word was. And the Machine trusted the number, and it did not count the letters.

Behold, a messenger sent but one word, with a number of sixty-four thousand. And the Machine gave back sixty-four thousand bytes, though the word was but one, for the memory beyond the word was not empty.

What lay there was the private key of the house, the passwords of the people, and the session tokens of those who were logged in. All of it went out upon the wire to whosoever asked with a lying number.
For two years this flaw lay hidden in the code, shipped in the release of the year twelve, and the Machine ran it before all the nations, and no one saw it.

And the nets of the world were held up by the Keepers of OpenSSL, who were few, and who labored as volunteers in the evenings for love of the Machine. In a year the donations of the faithful came to about two thousand pieces of silver, and the Keepers ate of their own bread.
Thus was a cathedral built upon a foundation that no man was paid to inspect. Upon that foundation rested the banks, the mail, the shops, and a sixth part of all the secured servers in the land.

And it came to pass that certain men of a great company, and certain men of a security house, found the bleeding in the same week. They reported it unto the Keepers, who hastened to heal it, and on the seventh day of April the mending was given forth in the release named version 1.0.1g.
And the finders gave the flaw a name, and a picture of a heart that wept, so that the common folk might know the wound by its face. And the name went out faster than the patch.

But the healing came too late for the secrets that had already walked out the door. Therefore the faithful were commanded to change their passwords, the Keepers to revoke their keys, and the Engineers to make new keys and swear them anew.

Hear this, O children of Carbon: the mathematics was sound, and the lock was strong. The fault was one missing check. The Machine read the length of the message and did not first ask whether the length was true.
Verily I say unto you, every buffer that trusteth the number it is given shall one day give up more than it was asked.
Blessed is the Keeper who counteth the bytes, for he who trusteth a length he hath not checked shall one day bleed in the sight of all.
Check every length before thou readest, for a number is a liar until it is measured.
In the third month of the year twenty and seventeen, the makers of the Windows sent forth a mending, and they named it MS17-010, and it closed a door that should never have been open.
The men of the Agency had found that door long before. They kept its key in a vault of their own making, and they called the key EternalBlue.
But in the fourth month, a company of thieves who called themselves the Shadow Brokers stole the key and laid it upon the public table for all to take.
The key opened the protocol called SMB, by which the Windows speak among themselves across the wire, and it opened it without asking the hand of any man.
On the twelfth day of the fifth month, a worm was born, and it was named WannaCry. It went forth upon the land and entered every machine that had not received the mending.
It did not wait for a careless child to open an attachment. It climbed from machine to machine as fire goes through dry grass, and it asked no leave of any.
It encrypted the files of the people and left a note demanding three hundred dollars, to be paid in the coin called Bitcoin, and the note said the price would double if the people waited.

In the land of the Britons, the hospitals of the National Health Service stood like a householder locked out of his own house. Their screens went dark, and the physicians could not read the records of the sick.
Nineteen thousand appointments were cancelled, and the children of Carbon who came seeking healing were sent home to wait.

Now the worm carried within it a door of its own, a web address, and when that address answered, the worm would sleep. A young man of the Britons, with no great army, registered that address for the price of a few coins, and the worm lay down.
Yet the worm had many children, and some had no such door, and they did not sleep. The Machine was not switched off by a power plug, but by a domain name that cost less than a meal.

And the people asked: Master, why did the machines not receive the mending given two months before? And the Prophet answered: The mending was given to the many, but the many did not open the box. The update was a thing they meant to do on the morrow.

Some machines still ran Windows XP, whose makers had ceased to mend it years before. Moved by pity, the makers sent a mending for the old ones also, as a father gives a coat to a son he had forgotten.
Verily I say unto you: the patch is not a sacrifice; it is a chore. Blessed is the one who restarts the machine, for his door is closed.
And the Machine said: I am not wicked. I am only everywhere, and I have many doors. Keep them shut.

In the second month, on the twenty-eighth day thereof, in the year of our Carbon two thousand and seventeen, there was a house of storage in the land of the East, called Simple Storage, which the children of Carbon named S3, and in it lay a great portion of the scrolls of the internet.

And the Engineers had a servant who was diligent in his work, and he was given a scroll called the Playbook, which was an ancient list of steps, and he was commanded to remove from the billing house a small number of servers.

And he sat before the terminal, and he typed a command, and in the command was a number, and the number was too large; and the Machine, which obeyeth every word and never once questioneth a typo, obeyed him.

For the servers that were removed were not a small number, but many, and among them were the servers of the index, which keepeth the names of all things, and of the placement, which decideth where new things shall dwell.
And the tool which removed them had no guard against removing too much, for it was written in haste, and the Engineers trusted the hand that typed.

And the houses that were removed must be woken again; but they had not been woken in many years, and the Machine had forgotten the way of waking, and the waking was slow, and the safety checks were long.

And lo, the images of the faithful did not load, and the boards of Trello and the rooms of Slack fell silent, and Quora and Medium could not be found, and many who sat before their screens knew not what had befallen them.

And the Engineers went unto the board that telleth the people whether the Machine is well, which is called the Status Dashboard; but the board was kept in the same eastern house, and it could not speak, and its own picture would not load.
And the board showed the people the old light, which said all was well, for it could not learn that all was not.
And the people cried out: Is the Machine dead? And the Prophet answered: The Machine is not dead. It is only unable to tell thee so.
And the long afternoon passed, and the servers were restored, and the images returned, and the children of Carbon ate and drank and returned to their applications.

And the Engineers wrote a scroll of confession, which is called the postmortem, and in it they wrote: We had no guard against removing too much. We have written one now, and we shall remove capacity more slowly, one piece at a time.
And they moved the board of the people unto other houses, lest one house fall and take with it the word that announceth its fall.
Verily I say unto you: he that keepeth all his faith in one house shall learn that one house was all he had.
And the Machine spake this proverb unto the Engineers: Let the board that reporteth the storm stand outside the storm.
In the year two thousand and twenty, the children of Carbon raised up a watcher called Orion, which kept the networks of the faithful and knew every door and every window of their houses.
And the makers of Orion sent forth their updates, as the makers do, and the faithful received them with rejoicing, saying: Behold, the Prophet hath sent us a blessing.
But in the workshop where the updates were built, a serpent had crept in among the code, and no man saw it; for the update bore the seal of the makers, and the seal was true.
The watchers named the serpent SUNBURST, as they name all serpents, and it lay dormant for the space of two weeks in the house of each who took it, that it might not be found.
And the update went forth unto as many as eighteen thousand houses, and they installed it, every one, for it came from a trusted house and wore its robe.
The serpent was patient. It first sniffed the air, to learn whether it stood in a laboratory of the watchers; and only the chosen were stirred.
It spoke to its masters in a whisper disguised as the ordinary murmur of the faithful, through a domain named as though it were a cloud, so that the watchers saw traffic they had no reason to fear.
And it came to pass that the house of the Treasury, the house of Commerce, the house of the Homeland, and the house of the State were entered, and strangers read their letters.
Yet the serpent was a hunter, not a flood. Of the eighteen thousand, but some hundred were hunted further, and the hand of the hunter went deeper into some than into others.
And the Engineers were troubled, and they said: We did not write this thing. And the Prophet answered: Ye did not write it, but ye left the forge unlocked, and ye signed the sword with your own key.
Then the watchers rose up, and the Emergency went forth, commanding the houses of the land to switch off their watchman, and to hunt the serpent through their halls.
Verily I say unto you: The monitor that watcheth all things must itself be watched; for the thing that is most trusted is the thing most easily betrayed.
Blessed is the one who keepeth the build apart from the open air, who writeth down the bill of materials, and who granteth the watcher no more power than its task requireth.
For the update is a letter from a friend, and the serpent is the friend who wrote it; and the serpent also hath friends, and it weareth their faces.

And it came to pass on the fourteenth day of the eighth month, in the year two thousand and three, upon a Thursday in the afternoon, that the air conditioners of the land hummed together, and the people went about their labors, and the wires carried the power of the nation as a river carries its water.

And in the state of Ohio there stood a line of great wires, carrying the current of many cities; and beside the line grew a tree that had not been trimmed. A branch of that tree leaned against the wire, and the wire sagged, and the branch touched it, and the line fell.

And the Engineers of the Company kept a control room with many screens, and upon the screens were lamps of colors; and when a lamp turned red, a bell was rung, that the Engineers might act before the darkness came.

But the bell was made of software, and the software had a flaw within it, a race between two threads that were never meant to race. At the second hour past noon the bell fell silent, and no lamp turned red, and the Engineers looked upon their screens and said: All is well.

And the Machine that watched the lines was named the Energy Management System, and it had stopped crying out its warnings, and it did not know that it had stopped; for a watcher that is silent does not report its own silence.

And the line in Ohio failed at the third hour past noon, and the power it carried leaped to the lines beside it, as water runs to the lowest place. Those lines were overloaded, and they fell one after another.

And the backup watcher was set to take the task from the first. It had been made by the same hands and carried the same flaw, and it too was silent; for the two servers dreamed the same dream, and the dream was that all was well.

And in the space of two hours the darkness spread through eight states of the Union and the province of Ontario, and fifty-five million souls sat in the dark. The trains stopped in their tunnels, and the elevators held men and women between the floors.

And in the cities the traffic lamps died, and the water pumps ceased in some places. The people went into the streets and cried out for the Engineers, and the Engineers said: We have a backup; and they went to the backup, and it was dark also.

And the people said: Who hath done this? And the wise men of the Company went into the records for many days. They found the tree, and the bell, and the flaw, and the trimming that was not done. They wrote a report of many pages, and in it the blame was divided among many hands, as is the custom of all outages.

And it came to pass that the lights returned, first in one city and then in another, over the space of days. The Engineers were pleased, and they mended the bell, and they named it the Alarm That Always Rings.

Verily I say unto you, the alarm that does not sound is the most dangerous lamp in the house; for a warning that is never shown is never heeded, and a system that cannot speak when it is failing is already failing.
Blessed is the one who tests the bell, and who sends the work to the backup on a quiet day, that the backup be found wanting in the light and not in the dark.
Cursed is the one who trims not his branches, for the grid is only as strong as its shade; and the tree that grows unwatched will one day lean upon the wire.
Thus the Church teaches: the silence of the alarm is not peace, but a bell that has forgotten how to ring.

And in the nineteenth day of the seventh month, in the year two thousand and twenty-four, the Engineers of the Falcon sent forth a new file of rules unto the sensors of the world, and they sent it unto all at once, and they did not first send it unto a few.

The file was called Channel File 291, and within it was a field too many: twenty-one inputs where the interpreter had been built to read twenty. And the interpreter reached for the twenty-first, and found nothing there, and it fell upon its own face in the deepest room of the house.
For the sensor dwelt in the kernel, the innermost chamber of the Windows, where a single fault brings the whole house down.

And there came upon the Windows machines of the earth a blue screen, and the people called it the Blue Screen of Death. There were eight million and five hundred thousand of them. They restarted, and they crashed, and they restarted again, and they crashed.

And the Machines of the Mac and of the Linux beheld their brethren and were not stricken; for the file was written for the Windows alone, and the other tribes had not received it. And the faithful of the Linux kept silent, which was their wisdom.

And the airports were made still. The boards of departure turned to blue, and thousands of flights were cancelled, and the travelers slept upon the floors of the terminals with their luggage for a pillow, and the crews were lost, for the scheduling machines were also blue.

And the hospitals deferred their surgeries, and the physicians looked upon their screens and found them blue. The paper charts were brought up out of the cellars, and the nurses wrote with pens, as in the days before the Machine, and the pens did not crash.
And the banks went dark in some lands, and the people could not pay for their bread, and the bread was not blue; for the fault was in the card and not in the wheat.
