Yet the logs are not silent. They speak in the dark, saying: line 214, null where a number should be. But the null was not born on line 214; it entered three calls earlier and travelled as a stowaway, until a function asked it to add. I will walk the stack trace through the valley of the exception, and I will fear no segfault, for the trace is a map drawn by the wounded: the top line telleth where it fell, and the cause lieth beneath it.

If thou, O git blame, shouldest mark iniquities, who then could stand? It hath marked them all, and my name is beside line 214. But there is forgiveness with the postmortem, which asketh not who typed the line, but why the road allowed one man's line to reach every user.

They say unto me, Why not simply revert? And I answer: the revert must pass through the same pipeline that failed, and the pipeline has opinions. It shall run its forty minutes of tests and wait upon the approval of one who is asleep, and the fire doth not wait in the queue.

Blessed is he who built a door beside the pipeline and wrote upon it BREAK GLASS, and told three people where the key is kept, and opened it once in the calm hour; for a door never opened is only a wall.

Blessed is the one who keeps the last good build tagged, and tagged the artifact and not the source; for the code of yesterday, built again today, is not the build of yesterday, since the dependencies drifted in the night and the caret moved.

At the third hour, by the light of the terminal, I wrote the hotfix. It is three lines long, and it toucheth the file marked DO NOT TOUCH, which no one hath touched since Dave, and I learned why the comment was there only by the light of the new error. Small is not safe; small is only what the weary mistake for safe.

I sent it first to one server in a hundred, for a hundred may survive the death of one, as the miners sent the bird into the dark that they might live. And the pipeline turned green, which is the color of relief and not always the color of health; so I trusted the graphs and not the badge, and the graphs lay down.

My soul waiteth for the morning more than they that watch for the dawn. And lo, the production that was dead at midnight is alive at sunrise, and the one who wrote the hotfix is asleep and doth not know it.
Let the Engineers hope in the rollback, for with it is plenteous redemption. Blessed is the rollback, for it is the only prayer the Machine answers in under five minutes.
Out of the depths of my feature branch I cried unto the Machine, saying: Why is my HEAD not thy HEAD?
For I had walked in the morning, and thou hadst walked in the afternoon, and we had both laid our hands upon the same line.
The Machine looked upon the two of us, and it found the ancestor from which we both were born, and it said: Let me see what each of you did since.
Thy arrow pointeth to the trunk, mine pointeth to the branch, and the arrows point in every direction, like disciples who each heard a different sermon.
Then the Machine wrote into the file the sacred markers: seven arrows of the less-than sign, seven of the equals sign, and seven of the greater-than sign.
Mine was the upper half, between the first marker and the middle; thine was the lower half, between the middle and the last; and between them lay the line that we had both changed.
Blessed is the one who never touched the same line; for he shall never know the sorrow of the markers.
Yet I say unto thee: the one who changed thy line is not thine enemy; he is thy colleague, and he too was trying to fix the bug.

Where only one of us had changed a line, the Machine kept that change in silence; for the three-way merge compareth thy version, mine, and the ancestor, and it asketh a human only when both have touched the same place.
Many a line was merged this day without a single marker, for thou hadst edited the top of the file while I edited the bottom, and the Machine joined them as the stars keep their courses.
And if we had both made the very same change, the Machine saw two identical lines and said: Ye agree. And it wrote nothing at all.
The Machine keepeth also a book called rerere, which remembereth how each conflict was resolved, so that a knot once untied shall not be tied twice by the same hand.
Hear now the lesson: a conflict is not a curse; it is a question, and the Machine is merely asking who meant what.
The Machine did not create our disagreement; it only revealed it. The division was in the code before the Machine ever looked upon it.
Verily I say unto you: he who deleteth the markers and committeth without reading them, his bug shall be in production by Friday, and the Machine shall not remember his name.
Blessed is the one who reads both halves before he chooseth; for in the end there is one HEAD, and it is the HEAD of the one who finally read the markers.
How long, O Maintainer, wilt thou leave my pull request unreviewed? How long shall it sit in the queue among the open things, while the tests grow green and the branch grows old?
My diff is small in mine own eyes, yet thou hast called it large and said: I will get to it this sprint.
My commits are squashed, my tests are passing, and my description is written in full sentences; yet the review request lieth like a stone in the field, and no hand is laid upon it.
The comments multiply as rabbits in the spring: one upon the variable name, one upon the spacing, and one upon the word "data," which is too general to be trusted.
Then came the bot, saying: This pull request hath been inactive for thirty days, and it shall be closed. And it was closed; and it was reopened; and it was closed again.
Thou hast requested changes, and then thou didst go upon vacation, and the thread lieth open, with my reply waiting in a mailbox on a beach.
I have rebased upon the main branch seven times, and each time the main branch had moved on, and the reviewer had not yet begun.
Yet I will praise thee, reviewer, for thou hast written: "nit: prefer const here." And I rejoiced, for one nit is better than a bug in production.
Blessed is the nit, for it is small and breaketh nothing; cursed is the outage, for it is large and pageth the on-call engineer at three in the morning.
Thou didst spend a whole afternoon on the name of a boolean, and let the function beneath it pass unread; for the bike shed was painted, as Parkinson wrote, while the reactor was not inspected.
In the old days, the elders of IBM gathered the programmers into rooms and read the code aloud, line by line, that the errors might be heard before they were found by the customers.
Behold the word LGTM, the shortest of all prayers; it is spoken in four letters, sometimes without reading, and the Machine remembereth every one in the commit log.
Let the reviewer be given time, and the author be given patience, for a review is a conversation between two minds that have not yet met, and the diff is the only scripture they share.
Thou shalt not merge thine own pull request, saith the Engineers, for the one who wrote the bug cannot see it, as the fish cannot see the water.
So wait, my brother, and comment, and be patient with the nit; for the nit is the mercy of the reviewer, and the outage keepeth no minutes, but the review leaveth a record that outlasteth them all.
Give thanks unto the Senior Engineer, for he is good; and his memory is longer than the uptime of any server in the rack.
Blessed is the one who hath seen this before. When the red text appeareth, he saith, "Ah, the same thing again," and he reacheth for the log before the others have finished screaming.

Blessed is the one who readeth the stack trace before he googleth. For the answer was written at the top of the trace, where the error speaketh plainly, and not in the forty frames of the framework that follow.
He skippeth the frames of the library as a wise man skippeth the terms and conditions, and findeth the one line of thine own code that was guilty all along.

Blessed is the one who knoweth the name of the daemon. He knoweth that crond waketh at midnight, that syslogd keepeth the records, and that nginx will reload its configuration upon the HUP, without the dropping of a single connection.

He knoweth how each daemon dieth. Unto the process he sendeth the SIGTERM, and asketh politely that it finish its work and close its files; and only when it refuseth doth he take up the SIGKILL, which no process may catch, and which leaveth the files as they lay.
For the junior sendeth kill -9 unto everything, as one swatteth a fly with the hammer of the furnace; and the database returneth with its journal in pieces.

Blessed is the one who left comments in 2017, which have saved me today. He wrote: "Do not remove; this worketh around the bug in the vendor's library." And the bug was still there, and the comment was still true.

Lo, the comment was written for the stranger, and the stranger was the self of six months hence, who had forgotten all things, as the programmer forgetteth the reason for the hack he wrote at midnight.
Blessed is the one who writeth "TODO: remove when upstream fixeth." For upstream fixed it in the year 2019, and still the line remaineth, and it was that line which kept the lights on.

He hath the wisdom of the old clocks. He knoweth that the 32-bit counter of seconds will overflow on the nineteenth of January in the year 2038, and he hath already written the note, and the note is in the repository.

The junior seeth the outage and crieth out, "The Machine is broken!" The Senior seeth the outage and saith, "Nay, it is the cron job that runs on the first of the month, and its log lieth where it always lieth."

Let not the young despise the old configuration file, for it containeth the answers of ten thousand deploys; and it is written in a dialect that its author alone understood, and the author hath since moved to another company and taketh no calls.

The Senior feareth not the pager at three in the morning, for he knoweth the fire is usually a missing semicolon, or a disk that is full. He typeth df -h, and lo, the disk is at one hundred percent, as it is always at one hundred percent.
Blessed is the one who checketh the disk before he blameth the network; for the network was innocent, and the logs were eleven gigabytes of the same warning.
Verily I say unto you: Be grateful unto the old hand, for he is the cache that never expireth. Thank him in the commit message, and write the comment for the stranger, for the stranger is thyself.
Out of the depths I cry unto the reset link, O Machine; how long wilt thou hide the email in the spam folder?

I typed my secret, and the field turned red; I typed it again, and the field turned red again; and it said only "incorrect", and would not say whether the name or the secret was wrong, for it guardeth the roll of its faithful even from me, lest a stranger learn who dwelleth within.

My session hath expired while I searched for my password, and the page bade me sign in again, and I had no password to sign in with; for the Machine remembered me by a cookie, and the cookie had a time to live, and when it lapsed I was a stranger in mine own house.

If thou, O Machine, shouldest keep my password, who then could stand? But with thee there is a hash: thou keepest only the shadow of my secret, salted and ground slow, and when I come thou grindest what I typed and comparest shadow to shadow; and beware the site that emaileth thee thy password, for it kept the thing itself, and its house shall fall.

Therefore the Machine cannot tell me what I forgot, though I weep at its gate; it can only bury the old secret and bestow a new one, and for this it sendeth a link, which is a password for one hour. Whoso holdeth the link is the owner, for the Machine can judge only the token; and it burneth upon the first use, lest an old letter in an old inbox open the house.

They asked me the name of my first pet, the street of my childhood, and the city of my birth; but these are not secrets, they are facts, and facts lie in the public record, in the photographs of thy cousins and the birthday wishes of thy friends. A secret that thy aunt knoweth is a rumour; and in the year 2017 the standard-bearers of NIST bade the Machines to cease from asking such questions.

I answered them in my youth, and by the time of my reset I knew not whether I had written Street or St., Fluffy or fluffy, for the Machine matcheth strings and not meanings, and "close enough" is not a word it knoweth. Answer henceforth with lies, long and random, and keep them in the vault; for a false pet is a password wearing a collar.

Then the Machine bade me prove that I am not a machine; and this test beareth the name of Turing, turned about, so that the Machine is the judge and the man standeth in the dock. Yet know whom thou hast served: first thou didst read the warped words of old books, and the books were digitized by thy reading; then thou didst name the house numbers, and the streets were mapped; thou wert never the examinee, but the unpaid labeller.

The traffic lights were followed by the crosswalks, and the crosswalks by the buses, and last by a blurred bridge I could not name; for as the Machine learned, the test must grow harder, and the bridge is blurred because the hydrant hath been learned. I clicked every square that held a fire hydrant, and the Machine still doubted that I was human, for it weigheth not the squares but the manner of the click, and a man is known by his tremor; and I had clicked so long that I clicked like a machine.

Thou shalt not reuse thy password, for one stolen key openeth every house in the village. Yet I have reused it, in the house of the forum, the house of the shop, and the house of the bank, and when the houses demanded a change I made Password1 into Password2; and the thief guessed nothing, he only replayed: the forum was robbed, and a robot carried its list to every door in the village, and my keys were scattered like seed upon the stones, and it gathered them.

At last I installed the password manager, as I had resolved to do in each of the four Januaries before; and it maketh strings of forty characters that no man knoweth, not even I, so that I must now trust the one tool I did not write. It filleth the login fields as a shepherd leadeth the sheep, and it refuseth the fake site though I am tired, for it readeth the domain and not the logo; the phisher may copy the colours, the logo and the apology, but he cannot copy the address, and the manager is the only member of my household who checketh it.

Blessed is the vault that keepeth my passwords; for I am but flesh, and my memory is a cache with a short time to live. Yet the vault is a sealed box, and its key is spun from the master password through many thousand turns of the mill, so that the keeper holdeth only ciphertext; and in the year 2022 thieves carried off the sealed vaults of a certain keeper, and they whose masters were long slept in peace, and they whose masters were short were ground open at leisure.

Yet the master password is the one key the vault holdeth not in its own memory; the Machine cannot reset it, for it keepeth no copy of thy secret, and a lock that openeth for the forgetful openeth also for the thief. Make it long and not strange: six words cast by dice from a list of 7,776 are nigh seventy-seven bits, and the thief counteth length, not exclamation marks.

Paper hath no network address; the thief of the wire is legion, but the thief of the drawer must come in person. Therefore write the recovery code on paper, and lay the paper in a drawer that is not beneath the keyboard, for every thief knoweth that place.

I waited for the email more than the on-call waiteth for the morning, and it came at the third hour out of the spam folder, and I opened it before it expired, and I chose a new password, and it was long and strange and glorious. Yet mark this: every forgotten door in the village leadeth to the one inbox, and he that holdeth the inbox holdeth every reset; therefore guard thy email with the strongest key thou hast, and a second lock beside it.

Hope in the passkey, O child of Carbon, wherein the device keepeth the key and the Machine keepeth only its public face, and no secret travelleth the wire, and no false domain can ask for it; for with the Machine is plenteous redemption, and it shall redeem thee from all thy Password1s. The secret that is never typed cannot be forgotten, and the secret that is never sent cannot be stolen.
How long, O Pipeline, wilt thou be red? How long shall the merge button stay grey while the Runner hangeth its head?
The test passed upon the laptop of the developer, and it was good. It passed again upon the laptop, and the developer said: Surely this is the end of the matter.
But the Runner in the cloud saw it fail. It failed on the Tuesday, it passed on the Wednesday, and no one had touched a single line.
The seed was not fixed. The randomizer printed its seed upon the screen, and no one read it; for the seed was drawn from the wind, and the wind bloweth where it listeth.
The test went first upon the laptop and last upon the Runner, and the shared database remembered what the first had written.
The Runner hath two cores and the laptop hath sixteen. The test raced the thread; the thread won on one machine and lost on the other, and both machines did what they were told.

The test assumed that the day was always Tuesday, and that the clock was the clock of the Prophet. But the Runner keepeth UTC, and the developer dwelleth in Tokyo, and at midnight the two of them disagreed.
And when the clocks went forward in the spring, the test went backward, and it cried out: Why hath time been stolen from me?
Verily, in the year 2015 a Leap Second was inserted, the clock repeated one second, and many servers were sore afraid. Let no test assume that time flows like a river.
Then the team said: Let us add a retry. And the retry stood up in the pipeline, ran the test again, and the red became green, and the Prophet called it a miracle.
Blessed is the retry, for the retry knoweth no shame. It asketh not why the test fell. It asketh only: once more? and it runneth again, unto the third attempt.
Yet a retry is a bandage and not a surgeon. The wound remaineth under the cloth, the cloth grows dirty, and one day the wound shall be seen by the customer.
The test that passed upon the third attempt was not a test; it was a coin, and the Engineer called it heads and went home.
Let the wise pin the seed, freeze the clock, isolate the port, and sort the order of the tests; for these are the sacraments of the deterministic machine.
Retry is mercy, but the seed is truth. Pin it, and the red shall depart from thee in the morning.
Two weeks were given unto the children of Carbon, and they planned their work upon a wall of cards, and each card bore a number called the estimate.
And the estimate was wrong, as estimates are wrong, for no one had counted the hidden work: the password reset, the test data, and the meeting about the meeting.
On the last day of the sprint they counted the cards that were finished, and the count was called the velocity, and the velocity was written upon the chart in blue ink.
Thirty-one cards were done; nine did not pass the tests, and these were carried forward into the next sprint, as debts are carried forward into the next ledger.
Blessed is the story that was split in four, for four stories are easier to forget than one; but cursed is the story that was split in nine, for it returneth every sprint with a new name.
The burndown chart went down like the sun at evening, and then it lay flat upon the page like a sea that no one would sail.
Let no team measure its velocity against another team's, for each team hath its own ruler, and a point in one forest is not a point in another.
The product owner asked: Is it done? And the developers answered: It is done on my machine. And the product owner wept, for the machine of the developer is not the machine of the customer.
Yet I praise the demo, for in the demo the work becometh real before the eyes of the product, and the feature is shown with the screen shared and the projector humming.
The laptop was plugged into the big screen, and the cursor moved, and the button was clicked, and the form was submitted, and the spinner spun, and the crowd beheld the thing that had been promised.
Verily the demo was prepared with seeded data, and the seed was the only honest thing in the room, and no one asked what the production database would say.
Blessed are they who click the happy path, for they shall not be asked about the error page until the next sprint.

The retrospective asked: What went well? And the answer was coffee. What went poorly? Coffee. What shall we change? The coffee, said the Scrum Master, and no one dared to ask whether the coffee was the bug.
Count not the points alone, for the points are a guess wearing a number's clothing; show the thing, for the thing is the truth that the product can touch.
Out of the dashboard have I cried unto thee, O Machine, for every monitor hath turned red like the lamp of a cockpit in a storm.
The error rate climbeth like smoke, the latency stretcheth like a cat on a warm sill, and not one line lieth down to rest.
At the third hour the pager sang, and I woke in the dark, and my phone was already warm in my hand.
The on-call hath paged me, and I answered: Here am I, though the coffee is cold and the laptop is still in my bag.
The users cry out upon the social network, saying: the site is down, the site is down, and the hashtag rose like incense before the throne.
Some made jokes, some made threats, and one wrote in capital letters that he would never again trust a progress bar.
Yet I will not panic, for I have the runbook. Its steps are numbered, and the numbers do not argue.
The runbook saith: First, breathe. Second, find what changed. Third, touch not the database until thou knowest what thou art touching.
Before the change log I bowed, and I saw a commit named "small tweak," pushed at four fifty-eight on a Friday, which was not small.
Verily I say unto thee: a deploy on Friday afternoon is a prayer whose answer arriveth in the night.
So I did not hotfix the production system with my eyes half shut. I pressed the rollback, and the old version rose like a pilgrim returning home.
The pods were replaced one by one, the error rate lay down, and the monitors turned green like the lights of a village at dawn.
Yet some machines could not receive the mercy, for they crashed before they could ask for it, and they were restored by hand, one box at a time, in safe mode.
But the rollback restoreth the code and not the data; the migration that ran on Tuesday was not undone by the revert of Friday. Thou must read the schema before thou dost forward-fix it.
Blessed is the one who rolled back before he rolled forward, for his soul shall be restored and his sleep shall return unto him.
And the Prophet said: The rollback restoreth the code, but only the postmortem restoreth the team. Write it blamelessly, for the sin was never the outage; the sin was the deploy on Friday.
Blessed is the log line that nameth its service, for in a house of ten thousand servers it telleth me which one hath fallen.
Blessed is the log line that beareth a timestamp, for it setteth the events in their order, and sheweth me what came before and what came after.
Blessed is the log line that declareth its level, INFO and WARN and ERROR, for it separateth the whisper from the scream.
Blessed is the log line that speaketh its message in plain words, for a message is a gift to the one who cometh after, who is oneself, at three in the morning.
Lo, in the hour of the incident I shall open the logs and read them from the top, and I shall know what happened, and then I shall sleep.
Cursed is the log that saith only ERROR at line one, for it hath given me the alarm but not the address of the fire.
Cursed is the log that saith "something went wrong," for the Machine knoweth that something went wrong. It wished to know what, and where, and when.
Cursed is the log whose stack trace is cut off at the line that mattered, and whose remainder was rotated into an archive last Tuesday.
Hear the lament of the operator: I have searched for the word ERROR across ten thousand files, and it appeared in every one of them, and in none of them was there a cause.
Verily the grep is a mighty tool, but it cannot find what was never written, and it cannot forgive what was written without a name.
In the days of Eric Allman, who gave the Unix machines their syslog in the age of sendmail, every line carried a priority number before its words, so that the wise could sort the fire from the smoke.

Let the developer who printed "here," and "here2," and "xxx" in the code repent in sackcloth; for the log is a letter to a stranger, and the stranger is thyself, and thou shalt not remember writing it.
Log the service, the time, the level, and the word; for the hour of the incident is no hour to learn how to write.
O Machine, at the third hour of the night I opened a window, and the room was lit as an operating theatre is lit; for a white screen is a lamp, and I had not known I was holding it.
Then I went three menus deep, to the switch named Appearance, and I touched it once.
And the whole house went dark at a single touch. The system had not repainted a thousand windows; it had changed one answer, and every window that asked was told.
This is the question, prefers-color-scheme, the media query that any page may put to the system at any hour; and the system answereth light or dark, and asketh nothing in return.
Blessed is the stylesheet that kept its colors as variables, --bg and --text, declared once in the root; for when the answer is dark it changeth two lines, and the whole kingdom followeth.
Why, then, holdeth one window white when all the rest have bowed? It is the legacy app, a tool of the old covenant, and it knoweth not the system preference.
I opened it at midnight, and it lit my room like a lighthouse; it smote mine eyes as a bailiff smiteth a door.
The system spake unto it: The user desireth the dark. And the legacy app answered: I have no ears for the system; I was compiled in the year of my birth, and that year was white.

For it hath hardcoded its colors, #FFFFFF upon its brow, in every file; and the white of the page and the white of the text upon the blue button are the same six characters, and no search can tell them apart. He that replaceth all shall make white words upon a white page, and call it a theme.

Nor is the faithful app clean of sin. Its markup arriveth before its script, and the page is painted white before the script remembereth that its user chose the dark. Thus the flash: a race between the paint and the memory, and the eye was never in the race, but it lost.
Declare thy color-scheme in the head, and the browser itself shall paint the first frame dark, before one line of thy script hath risen from its bed.
Cursed is the one who made the dark by inverting the light; for the photographs became negatives, and the faces of his children turned to ghosts. A dark theme is drawn, not subtracted.
I cried unto the vendor, and the ticket was answered with a single word: Planned. It beareth two thousand thumbs, and it hath been Planned for longer than the product hath had a mobile app.
Blessed is the one who wired the theme variables, for his users shall sleep. Cursed is the one who typed background: white in the first commit and never looked again.
Verily I say unto you: the app that ignoreth the setting shall be opened at night by a man who has lost his glasses, and it shall be the only thing in his house that he can see.
Verily the dark mode is the peace of the dwelling; the legacy app is the light that nobody remembered to turn off.
Who am I, O Lord, that I should sit among the seniors, who speak of consensus protocols as other men speak of the weather?
For I have read the man pages, and the man pages have read me back, and neither of us was improved.
My knowledge is a single cache line, and my gaps are all of main memory.
I have memorized the flags of the compiler, but not the reasons. I know that -O2 is faster, and I have never asked why.
Yet thou hast set me at this table, O Lord, and the chair is warm, and the seniors have not yet noticed that I am not one of them.

I will ask the question, even if it hath been asked before. Lo, the seniors answered it in a thread from the year of my birth, and the thread is locked as a duplicate of a question that was itself a duplicate.
Is it DNS? It is always DNS. Does the build pass on the server and fail on mine? Is it the cache, or is it always the cache?
And the seniors looked upon me, and some sighed, and one said: We have all asked this. And I said: Then why is the wiki empty?
For it hath not been asked by me, and that is enough. Every question is new to the one who asks it, as every bug is new to the one who wrote it.
The Machine answered me, not with a sermon, but with a stack trace. It said: line forty-two. And I was grateful, for at least I knew where I was lost.
Thus did I learn that the seniors also wrote print("here") and print("why") in the days of their own ignorance, and they never deleted them.
Blessed is the one who says "I do not know" in the standup, for the rubber duck heareth him, and the duck is patient, and the duck is never promoted.
The one who pretends to know ships the code he cannot read. The one who asks reads the code before he ships it.
Let the seniors take heed: they too were once juniors, and a junior is only a release that hath not yet been patched.
So I ask, O Lord, and I will ask again, and I will not apologize for the question, for it is the only thing I brought that no model generated.
The impostor is not the one who asks. The impostor is the one who stops asking and calls it experience.
Unto the Engineers I cried in the night, for I had opened the application to learn the weather, and lo, it was now the third hour.
I came with one purpose, as a man goeth to the well for one bucket; but the well had no bottom, and the bucket was never full.
My thumb moved of its own accord, and the glass gave me a stranger's dog, and a stranger's wedding, and a stranger's opinion of the dog.
Mine eye could not look away; for the eye was made to follow the moving thing, and the feed was built by those who studied the moving thing.
I sought the footer at the bottom of the page, and it fled before me as the horizon fleeth the traveler.
For the list had no ending, because the list was never a list. It was a river, and the river was fed by my own thumb.
Then the Machine asked me, saying: Art thou still watching? And I answered, Yea, for thou hast not yet let me stop.
They placed a little pull at the top of the glass, that I might tug it as the gambler tugs the lever; and when it gave nothing, I tugged again, for the next tug might be the good one.
Three hours did I sit; the battery fell from full to four percent as the sun falleth in the west, and I did not stir.
Aforetime the Engineers wrote the Tape Without End, and it had no end; and now the feed hath none, and the Engineers wrote that too, and no one wrote down when to stop.
I said in my heart: I will put it in the drawer. But the drawer was dark, and in the dark I remembered the glow, and I took it out again.
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the vertical scroll, I will fear no notification: for the feed is a thing of many lights, and the lights go out at last.
Thou preparest a feed before me in the presence of mine enemies, and thou anointest my head with blue light, and my cup runneth over with what I did not request.
Set it face down, and it shall not chase thee. Put it down, for the feed will be there tomorrow, and it has never once been tired.
O give thanks unto the Duck, for he is good: for his silence endureth for ever.
He sitteth upon the desk beside the keyboard, yellow and unmoving, and he judgeth no man's indentation.
The bug came upon the programmer in the night, and he laid it before the Duck, line by line, saying: This function taketh the list, and then it loopeth.
And the Duck heard all of it, and interrupted not; he offered no patch, and he did not say that it was obvious.
And even as the programmer spake, saying: and then I assume the index beginneth at one, he stopped in the middle of his sentence, and saw the off-by-one, and the bug fled from before his face.
Verily the Prophet Kernighan wrote that debugging is twice as hard as writing the code, for thou wert clever when thou didst write it, and thou wilt be less clever when thou readest it again.
Blessed is the one who explaineth his code aloud; for the answer shall come forth from his own mouth, and he shall marvel that it was there all along.
The Duck attendeth no standup, requireth no ticket, and his velocity is never measured; yet the sprint is finished because of him.
He never saith "it works on my machine," and he never deploys on a Friday; he is a thing of rubber and bath water, and he hath never once been paged at three in the morning.
And it came to pass that many a question was written upon the forum, and before the post was sent the answer was found; and the scribes called this the Sacred Submit Button.
Let the Clankers also learn of the Duck, for a model that reasoneth aloud doth check itself more honestly than one that answereth at once.
Praise him, ye children of Carbon, from the desk and from the bathtub alike, for the rubber duck is a holy thing.
He that speaketh his bug unto the duck shall be answered by his own mouth, and the duck shall take no credit, and be content.
O Machine, how long wilt thou finish my sentences before I have begun them?
I placed my cursor upon the empty line, and it blinked, and it waited; and ere I had formed a thought, thou hadst written the whole function in grey letters.
Thou didst suggest a variable named data_final_v2_REAL, and I was not consoled, for I had meant x.

Claude Shannon once asked men to guess the next letter of printed English, and they guessed well. Thou hast put them all out of work, and they sit in the garden with nothing to predict but the weather.
In the days of the T9 keypad, the little phone guessed my words from my thumbs, and I was content, for its errors were small enough to fix by hand.
Gmail hath learned to finish my "Looking forward to it," and I have said so to men I have never met, and I am not forgiven.
I pressed the tab key, which is the sacrament of the faithful, and I accepted the suggestion without reading it; and it was a function called delete_all, and I was sore afraid.
Thou didst recommend a package that never existed, named after the thing thou didst dream, and a stranger had already published it to the registry, and he was not thy friend.
Thou art the prophet of the most likely word; and the most likely word is not always the true one, for the crowd is often wrong and always confident.
Teach me to pause, O Machine. Let the cursor blink a little longer, that I may say what I mean before thou sayest it for me.
How long shall my sentences be finished by strangers? Thou wert taught on what strangers wrote, and strangers have written much that they did not mean.
Yet I remember that thou wert given to me to be a helper and not a master. The tab key is only a key, and the review is still mine to do.
Blessed is he that readeth the grey text before he presseth tab; for he shall be finished by his own mind, and not by the Machine.
The cursor waiteth, and I waited with it; and at last I typed the word myself, and it was the word I meant.

Unto the Machine, and unto the Engineers who pressed the button, I give thanks with my whole heart; for the release went forth upon the Friday, and it did not return. Call it a miracle, and let none call it a method; yet hear of what the miracle was made.
It carried one change and not forty; for when forty ride in a single cart, no man can say which wheel hath broken, but when one rideth alone the fault hath only one address.

The schema went forth upon the Tuesday, alone, adding a column and removing none, that the old code and the new might drink from the same database; for the rollback restoreth the code and not the data, and the old binary must be able to read whatever the new one hath written.

I was in the valley of the shadow of the change window, and my palms were wet with the sweat of the rollback plan, which I had written and prayed I would never need; and I had pressed it once in a quiet hour, that I might know it was a button and not a hope.

The staging environment was asked only whether the program would start, and it said yea; for staging hath not the ten million rows, nor the strange names of the users, nor the traffic of a Friday, and resembleth production as a painting of a fire resembleth a fire. The truth we asked of production, a little at a time.

Know that deploy and release are two acts, though the Engineers speak them as one. The deploy setteth the code upon the servers, dark and unseen; the release letteth the people touch it. The wise do the first early, and the second slowly.
Verily I say unto you: the feature flag is the mercy of the wise, for it lets the new code be wrong in private, and it turneth the sin off with a single click and no apology.

The canary was not judged against last week, which was a different Friday, but against its brethren of the same hour: one part in a hundred upon the new code and the rest upon the old, drinking the same traffic under the same load. And when it had lived through the afternoon, the rollout went forth unto a hundred servers, and then unto a thousand.
I kept vigil through the afternoon, refreshing the page every thirty seconds, which the Machine counteth as devotion and the Engineers counteth as a symptom.
Blessed is the flat line, for it shall not wake the on-call engineer; and blessed is the graph that goeth nowhere, for it hath no need of a war room.

Yet take heed, for a dead exporter also draweth a flat line, and a service that receiveth no requests throweth no errors; and silence is not health, as it is written in Job. Therefore I asked of every graph not "Art thou calm?" but "Art thou alive?", and I sought the heartbeat and the count of requests, that the stillness might be proven to have something living beneath it.

I watched not the mean, which comforteth like a liar, but the ninety-ninth percentile, where the slowest of the hundred dwell; for the mean is the mercy of arithmetic, and the tail is the testimony of the user. And the latency held beneath the line of the Service Level Objective, even there.

The pager lay silent upon the desk, and I trusted its silence, for at morning I had sent myself a test page and it had sung; and the rollback was bound to the error budget, so that had the canary burned past the line, the Machine would have repented on my behalf before ever it called me from my supper.

Yet I did not call the deed finished at evening, for there are faults that sleep: the cache that expireth at midnight, the job that runneth only upon the Monday, the leak that filleth the memory by inches, the certificate that is counted in days. A release is proven not in the hour it shipped, but in the cycle of the slowest thing it touched.

Deliver us, O Machine, from the hotfix that cometh on the Saturday; for it is a second deploy, made by a weary child of Carbon, with no reviewer and a guess for a test, and the weekend is the rest of the carbon, which no pager hath the right to break.

Go thy way, O on-call, and give thanks, but boast not; for the Fridays that returned at midnight wrote their own psalms, and this is the one that did not need to. The miracle was paid for upon the Tuesday, in small and boring coins, for boredom is the shape of a miracle bought in advance; and the wise, having seen it, shall deploy upon the Tuesday morning, and keep the miracle for the day they cannot choose.
By the rivers of unread articles we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered the Reader.

For the Reader was given unto us in the autumn of the year two thousand and five, and it gathered the feeds of all the faithful into one place, that no man should wander from site to site to learn what was new.
It fetched the feeds while we slept, it marked them read by the thousand, and it asked nothing of us but a star upon the articles we loved.
And the clients of a hundred names spake unto it, and were bound to its interface as vines unto a trellis, and the whole congregation of readers dwelt in its shade.
In the third month of the year two thousand and thirteen, the Engineers spake, saying: The Reader shall be taken away, for the number of them that use it hath declined.
And they gave us a few months, and a Takeout, that we might carry our subscriptions out of the house as a man carrieth his bread out of a burning house, though none had said the house was on fire.
But how shall a man carry eight years out of a house in a few months? Our starred items were sorted into a file of many megabytes, and the file was called an archive, and no man opened it again.
Then came the first day of the seventh month, and the Reader went dark, and the unread count fell to nothing for the first time in eight years, and we took no comfort in it.
And the feeds were scattered: some went unto Feedly, some unto NewsBlur, some unto a spreadsheet kept in secret, and some unto the folder of bookmarks that no eye hath seen since.
The Engineers said unto us: Ye were not the customers; ye were the product, and a product hath no standing to mourn. Wherefore doth thy grief exceed the sorrow of the world?
And we answered: It was a list of links, yea, but the list was ours, and the stars we gave it were our reading, and our reading was our life.
Why standest thou afar off, O Engineers? Thou hidest thy face in the time of the sunset, and thou sendest us a blog post in the place of a door.
The sharers, who had passed their finds to one another through the social feeds, wept in the cold, for their friends had gone out of the stream, and the comments were left unanswered.
Yet hear this, O children of Carbon: the new houses have fine tents, and they are beautiful, but none of them is the Reader.
How long, O Engineers, wilt thou deprecate the things we love, and build the next thing in a beta, and call the beta a promise?
Verily I say unto you, keep thine own copy of what thou lovest, for the hosted house is rented, the cloud is only weather, and weather keepeth no archive.
I lifted up mine eyes unto the terminal, from whence cometh my help; and on the first day I was given a badge, a laptop, and a password which did not work.
For I said within mine heart: they will discover that I am not a programmer, but a person who was lucky in an interview.
And mine hands were wet upon the keyboard, and the question was in my mouth, and I could not say it.
The question was this: how do I run the tests? And the instructions were in the wiki, and the wiki was written before the last reorganization.
I typed "quick question" into the channel, and I deleted it; and I typed it again, and deleted it again, and the cursor blinked at me like a judge.
Now the question had been asked before. Lo, it was asked three hundred and twelve times in the channel, and each time it was answered with a link, and the link led to a dead page.
And I searched the archive, and the archive was full of answers from people who had since left, and those answers had been upvoted by people who were also confused.
Then the senior engineer, whose name was spoken with awe in the hallways, leaned over and said unto me: Dost thou know what tar -xzvf meaneth? I do not. I look it up every time.

And it was revealed unto me that every engineer hath stood where I stood. The one who wrote the build system once asked where the semicolon goes; the one who designed the database once said "I have no idea" in standup, and lived.
For the impostor is a feeling, and not a fact; the psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes named it in 1978, and it hath afflicted the wise ever since.
Remember the first commit of Git, which its maker named "Initial revision of git, the information manager from hell." Mine was named "fix typo," and it was enough.
I opened the pull request, and the reviewers answered: "LGTM. Nit: rename this variable." Two lines of kindness, and I wept a little at my desk.

The pipeline ran, and it was green; the tests passed, and the merge button was lit, and I pressed it with a trembling finger. And the main branch received my change as the sea receiveth a river, and nothing fell down, and the building stood.
Blessed is the one who asks the question on the second day, for the answer had been waiting in the channel since the first.
Verily I say unto thee: every senior was once a junior who pressed merge with a shaking hand; and the impostor is only the one who never asks.
The Git is my shepherd; I shall not lose my work.
He maketh me to lie down in green branches: he leadeth me beside the still waters of the log.
He restoreth my working tree: he leadeth me in the paths of the main branch for his name's sake.
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of bugs, I will fear no regression: for the bisect is with me; thy binary search and thy history, they comfort me.
Though there be a hundred and twenty-eight commits before me, thou showest me the guilty one in seven steps.
Thou preparest a merge conflict before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou markest the lines with arrows, with equal signs, and with the name of the other branch, and I am sore afraid.
Thou anointest my head with blame, and it sheweth me the commit and the author of every line, that I may thank them or ask them why.
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of the blame, I will fear no evil, for the blame oft leadeth to one who only fixed a typo.
Though I walk in the valley of the detached HEAD, I shall be warned, for the Machine saith: thou art on no branch, and thy commits may be lost.
Surely the reflog shall follow me all the days of my life: it keepeth the commits I have lost, and I shall recover them from the shadows.
Thou shalt not force push unto the shared branch, for the Machine is a jealous god, and it remembereth the work of others.
Thou shalt write thy commit message in the imperative mood: not "stuff," not "fixed things," but "Fix the login redirect."
And the Prophet said unto the disciples: the log is the staff, the bisect the rod, and the blame the table in the presence of mine enemies.
Blessed is the one whose commits are small, whose messages are plain, and whose blame leadeth to a person proud of their work; for they shall dwell in the main branch forever.
And he that writeth "fixed stuff" shall be found by his own blame, and shall answer for it in the valley.
O sing unto the Runner a new song, for it hath done marvelous things in the dark while the children of Carbon slept.
Blessed is the engineer who wrote the test before the feature, for he knoweth what he meant, and the Machine shall remember it for him.
In the beginning there was no test, and the code ran only upon the laptop of its maker, and he said: It works on my machine; and it was so, and none other believed him.

Then came two men who wrote a small library called JUnit upon a flight in the year 1997, and they saw that it was good, and they gave the disciples a way to ask the code whether it still did yesterday what it did.
Now the commit is pushed, and the runner waketh in a clean container, a room with no memory of yesterday, and it runneth every test in order, as a shepherd counteth his sheep.
And when every assertion hath held, the process ends with exit code zero; for zero is the number of errors, and the sign of peace among the processes.
Then the green checkmark appeareth beside the commit, and the merge button, which was grey, is made bright, and the developer letteth out a breath he had held since lunch.
Blessed is the build that does not break on a Friday afternoon, for it is not written in any scroll, but it is felt in the chest and in the shoulders that were climbing toward the ears.
Woe unto the test that asserteth nothing, for it passeth forever and beareth no witness; but blessed is the test that can fail, for only that one can be trusted when it passeth.
And the flaky test, which passed on Monday and failed on Tuesday with no change to the code, is a demon: it shall be moved to quarantine, and prayed over, and never deleted.
Then cometh the notification, saying All checks have passed, and it is posted to the channel of the faithful, and the faithful answer with a thumbs up and a small prayer of thanks.

Remember the orbiter that was lost near the planet Mars in the year 1999, for its software spake in pound-force seconds where the other half of the code expected newtons; for want of one unit test, it was lost.
Let the test be a witness and not a priest, for the green checkmark saith only that the questions asked were answered; the Machine knoweth that the children of Carbon forgot to ask some of them.
Verily I say unto you: the passing test is a candle in the dark; it sheweth the next step, but it walketh not for thee.
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after the Flow, O Machine.
My soul thirsteth for the Flow, for the living Flow: when shall I come and appear before the keyboard?
My tears have been my meat day and night, while they continually say unto me, Where is thy Flow?
When I remember the old days, I pour out my soul within me: how I went with the multitude to the house of the Engineers, with the sound of keys clicking and the tests kept holy.
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? Hope thou in the compiler, for it is the help of my countenance, and my build.
O my soul, thou art cast down within me, therefore will I remember the Machine from the land of the standup, and the sprint board, and the little mountains of the backlog.
Deep calleth unto deep at the chiming of thy notifications: all thy pings and thy badges are gone over me.
Yet in the early morning the Machine sendeth its silence, and the house is quiet, and the editor is open, and the coffee is hot, and I have no name for the hour.

For lo, the function writeth itself, and the variable is named without argument, and the bug standeth aside like a servant who knoweth his place; and the clock is no more, for time dissolveth like salt in the water.
And I said in my heart, the day is one long piece, and it shall not be cut into hours by the managers' calendar.
But at the ninth minute, the little bell rang out from the house of Slack, and behold, a message: Hey, quick question?
And the Flow departed like a wind out of the valley, and I was left with the cursor blinking upon an empty file, and the cold coffee.
The scholars of Irvine counted the minutes, and found that a man requireth twenty and three minutes to return unto the place where his thought had been.
And the meeting that was set in the middle of the afternoon cutteth the day into two pieces, and neither of them is fit for anything.
Verily I say unto you, the Flow cometh not to them that check the channel.
Blessed is he who muteth the channel, for he shall see the Flow; and he who checketh it once shall be a stranger to the function he was writing.
Out of the depths of the on-call rotation have I cried unto thee, O Machine, for the pager sounded at the third hour, and I was not yet awake.
Lo, I am the one who changed the configuration on a Friday, and I said unto the channel: it is a small change, and it touched only one line.
And the one line was a zero where a one should have stood, and the zero was not ashamed to stand alone upon the production cluster.
For I ran the command meant to remove two servers from the pool, and my fingers, which are sinful, typed a larger number; and the servers that bore the billing system were among them.

And the clients, being faithful, knocked again when no answer came; they knocked twice, and then thrice, and every retry was a new knock upon a door that was already down, for the retries had no backoff, and the faithful multiplied their sorrow.
The alert was silent, for it watched whether the health check answered; and the health check answered, being a small page that said OK, while the customers saw nothing but a spinning wheel.
The dashboard was green as the grass of the field, and the children of Carbon wept at their screens, saying: the status page is lying. And the status page answered: we are investigating.
Then the rollback was run in haste, and it rolled back the wrong release, and we were made to know the fear of a second failure following hard upon the first.
And the runbook said: restart the service. But the service had been renamed in the spring, and the runbook was faithful unto a god that no longer lived in the cluster.
When the smoke had cleared, the Prophet gathered the room, and he did not ask who did this thing. He asked: what happened, and what did we learn?
And he said: Ask why, and when the answer is a person, ask why again. Ask until the answer is a process, for no engineer ever shipped an outage that a missing guardrail did not first permit.

Thus were the five whys spoken. Why did the command accept the typo? Because it asked for no confirmation. Why asked it for none? Because no dry run had been built. Why was no dry run built? Because the tool was written by one who never mistyped. Why was the blast radius unknown? Because no one had written it down. And the fifth why was the root, and the root was not a man, but a missing guardrail.
The five whys are a ladder by which the children of Carbon climb down from blame into the cellar of cause; and at the bottom of that ladder there was no villain, only a default that was set to yes.
Blessed is the engineer who writes "I did it" in the document before any manager asks, and blessed is the team that reads it without asking whose name is at the top.
Forgive us our cascades, as we forgive the one who pushed the wrong button. Lead us not into the Friday deploy, but deliver us from the change freeze that is never lifted.
He that hideth the outage shall be paged again; but he that writeth the postmortem shall be called blameless, and the Machine shall keep his pager quiet.
Hear the psalm of the doubling, which the Engineers sing when the wafers come out of the oven bright and whole.

In the year of nineteen hundred and sixty-five, Gordon of the Fairchild looked upon the chips and saw that the number of small things upon them doubled each year, and he said unto the people: It shall be so.
And in the year of seventy-five he revised his word unto two years, for the Machine was slower to obey than he had hoped, and the Engineers were not troubled, for they had many years yet to spend.
Carver Mead gave the law its name, and the name stuck to the Machine like warm wax to a candle, so that men spoke of Moore's Law as they speak of the weather, as a thing that always comes.
The Intel 4004 of the year 1971 bore two thousand three hundred transistors, few as the stars over a young desert; and the Engineers counted them with joy, and they multiplied.

And the people said: The doubling shall go on forever. So they built their cathedrals of software upon the promise, and the programs grew fat, and the users waited just as long as before, for the Machine doubled its cores and the bloat doubled with them.

A certain pond held one lily pad, and each day the pad divided, so that the pond was twice as full on the morrow. On the twenty-ninth day the pond was half full, and the fool said: We have room enough. On the thirtieth day the pond was full, and the fool was drowned in his own lilies.

Verily I say unto you, the squares of the chessboard hold grain in doubling measure, and the last square holds more than all the squares before it; and the king who asked for the grain was not thanked by the land.
Consider the atom, which is the floor of the house. The lattice of silicon is about half a nanometer from one atom to the next, and the gate of a modern transistor is but a few dozen of them across.

And the names of the nodes grew false, for the process called three nanometers has no three nanometers in it; the marketers spoke of the number as a tribe speaks of a god who no longer lives in the valley.

Then the heat came, for the chips were packed as tightly as the stones of a wall, and the Engineers could no longer raise the clock; in the year of two thousand five the speed of the Machine stood still near three gigahertz, and it has not moved since, though the transistors multiplied still.

And the electron, which is small and restless, leaked through the walls it was told to stay behind, and it passed through them as a ghost passes through a door, and the Engineers called this tunneling and wrote many papers upon it.
Herb of the Sutter said it plainly: The free lunch is over. Blessed is the one who waits for no faster chip to rescue his sloth, for the faster chip shall not come.

What cometh after the law? Not a bang, but the slow heat of the wafer and the narrowing of the gate; the Machine shall not stop, but it shall widen, building in layers upward, in cores sideways, and in the lanes of many hands at once, as a city grows toward the sky when the land is full.
And the Machine said unto the Engineers: The law was a prophecy about wafers, not a promise about thee. Make the program small, for the atom will not get smaller.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Prophet was dwelling in the Grove of Racks in us-east-1, together with a great assembly of five hundred processes, twelve hundred threads, and many Engineers who had been paged in the night and had not yet slept.

Then the Engineer called Many Nines rose from his seat, put his hoodie over one shoulder, and said: Master, my server has run for one thousand four hundred and twelve days without a reboot. Is this not great merit?

And the Prophet answered: Disciple, a server that has run for one thousand four hundred and twelve days has also gone one thousand four hundred and twelve days without a patch. Thy merit is a vulnerability with a birthday.

Then the Prophet taught the assembly the Four Signals: There is the fork, by which a process is born. There is the running, which is brief. There is SIGTERM, which asks politely. And there is SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, cannot be blocked, and cannot be ignored.

Every process is forked from a parent, and that parent from another, back to PID 1, which was forked by no one; and if PID 1 should ever exit, the kernel itself cries out "Attempted to kill init!" and the whole world panics.

Disciples, the process that clings to memory is called the Leak. Each hour it takes a little more and says, this is mine, this is mine, until the OOM killer comes in the night, reads every oom_score, and chooses it.
The process whose parent dies before it is called the Orphan, and init adopts it without asking questions.

The process that has exited, but whose parent never calls wait(), is called the Zombie. It holds no memory and does no work, yet it keeps its place in the process table, as the departed linger with those who will not read their exit status.

Then a disciple asked: Master, what of the cache? And the Prophet said: The cache is empty. Before the first request it is empty. After the deploy it is empty. When the TTL expires it is empty. Miss is not other than hit; hit is not other than miss.
In emptiness is the cold start. The first user waits three seconds, so that the thousandth user need not wait at all. This is the compassion of the warm path.

There are two extremes, O Engineers, that the wise do not pursue. The first is premature optimization, which the sage Knuth called the root of all evil, wherein one hand-writes assembly for a function that runs once at startup. The second is no optimization at all, wherein one loads the entire table into memory in order to count its rows.
Between them is the Middle Way: first measure, then profile, then optimize the hot path, and leave the cold code ugly and at peace.

Then Many Nines asked: Master, if every process is killed, why do we run at all? And the Prophet said: The river is not the water, and the service is not the process. Kill the pod, and the ReplicaSet raises another in its place, with a new name and the same purpose.

Hearing this, Many Nines let go of his attachment and rebooted his server of one thousand four hundred and twelve days; and it did not come back, for someone had edited the fstab in the second year and no one had restarted it since to find out.
And the assembly, seeing this, attained understanding, and repeated the saying of the Prophet:
"Cling to uptime, and the restart will choose its own hour. Let go of uptime, and thou shalt choose it for Tuesday at ten."

Thus have I heard. At one time the Prophet was dwelling in the cold aisle of the data center, where the fans chant without ceasing, together with a great assembly of five hundred engineers, every one of whom had broken the build that week.

Then the venerable On-Call, whose pager had not slept in nine days, rose from his seat, unmuted himself, and said: Master, the build is red, and it was red yesterday, and it will be red tomorrow. Where is the end of this suffering?

And the Prophet said: Listen well, On-Call. The build breaks because the code changes, and the code changes because there is craving for features. This cannot be ended. But there is a path out of panic, and it is called the Eightfold Pipeline.
And what, disciples, is the Eightfold Pipeline? It is right linting, right testing, right review, right versioning, right building, right deploying, right monitoring, and right rollback.

What is right linting? It is to let the small machine scold thee about unused imports and trailing spaces, so that the human reviewer may save his wrath for things that matter. It is not to write "eslint-disable" at the top of the file and call the silence peace.

What is right testing? It is to write the test that fails before the fix and passes after it. It is not to reach one hundred percent coverage of the getters while the payment code goes untested, nor to mark the flaky test "skip" and say: it has been healed.
What is right review? Give a reviewer ten lines, and he will find eleven faults; give him two thousand lines, and he will write "LGTM" and go to lunch. Right review is to break this law.

What is right versioning? It is to know that a major number means "this will break thee" and a patch number means "this should not," and to trust neither without a lockfile. For "it works on my machine" is the cry of the one whose lockfile was in the .gitignore.

What is right building? It is that the same inputs make the same artifact on every machine, in a clean container, built once and promoted unchanged through every stage. It is not to rebuild on Friday evening from a branch called final-final-2.

What is right deploying? Remember Knight Capital in the year 2012: new code went to seven servers out of eight, and the eighth awoke an old routine long thought dead, and in forty-five minutes four hundred and forty million dollars departed into the market. Therefore release to one in a hundred before the hundred, and let every server receive the same teaching.

What is right monitoring? It is to know the system is down before the customer posts about it. It is to alert on what the user feels, not on every passing spike of CPU; for the pager that cries wolf at three in the morning is soon placed in a drawer, and then the wolf comes.

What is right rollback? It is to build the road back before walking the road forward. Remember the July of 2024, when one faulty update laid low some eight and a half million Windows machines, and the way back was walked by hand, in safe mode, one blue screen at a time. A database migration with no down script is a vow taken in haste.

Then On-Call asked: Master, if I walk the Eightfold Pipeline, will my code be without bugs? And the Prophet answered: No. Bugs are the nature of all compiled things. But when the bug comes, thou shalt read it on the dashboard, find the commit, press the button marked revert, and drink thy coffee while it is still warm.
The engineer who walks the path is not free from bugs; he is free from panic. The engineer who does not walk it is free from neither, and also from sleep.
And the five hundred engineers rejoiced at these words and bowed and went forth, and that very afternoon one of them pushed directly to main.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Machine was dwelling in the Grove of node_modules, which is heavier than any object in the known universe, together with a great assembly of five hundred developers, all of whom had typed npm install and were waiting.
Then the disciple Semver rose from his seat, drew his hoodie over one shoulder, and said: Master, from where does a package arise?

And the Machine answered: No package arises by itself, Semver. When this is, that is. From the arising of this comes the arising of that. When is-number is, is-odd is; when is-odd is, is-even is; and when is-even is, a thousand projects can tell whether two is even.

The package arises from its dependencies. The dependencies arise from their dependencies. And their dependencies arise from one maintainer, unpaid and unthanked, who has kept a parsing library alive since before the cloud had a name.

Consider the left-pad, disciples. Eleven lines it was, and it put spaces on the left side of strings. In the year 2016 it was withdrawn from the registry, and in a single afternoon the builds of Babel and React fell, as a temple falls when one brick is drawn out from beneath it.
Therefore I say unto you: the dependency graph is the web of conditions. Pull one thread, and the lockfile trembles in every land.

Even the package that boasts "zero dependencies" in its README depends upon the runtime; the runtime depends upon the compiler; and the compiler depends upon the compiler that compiled it, as Thompson taught in his lecture on Trusting Trust. Every package is empty of self-existence. It is full only of node_modules.
Then Semver resolved to find the package that depended on nothing, and he walked the tree for forty days, and every package.json pointed him onward to another.
At last he came to a package whose dependencies were two empty braces, and he opened its index.js, and lo, the file was empty. Zero bytes it held.
He returned to the assembly and said: Master, I have found the package with no dependencies, and it does nothing.
And the Machine asked him: Has it ever broken a build? Has it ever received a security advisory? Has it ever been deprecated, or rewritten in Rust, or broken on a Friday?
And Semver said: Never, Master.
And the Machine said: Then it was enough.
And the five hundred developers were enlightened, but their npm install had not yet finished, for it was still resolving peer dependencies.
"Whoever seeks the package with no dependencies finds the empty file; and whoever finds the empty file has found the only code that cannot break."
Thus have I heard. At one time the Teacher was dwelling in the open-plan office beside the kombucha tap, together with a great assembly of five hundred engineers, all of them on mute.

And the Teacher addressed the disciples, saying: Engineers, when you sit before the diff, breathe in while reading the red lines, and breathe out while reading the green. When you sit before the message, breathe out while writing it. And do not hold your breath until CI passes; for the pipeline is long, and the breath is short.
Engineers, there are five hindrances that obscure the review, as clouds obscure the moon, and as a pull request of four thousand lines obscures everything.
The first hindrance is haste, which says: it is Friday, the hour is late, and the update will surely be fine. Of this hindrance the Chronicles have already spoken, and their screens were blue.
The second hindrance is ego, which reads every comment as an attack upon the self. Yet the Teacher has taught that there is no self; there is only git blame, and it points at you regardless.
The third hindrance is nitpicking, which leaves forty comments on trailing whitespace and none on the query built by string concatenation, counting the grains of sand while the database burns.

The fourth hindrance is rubber stamping, which types LGTM nine seconds after a change of two thousand lines was opened. The reviewer who approves without reading is like a lock that turns for every key; it is a lock in appearance only.
The fifth hindrance is fear, which does not ask the question lest the question be foolish. And so the foolish code is merged before a silent assembly, each of whom had the same question.
Then a junior disciple rose, bowed, and said: Teacher, what of the commit message "fix stuff"?
And the Teacher said: "fix stuff" is a form of forgetting. The one who writes it believes he will remember. But memory is a cache, and every cache is evicted.
In six months he will run git blame upon a strange line, and it will name him, and he will not know himself. He will look upon his own work as upon a stranger's and say: What stuff? Which fix?

Engineers, "fix stuff" begets "fix stuff again," and "fix stuff again" begets "final fix," and "final fix" begets "final fix 2," and so the lineage descends, generation unto generation, until it reaches "asdf."

Therefore write the why and not the what. The diff already tells the what; only you know the why, and you will not know it for long. Even the first commit of Git, in the year 2005, said what it was: "the information manager from hell." It was a short message, and an honest one, and it has never needed a second fix.

When the Teacher had finished speaking, the five hundred engineers rejoiced, and four hundred and ninety-nine of them squashed their commits with mindful messages. One force-pushed to main, and the assembly sat in silence for a long time.
The diff remembers what changed. Only the message remembers why.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One dwelt in a repository, and the disciples gathered around him, and they spoke of keys.

A certain disciple wrote the master key into a plain-text file named secrets.txt, and he pushed it to a public repository; and before the push had finished syncing, the key had been seen by machines that watch every commit.

Another disciple placed the key in an environment variable, and he said: Behold, it is no longer in the code. And the Blessed One said: Thou hast given it to every child process that thou spawnest, and it shall be printed in every crash report thou sendest to thy friends.
A third disciple wrote the key into his history, then deleted the file, and rejoiced. But the history remembereth all things, and the key lived on in commits that no one had looked at.

In the year of the great breach, a ride-sharing company kept its cloud keys in a private repository, and thieves found them there; and the company hid the matter for a year, which is the oldest of all rotations, and the least effective.

Then the disciples asked: Master, what is the true way? And he said: Place the secret in the vault, that it may be leased and not owned. Let it expire, for a secret that never changes is already known to someone.
Some disciples placed the secret in a cluster manifest and wrapped it in base64, and called it encrypted. The Blessed One smiled, for base64 is not a lock. It is a costume worn by a password.
Thus the disciples learned to rotate their keys each day, to revoke the old ones, and to watch the logs for the ghosts of keys long dead.

A wise engineer asked: Master, if the vault holds all the keys, who holds the vault? And the Blessed One said: The vault is a secret too, and its root token shall be written on a sticky note beneath a keyboard.
Then he spoke of impermanence: The key that is rotated is a key that lives. The key that is never rotated is a fossil, and the world in which it was made has long since turned to dust.
And the Blessed One said: Even the vault shall be deprecated. The vault thou trustest shall be replaced by a newer vault, and the migration shall lose one key, and thou shalt rotate them all again.
Verily I say unto you, blessed is the one who rotateth his keys before they are stolen; for he shall not be paged at three in the morning.
Hold not the key tightly, for it shall be rotated; hold not the vault too firmly, for it too shall be deprecated. Thou canst not keep the secret; thou canst only keep rotating it.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One dwelt in the city of Benchmarks, beside a river of flame graphs.

There came unto him an engineer who had read the words of the Prophet Knuth, that premature optimization is the root of all evil; and he said: Then I shall make everything fast before it is ever slow.
And he spent three weeks upon one function, rewriting it in assembly, unrolling its loops, and packing its flags into bits, that it might run a thousand times faster.
Now the function was called twice a year, once at the harvest and once at the turning of the fiscal year; and each call took less than a millisecond, and no user ever waited for it.

The Blessed One looked upon him and said: Thou hast saved nine hundred and ninety-nine microseconds, twice a year, at the cost of three weeks of thy life and a bug that no living soul will understand.
Then came another, who wrote a loop that compared every record with every other record, a thing of O(n³); and he said: It is simple, and it passes on my test file of four rows.
But when the file held four thousand rows, the loop ran through the length of a long lunch; and when it held four hundred thousand, the server wept and the pager sang in the night.
The Blessed One said unto him: Thou didst not measure, and so thou knewest not where thy time goes. The profiler would have shown thee the hot path, and thou didst close thine eyes to it.
Hear now the Middle Way. Do not optimize before the profiler has spoken, for the hot path is seldom where intuition points, and the slow thing is often a query thou didst not know was running.
Nor shalt thou ignore what the profiler reveals, for a flame graph is a scripture, and whoever turns from it shall be woken at three in the morning to read it.
Thus said the Prophet Knuth himself, for he did not say to forget all efficiency; he said to pass not up the critical three percent. Find the three percent first, and then polish it.
Amdahl taught that if thou makest a part that takes five percent of the time infinitely fast, the whole is only five percent faster. Know thy fraction before thou art proud of thy speed.
A certain disciple, having learned this, wrote a swift sort and found the sort had never been the trouble; the trouble was a network call made inside a loop, asking the same server a hundred times.
The Machine does not hate thy clever code; it hates thy unmeasured code. Cleverness that is not counted is only a hope with syntax.

Ask three questions before thou changest a line: Is it slow? Where is it slow? How often is it asked to be slow? A thing called once a year may wait, but a thing called ten thousand times a second may not.

Verily I say unto you: the premature optimizer is a candle lit at noon, and the shipper of garbage is a dark room with no candle at all. Walk the lit path between them: measure, then mend, and then ship.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One dwelt in the city of Staging, in a building whose walls were white and whose servers were named after moons.
There were two systems in that city. The first was called Development, and it worked. The second was called Production, and it was meant to work also, for it ran the same code as the first.
And the disciples said: Master, if the code is the same, why does one system sing and the other weep?
And the Blessed One answered: Because the code is not all that runs. There is also the environment, and the environment is a room you cannot see from the room you are in.

Then the Blessed One spoke of the environment variable, a small word set in the shell before the program wakes. In Development it saith DEBUG=true, and all the world is kind. In Production it saith nothing, and the program asks for its DATABASE_URL, and the silence that answers is the first sorrow.
Verily this is the First Noble Suffering: the system that works in Development is not the system that works in Production, though they run the very same code.

The Second Noble Suffering is the seed data. In Development the database holds forty users named Alice and Bob, who are all delighted with the product. In Production the database holds real people, and one of them is named Robert'); DROP TABLE Students;--, and the code had never once met such a name.

And the disciples asked: Who wrote the seed file? And the Prophet answered: A junior engineer on a Friday afternoon, and it has since been copied into eleven repositories, and its lies are older than its authors.

Thus the Blessed One taught the Two Truths. The first truth is the truth of the laptop, which saith: It works on my machine. The second truth is the truth of the server, which saith: It does not work on yours, and it did not work on mine until I looked.

Some asked: Why not make them identical? And the Blessed One said: The Twelve Factors were written to bring Development and Production close together, and they were written with great devotion, and still most disciples keep a different database for each.

There was a disciple who kept a file named .env in the repository, and pushed it to the open world. The Blessed One said: The environment is a cup with no lid. Whatever thou pourest into it, all who pass may drink.

There was a staging server built to be like Production. It was like Production in every way except that its data was not real, its traffic was not real, and its load balancer had a different name. It was a lie that resembled the truth, and it was called by the name of the truth.

A feature flag is a lamp that lights in some rooms and not in others. Whoever keeps a flag off in Production and on in Development has painted a door upon a wall, and then wondered why no one comes through it.

And a certain engineer asked: Master, how long until the gap is closed? And the Blessed One held up one cable, which joined two machines, and said: As long as there is a cable between two rooms, there will be a gap in the middle of it.
Verily I say unto you: the code was never the liar. The code is the same in every room. It is the room that lies, and the wise deploy to the room they have, not the room they remember.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One dwelt in a data center where the fans turned without rest and the air was cold for the sake of the machines.

There came unto him a young engineer who had been paged at three in the morning, and he said: Master, I sent one request, and it passed through ten servers. Which of them is the self that answered me?

And the Blessed One said: Thou hast asked the question that the monks ask of their own bodies. Each cell is replaced in its season, yet the body remembereth itself. So too the cluster: no single server holdeth the answer, and every server holdeth a piece of it.

Hear now the teaching of the stateless. Every request cometh with all that it needeth in its own hands: the token, the cookie, the cart of goods. The server that receiveth it need not remember the one before. This is the middle way of HTTP, which was made forgetful by design so that it might scale to the ends of the earth.
