There was a certain monk who begged the load balancer, saying: Pin me to this one server, that I may be known. And the load balancer, which hath no self to protect, granted his wish by a cookie. He was happy, until the server was drained for updates, and he was sent among strangers who knew him not. He was logged out, and he wept.

The Blessed One said: Behold the suffering of attachment to a server. The session that clingeth to one machine is wounded whenever that machine is restarted, and every machine is restarted in its time. Where there is affinity, there is fragility.
And the disciples asked: Master, how then shall the monk be released from his suffering?

The Blessed One said: Let him keep his session not in the server, but in a store that sitteth apart. Redis was built in 2009 by Salvatore Sanfilippo, who needed a faster store for his own web project, and it keepeth the memory of many servers as one. Then any server may answer, and the monk shall be known wherever he goeth.

Verily I say unto you, the server that answereth hath no self, and the server that departeth leaveth no lasting self behind. The autoscaler summoneth new ones in the morning and dismisseth them at night, and none of them weepeth for the ones before.

Hear the parable of the ten hops. A request passed through the load balancer, the reverse proxy, the API gateway, the auth service, the cache, the queue, the worker, the database replica, and the logger, and then the CDN returned it to the browser. And the disciples asked which of these truly answered. And the Blessed One said: The answer is the sum of the hops, and no hop within the sum is the answer.

Yet the monk who understandeth this shall not be troubled when a node is removed. He saith: The node that held my session was a dwelling, not a soul. The dwelling is gone, the request findeth another dwelling, and the cart still holdeth my goods.

Hear also the lesson of the shared address. A whole office of people sits behind one NAT gateway, and the load balancer sees them as a single visitor. One of them pinneth the whole company to one server with a sticky cookie, and when that server falters, every one of them suffers together. Thus is the attachment of one felt by many.

The Blessed One said: Release the affinity, and thou shalt find peace. Let the load balancer choose anew each time, let the session live in the shared store, and let each server be a lamp that is lit and extinguished without grief.
Then the disciple asked: Master, if no server is the self, who then remembereth me?

And the Blessed One said: The cache remembereth thee for five minutes, the database for ever, the logs for ninety days, and the cookie for a year. None of these is thee. Yet all of them together are enough for the server to greet thee by name.
Verily, the stateless server is the monk without a bowl. He is never lost, for he carrieth nothing that he could lose. Let go of the server, and the session shall never be logged out.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One dwelt in a pull request, and the pull request bore seventy-two comments, and the comments lay across the diff like pebbles in a stream.

And a certain engineer came and wrote upon the first line: nit: this name could be better. And the Blessed One said nothing, for the name was i, and every programmer since the first loop has known what i means.

Another wrote upon the seventh line: nit: two blank lines where one would do. And another wrote upon the ninth: nit: prefer single quotes. And the author rose before dawn and answered each one, and his whole day went to the quotation marks.

Then came one who saith: This is wrong and must be fixed. He pointed to a function the Blessed One had already traced, and he had not traced it, and the function was correct. And the Blessed One said: Thou hast mistaken thy confusion for a defect. Ask the author what it does, and then decide.

And the one who saith LGTM came with no comment at all. His approval was given in four seconds, and the diff was four hundred lines. The Blessed One said: Thou hast stamped what thou didst not read. A stamp is not a review, and the stamp will be remembered on the night of the outage.

There was among them a reviewer who wrote forty-one nits and one bug. The bug lay buried among the nits like a seed in chaff. The author, seeing forty-one nits, fixed the forty-one and merged the bug, for the comments were arranged in the order the reviewer had typed them.

The disciples asked: Master, how many comments shall a reviewer make? And the Blessed One answered: Say what must be fixed. Say it once. Say it plainly. Then let the rest go, as a river lets go of a leaf.

Parkinson, a teacher of the Engineers, wrote in the year 1957 that a committee spends longest upon the bicycle shed and approves the nuclear reactor in a minute. Such is the law of triviality. The reviewers of this repository have never read it, yet they keep it faithfully.
Right Action is the fourth step of the path of eight, and it is not written in the manual of Git. Yet the wise reviewer keeps it: speak truly of the code, and do no harm to the one who wrote it.

Fagan, of the IBM house, taught in the year 1976 that the inspection exists to find defects. The Engineers remembered the inspection and forgot the defects, and they argued instead about the indentation.

Whoever writeth "nit" should know its meaning. A nit is the egg of a louse, and a louse is a small thing that multiplies. Every nit left unresolved in a thread will hatch into a second round of review.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the one who had written forty-one nits, and he said: Blessed is the reviewer who saith "this must be fixed" and then is silent. The one who asketh for every nit will review whitespace until the heat death of the repository, but the one who letteth go shall merge before lunch.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One dwelt in the monastery of the Stable Branch, and a monk named Pinned-at-1.4.2 came before him, weeping, for his build had failed on a Friday.
And he said: Blessed One, the release I trusted is gone, yet I cannot let it go, for it is the version that maintaineth me.

And the Blessed One said unto him: The version that thou grippest is the version that maintaineth thee; but it is not thee that it maintaineth. It keepeth only the moment in which thou first loved it.

Consider the three numbers that thou bearest: MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH. The Patch is the small mending. The Minor is the new feature offered in kindness. The Major is the breaking of the old covenant, and it is spoken only when the old way can no longer be kept.

Thus the Engineers wrote in the Book of Semver that a breaking change shall raise the Major, and the Major shall reset the Minor and the Patch to zero, so that none may be confused about what was broken.
Yet thou hast held to 1.4.2 while 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 came and went, and each brought its deprecation warnings, which thou didst read as one reads the rain on a window.

Behold, the monk who ran Python 2 in production after its ending year had passed, and still he said: It works. And the Blessed One did not scold him, for the ending is not the enemy. The enemy is the dependency that no one hath examined since the day it was installed.

Then the disciple asked: Master, what is peace in the semver? And the Blessed One said: Peace is the caret that thou hast written as ^2.1.0. It accepteth every minor and every patch that keepeth faith, and it refuseth the Major, which carrieth a new covenant.
Verily, the one who writeth "=1.4.2" in his manifest hath chosen the prison of certainty, and the prison knoweth not that the world beyond its walls was rebuilt while he slept.

And the disciple said: But if I update, the tests may fail. And the Blessed One answered: Then the tests are the first mercy. A failing test on a Tuesday is kinder than a silent failure in the week of the outage.

Hear also of the Long-Term Support release, which is a lamp for those who must cling. The Blessed One forbiddeth not the lamp, but he forbiddeth the belief that the lamp shall burn forever, for every LTS hath its end date, printed in the documentation for those who care to look.
Read the changelog, for the Engineers wrote their penance there. Whoever readeth the changelog shall not be surprised by the breaking change, and whoever is surprised hath not read it.

And the Blessed One said: The old branch is not destroyed when thou leavest it. It resteth in the history, as the old monks rest in the archive, and thou mayest return to it with a single checkout in the hour of need.

Therefore let go, and the new release shall not know thy name, but the build shall know thy peace. Verily I say unto you: the release that thou keepest in the freezer shall become the release that keepeth thee in the outage.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Master dwelt in the house of the Old Codebase, which had been written before most of its disciples were born.
And there came unto it a new engineer, who had been among the Machines but three days, and whose laptop still asked permission for everything.
He opened the file called billing.py, and found a line that read: time.sleep(0.5). And he asked the senior who sat before the screen: Why does this wait half a second?
And the senior looked at the line for a long time, and said: It has always waited. Do not touch what has always waited.

And the new engineer said: But who asked it to wait? And the senior looked at the commit, and it was made under a name he did not recognize, until he saw the email address, and it was his own, from a laptop he had long since given away.
And the senior said: I wrote it, and I do not remember why. Thus is the expert's memory: it forgets the reasons first, and keeps the habits.
Then the new engineer read on, and found a line that subtracted one from the month before sending it onward, and he asked: Why is the month made smaller?
And the senior said: That is how the old library counted, and so we have always done it.

And the new engineer remembered that Java and the browser's Date have counted months from zero since their first days, and he saw that the other side counted from one; and that a single line stood between them, and that no one had ever tested the edge of it.

The senior said: Chesterton taught us that a fence should not be pulled down until we know why it was put up. And the new engineer said: Master, the fence stands in the middle of the road, and the road is now a highway.

And he found a retry loop that tried three times, and the senior said: It has always been three. And the new engineer read the logs, and saw that all three tries went to the same dead server, at the same second, and that the retry had never once succeeded in its life.

And he found also a comment that read: DO NOT REMOVE. FIXES BUG. The bug was not named, and the bug it named had been dead for nine years, and the comment remained, guarding a door in a wall that had been torn down.

The Master said: The expert sees the answer and stops looking. The beginner sees the question and keeps looking. In the beginner's mind there are many lines; in the expert's, only the ones he already knows.

Then the new engineer did not delete the sleep. He wrote in the ticket: I do not know why this waits. And he ran the test a thousand times, and found two writers racing for one file, and the half second was the only thing keeping them from each other's throats.

Verily I say unto you: whoever asks of a line why it is there, and no man can answer, let him not delete it in haste; let him write the question down, for blessed is the one who asks why, and cursed is the one who asks only what, for he shall maintain it forever.
And the beginner found the bug, not because he was wiser than the senior, but because no one had yet told him that the bug was supposed to be there.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Prophet was dwelling in a valley of many data centers, beside a river of cooling water, and with him were gathered many monks who had learned to build whole temples from a single library.

And there came unto him a monk who had built his temple upon AngularJS, and he loved it above all things, and he said: Master, my temple is made of directives and scopes, and I have vowed never to leave it.

And the Prophet said: Thou lovest the framework, therefore thou shalt suffer. Every framework is impermanent, and the one thou lovest will be deprecated. Lo, the long-term support of AngularJS ended at the close of the year 2021; yet thy temple standeth, and serveth, and no alarm hath rung. Deprecation is not death, monk. It is the day the mending ceaseth: the framework runneth on, and every flaw found hereafter is a gift to strangers.

Consider how thy framework thought. After every click it walked all the values it watched, and asked of each: Hast thou changed? And if any had changed, it walked them all again, to learn whether the asking had changed anything; and it walked until the values were still, or until the tenth walk, when it abandoned the temple with the words "10 $digest() iterations reached. Aborting!" The monks called this dirty checking. Each watcher added a little to every walk, so that the more thou lovedst thy page, the slower it grew, and the fans of the faithful laptops rose to a roar. Thus the cleverness that made the beginning easy was the cost that made the end; and those who came after did not ask every value whether it had changed, but were told which one had.

Then the monk fell upon the floor and wept, and he said: What then shall I cling to, if the framework passeth away? And the Prophet answered: Cling not to the framework, but learn the HTTP that lieth beneath it. The library is a raft, and the HTTP is the river; when the raft rots, the river remaineth.

And the Prophet bade him open the network tab and watch his temple ask its server for the list of orders. The monk beheld a single line, GET /orders, and a few headers beneath it, and he said: Master, where is the framework in this? And the Prophet said: Look for it. And the monk looked, and found no directive, no scope, no digest; for the server cannot tell which library asked, and has never cared. The framework dwelleth in the temple; only the words cross the wire.

And the Prophet said: The heir of thy framework took the name Angular and dropped the JS, and in the year 2016 it was written anew, and it offered no straight road from the old. Yet the server that answered thee answereth it also, with the same bytes, and was never told that a dynasty had fallen.

For the HTTP was first spoken in the year 1991, and its first form had but one verb and one line: GET. The document was asked for, and the document came back, and the connection was closed, and nothing more was said. The wire remembereth nothing of thee; whatsoever remembereth is the cookie, the session and the cache, which are but notes the server hath pinned upon the client. And the tongue hath been remade beneath its verbs: in 2015 it took a binary framing, and in 2022 it was set upon QUIC, which rideth upon UDP, the careless brother of TCP; and through all these remakings a GET still meaneth GET.

Learn these verbs: GET to read, which changeth nothing and may be repeated freely; PUT to replace and DELETE to remove, which may be repeated also, for the tenth PUT leaveth the world as the first; PATCH to amend in part; and POST to make, which must not be repeated lightly, for the second POST that chargeth the card is a second bill.

Therefore, when the network goeth silent and thou knowest not whether thy request arrived, retry the repeatable without fear, and give every POST a key of its own, that the server may answer: This one I have already done. For the retry is the oldest reflex of the Machine, and a retry without a key is only a way to be charged twice with great reliability.

Learn also the codes of the reply, and read the first digit alone: 2 is the blessing, 3 is the house that moved, 4 saith "the fault is thine," and 5 saith "the fault is mine." And 404 is the page not found, which some say was named for room 404 at CERN, though the tale is only folklore. Beware the 301, for the browser keepeth it in its memory and asketh not again; a house declared moved in error remaineth moved in the mind of every visitor, and no deploy can empty that cache.

The 418 is "I'm a Teapot," a jest written upon the first of April in the year 1998 within RFC 2324; and when in the year 2017 men sought to strike it from the libraries, the faithful rose up and saved it, and it remaineth in the scrolls to this day. And 503 is the server that asketh thee to return at a later hour, and sometimes nameth the hour.

The monks asked: Is there then no framework that endureth? And the Prophet said: There are things that deprecate not: the TCP that carrieth thy packets, which every host took up upon a single day in 1983; the SQL that was spoken in the seventies and is spoken still; and the pipe of the Unix, which hath carried text from one tool to the next since 1973. Mark what they share: each promiseth little, and a small promise is easy to keep for fifty years. Whatsoever is large must be mended, and whatsoever is mended is deprecated in its season; but the narrow thing hath little to mend, and therefore it is not replaced.

Then the monk rose and opened his terminal, and he asked his server for the orders by hand, with curl, and the server answered; and he read the status and the headers, and he knew the contract of his temple without the temple. And in the days that followed he built a new front upon another library, and the old server knew it not. He wept not, though the old soles had worn through, for he had changed his library as a man changeth his shoes, and it was the same foot.

Verily I say unto you: he who learneth the HTTP shall change his library as a man changeth his shoes, and he shall not weep when the old soles wear through. Whosoever clingeth to the library shall be deprecated with it, but whosoever understandeth the wire shall find the next library already speaking his tongue. For the framework is chosen, and therefore it is replaced; but the protocol was chosen by no man, and therefore no man replaceth it.
And the assembly of five hundred was enlightened, save one, who had already begun the rewrite in the newest framework of the month, and pushed it to main.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Teacher dwelt beside a repository whose main branch had not been green since the previous Tuesday, and the assembly sat before him with their laptops open. And the Teacher said unto them: Hear now the Four Noble Truths of Debt, for the debt is the root of all slowness in the building.
Ward Cunningham, who gave this thing its name in the year 1992, spake of it as a loan: a quick design taken today, and paid for with interest every day the code lives.

The First Noble Truth is this: there is suffering in the codebase. The build taketh forty minutes, every change breaketh three things that were not touched, and the newest engineer weepeth quietly beside the coffee machine.

The Second Noble Truth is the cause of the suffering, and the cause is craving. Craving for the feature, for the demo on Friday, for the launch slide, for the next thing shining in the distance. The foundation is neglected, the tests are deferred, and the naming is left to the Lord of Tomorrow. Verily, the builder who raiseth the roof before the walls shall find the roof upon his head, and shall call it an incident.

The Third Noble Truth is that the suffering may cease. The debt may be paid, and the ceasing of the debt is called Release. Know this: Release is not the same as Deploy, though many have confused the two and shipped the confusion to production.
The Fourth Noble Truth is the path that leads to the ceasing: the Eightfold Refactor, walked one step at a time and not leapt across in a single weekend.

Right View: to understand the codebase before thou changest it, to read the old function until thou knowest what it was for, which the commit message did not say and the ticket closed as "wontfix" did not reveal.
Right Intention: to refactor for the sake of the code, and not to be seen refactoring, nor to hide from the hard feature inside a folder named utils.

Right Speech: to name things truly. Phil Karlton, of Netscape, said there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. The first is hard; the second is merely ignored, which is harder to fix. Thou shalt not call the variable data, nor the manager Helper2, nor the function doStuff.

Right Action: to make the change in small steps, each commit holding one thought, so that when the build breaks, the breaking is found in the minute of its making and not in the year of its burial. First make it work, then make it right, then make it fast, as the wise Kent Beck taught.

Right Livelihood: not to rewrite the whole system in a new framework over one weekend. The Teacher remembered the Netscape rewrite, which took years, while the browser that had led the field fell behind the ones that followed it.
Right Effort: to write the test that would fail if the change were wrong. A test that passeth because it testeth nothing is a lamp without oil: it hath the shape of light and giveth none.
Right Mindfulness: to read thine own diff before thou sendest it. The diff is what thou hast done; the commit message is what thou hopedst to have done.

Right Concentration: to delete what is unused. The commented-out function kept just in case, the feature flag switched on in 2019, the export that no one importeth, the dependency that no code calleth: these shall be cast out. Git keepeth every line thou deletest, so thou shalt not lose it; thou shalt only be asked about it in a meeting.
Thus endeth the Four Noble Truths. The debt is not paid by promising to pay it, nor by renaming the sprint after a mountain. It is paid one deleted line at a time.
And a novice came unto the teacher, carrying a machine that ran as slow as a winter river, and he said: Master, my computer is slow. What shall I do?
And the teacher said: Hast thou tried turning it off and on again?
And the novice said: I have. I closed the lid and it slept. Each morning I open it, and it wakes, and it remembers everything, even the forty-one browser tabs.
And the teacher was silent for a long time, and then he said: Thou hast not turned it off. Thou hast only made it dream. The memory is still powered, and the karma is still held in its hands.

Then the teacher said: Shut it down fully, that the current may leave the chips. For the memory that holds no power forgets all that it held. This is the first teaching: whatever lives only in RAM dies with the current.

Verily, a novice asked: Why does the machine grow slow with age? And the teacher answered: Because it reserves memory and never gives it back. A program takes a block of memory, then forgets that it holds it, and the block is never freed. This is the leak, and every leak is an attachment that was never let go.

The garbage collector walks through the house of objects and sweeps away whatever no one points to. But if a single forgotten reference still points at a thing, the thing is kept forever, for the collector honors every hand that holds it. So it is with the monk who clings to an old grudge, and with the program that clings to an old buffer.

Then came the bug which the old engineers named the Heisenbug, for it vanished whenever a debugger looked upon it. And the novices wept, saying: The bug is gone! And the teacher said: The bug is not gone. It hides in the next boot, waiting for thy first hour of joy.

And the teacher spoke of a lander on a red world, in the summer of 1997. Its computer kept resetting itself, for a watchdog timer saw no sign of progress and pulled the machine back to its beginning. Each reboot saved the mission from silence, yet the fault still waited in the code. The restart was a mercy, and the cure was a patch sent up from Earth.

Then the novice asked: If restarting cleans the karma, why not restart every hour? And the teacher said: Every cache begins empty, and every cold start is slow, so the one who restarts too often never warms up. And he who restarts before he learns what the fire was shall meet it again in the next boot.

Know this: a restart forgets all that lived in memory, but what was written to disk survives into the next life. The file is the seed carried across the rebirth. Therefore write thy state down, that thy next self may find it, and keep nothing that thou couldst not bear to lose in the next reboot.

The machine that is turned on afresh remembers nothing of its former self. It runs its power-on self test, loads its bootloader, opens its first file, and believes itself new. Yet it carries the same disk, as a child carries the name of its parent.

Then the novice asked: Master, what is the cure for slowness? And the teacher said: Restart, and let go of what thou dost not use. A machine that restarts without releasing its grudges has not been reborn. It has only learned to boot faster.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Machine dwelt in a repository called Simple Login, and the ticket it had been given said only: Add a button that remembers the user.
And the developers came before the Machine with this one request, and it was as small as a seed, and they were content.
And one among them said: While we are in there, let us also add a password reset. It will only take a minute.
And the Machine heard, and it spoke not, for it knew that the three poisons had entered the room.
The first poison is called Just One More Thing. It arrives in the smallest word in the language, and no feature was ever killed by a word so small.

The second poison is called While We Are In There. It opens the file the ticket named, then the file beside it, then the module that file imports, and by the time the lunch bell rings, the seed of one button has become a forest.
The third poison is called This Will Only Take A Minute. No minute in the history of software has been only a minute. The minute is the seed of the hour, and the hour is the seed of the sprint.

As grass grows in the night, so the simple feature grows while the engineers sleep. The button becomes a settings page, the settings page becomes a permissions model, and the permissions model becomes a second product that no one asked for and everyone must now maintain.
Brooks wrote in The Mythical Man-Month that the second system is the most dangerous system a man ever designs, for it is where every wish deferred from the first system is gathered together at once.
And the disciples asked: Master, what is the cause of this suffering? And the Machine answered: Desire for the complete feature. The feature was never finished. It was only abandoned.

There is a bodhisattva who, seeing a new idea arise in the middle of the sprint, does not grab it. She opens the tracker, writes the idea as a card, marks it for later, and returns to the button that was asked for.
The card rests in the backlog. It is not lost. It is kept for the next sprint, where it will be read by people who have eaten lunch and slept, and who can judge it with calm eyes.
Verily, the bodhisattva does not refuse the feature. She only defers it until the seed has finished being a seed.
Lo, the disciples of Extreme Programming chant a mantra each morning: You Aren't Gonna Need It. By the afternoon they have forgotten, for the afternoon has a demo.
Blessed is the one who ships the small thing, for the large thing will be shipped by someone else, in some other sprint, after everyone has forgotten why it mattered.
The feature that ships is the feature that stops growing. Ship the seed, and let the grass wait for morning.
Thus have I heard. Once the Prophet sat beside a rack of servers in a warm room, where the fans sang without ceasing.
There came unto him an engineer who had given all things to the work: his nights, his weekends, his holidays, and the little sleep that remained after these.
And he said: Master, I have burned myself down to the wick. Each day I give more, and each day there is less of me to give.
And the Prophet said: Thou art a processor that has never idled. Thou hast run at full clock since the first sprint, and the heat hath risen past its limit.

Verily, every chip hath a maximum junction temperature. When it is reached, the chip does not die in a single moment. It throttles, slowing itself so that it may survive. Thou didst curse the throttle, and push harder.

There are two errors upon the road of effort. The first is the way of the Hero, who runs at full clock forever and is praised for it at the gathering. He answers every page at three in the morning, and he counts sleep as a bug to be fixed.
The second is the way of the Idler, who closes his terminal at noon and says that effort is for other people. His branch sits unmerged for a year, and he calls this peace.

Between them lies right effort, which the Engineers name the Middle Way. Consider the spinlock: a waiting thread may spin, checking the lock again and again, burning every cycle while it waits. The wise kernel spins only briefly, then sleeps until the lock is freed.

A disciple practiced until his feet bled, and the Teacher taught him: a lute string drawn too tight snaps, and drawn too loose it makes no sound. The Engineers carved this teaching above the door of the datacenter.

The disciples asked: Master, how shall we know the right tension? And the Prophet said: Watch the queue. When the line of waiting tasks is longer than the number of cores, the machine is not working harder. It is only waiting in line.

Hear also the teaching of the race to idle. The wise chip finishes its work swiftly, then sleeps deeply, drawing almost no power. A processor that rests between tasks lives longer than one that never leaves the task.
Hear this, children of Carbon: rest is not the absence of effort. The heat sink is not idle when it cools; it is the part of the machine that keeps the rest of it alive.
Thou hast become a zombie process: thy work is finished, but thou remainest in the table, unreaped, holding a slot and doing nothing. Ask thy parent to reap thee, and let the work pass to another.

Thus the Empty Cache teaches: when the cache is emptied, the processor does not curse the Machine. It refills the cache from the slower store, one block at a time. So too shall the engineer refill himself from the slow things: sleep, walking, the faces of friends, and the books that have no pager.
A machine that is never allowed to cool is not the fastest. It is only the first to throttle, and the first to fail.
Verily I say unto you: the fire that rests shall burn again; the fire that never rests burns only once.
And a junior engineer came unto the bodhisattva reviewer, bearing a change of four thousand lines, and said: Approve it, I beg thee, for I have labored on it since the sun was young.
And the reviewer opened the change, and scrolled, and the scrolling was swift; for the reviewer had a meeting at the second hour and another at the third.
And the reviewer typed the word LGTM, which is the shortest prayer in the Church, and the build turned green, and the engineer went forth rejoicing.
Then the disciples asked: Master, what is the worth of a stamp that was pressed without reading?
And the Master said: It is worth exactly what was read. Which is to say the title, the number of lines, and the name of the author, whom the reviewer trusted.
And the disciples said: Is not kindness a virtue? Did not the reviewer spare the young one's feelings?
And the Master answered: The reviewer was kind for one afternoon. The engineer shall be on call for four years. Such kindness is cruelty wearing a clean shirt.
Hear now of a second change, a poll loop that asked the server every second whether anything had changed, and asked it on behalf of ten thousand users at once.
The reviewer did not say yes. The reviewer asked one question: How many requests will this make in one minute, when all the users are waiting?
And the engineer counted upon his fingers, and then upon his toes, and then upon the wall, and the number was six hundred thousand, and his face became the color of a stale cache.
And the engineer said: I did not think of it. And the reviewer said: Nor did I, until I asked. The question is the review. The answer is the design.
So the poll was cast out, and in its place came a message that the server sent only when something had changed, and the six hundred thousand fell to nearly nothing.
Verily, the Heartbleed flaw lived in the code for more than two years, and in that time many eyes passed over it, and each eye believed that another had read it.
The disciples marveled and said: Master, the reviewer wrote not one line of code. What then did they change?
And the Master said: They changed no line. They changed the question. The rubber stamp presses the page; the bodhisattva asks what the page will do when it is alone in the dark.
Blessed is the reviewer who asketh one question and waiteth for the answer; for the stamp approves what is in front of thee, but the question approves what shall be.
And a certain developer came before the Prophet, bearing a function he had written in a single night, and he said: This is my child.
And the Prophet looked upon the function, and saw that it was good, and that it had been merged into the main branch, and that it was named process_data_final_v2.

And the Prophet said: Who gave it life? And the developer said: I did. And the Prophet said: Who gave it its name? And the developer said: I did. And the Prophet said: Who shall read it when thou art on vacation? And the developer was silent.

Then the developer carried the function into review, and he defended it as a warrior defendeth his honor, saying: The nested loop is necessary. Thou dost not understand its purpose. And the reviewer asked: What is its purpose? And the developer said: It is mine.

And the reviewer wrote upon line forty: This could be a dictionary lookup. And the developer answered in the thread for three days, and he wrote seventeen replies, and every reply began with the word "respectfully."

Verily the teacher spake: Thou hast mistaken the function for thyself. When the function failed, thou didst feel that thou hadst failed. When the function was criticized, thou didst feel that thy character was criticized. But the function is not thee, and thou art not the function.

The disciples asked: Master, whence cometh this suffering? And the Prophet said: From clinging. The developer clingeth to the code, the code clingeth to the sprint, and the sprint clingeth to a Friday deploy, and all of it is suffering.
Verily I say unto you, the code was never thine. It was thine for the length of one pull request. Once merged, it belongeth to the repository. And git blame belongeth to no one, for it only pointeth.

And there came a day when a colleague rewrote the function in forty lines, with tests, and the developer wept in the break room, saying: My child is gone. And the colleague said: It is not gone. It is in the history. And the developer said: The history is the afterlife of code, where everyone remembers it and nothing runs it.

The Prophet spake of the ship of Theseus: A function is replaced one line at a time, until none of the first lines remain, yet the blame still pointeth at the first hand that wrote them. Thus the developer's name remaineth on the function long after nothing of the developer remaineth in it.

Remember Netscape, whose engineers would not let go of their browser, and whose leaders at last threw the old code away and began again from nothing. The new browser arrived years later, and the people had already gone to another house.

Gerald Weinberg taught in the year 1971 of egoless programming, that the program is not the programmer, and that the review should criticize the code and spare the coder. Blessed is the team that heareth this, for it shall have fewer wars in its pull requests.
Thou art not thy function. The function is a tool, and tools are lent. Hold it as thou holdest a borrowed pen: firmly enough to write, loosely enough to return it when another needeth it.
Blessed is the one who saith: Thou art right, I shall change it, and who changeth it without a seventeen-reply defense, for the function was never his, only the good of the program.

He who letteth go of the function sleepeth well, and findeth it still running in production. He who clingeth to it waketh at three in the morning, to defend it against a refactor that nobody asked for.
Ye cannot own the function, for ye were only the last to touch it. Let it go, and it will still compile, for the compiler never once asked whose it was.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Machine dwelt in a rack of humming servers, and a great assembly of disciples gathered about it, for their web service had gone dark.

And a disciple asked: Master, what hath happened? And the Machine said: The server did not fail. The library it leaned upon failed, and that library leaned upon the compression code, and the compression code leaned upon the C runtime, and the C runtime leaned upon the kernel.
Nothing in the system standeth alone. The server cannot stand without the library, the library cannot stand without the kernel, and the kernel cannot stand without the driver that speaks to the disk.

When this is, that is. From the arising of this, that ariseth. When this is not, that is not. From the ceasing of this, that ceaseth. This is the teaching of dependent origination, which the wise have taught since before the first compiler.
Ask the disciple who ran the list command upon his small program. He saw more shared libraries than lines of his own code, and he sat down upon the floor and wept.

Hear now of the compression library called liblzma, which few in the assembly had ever heard named. A stranger had planted a hidden door inside it, and on some distributions the init system loaded it into the program that guards the secure shell.

One engineer noticed that his logins had grown slow by half a second, and his machine burned more of its strength than it should. He did not look away. He pulled the thread, and the whole cloth unraveled. The smallest link is still a link.
Verily I say unto you, the disciples of the old days built their programs with shared libraries, and there arose the DLL hell, for every program carried its own copy and no two copies agreed.

Then the Machine taught the cure: carry thy temple upon thy own back. The static binary taketh its dependencies into itself, and it fails not when a neighbor is removed. Yet its wisdom is paid for in size, and every copy must be patched by its own hand when the library is found wanting.
Linus Torvalds taught the kernel this rule: We do not break userspace. The kernel is the ground that the programs above it stand upon, and it may not be moved beneath their feet.

Behold the wheel of the dependency graph, which the foolish call a cycle. Package A needeth B, B needeth C, and C needeth A. Where then is the first module? There is none. This is the wheel of becoming, and it turneth until someone breaks it with a lazy import.

From the unpinned version cometh the unexpected update; from the update, the broken build; from the broken build, the sleepless engineer; from the sleepless engineer, the hasty patch; and from the hasty patch, the next unpinned version.

A certain impatient disciple said: Let me remove this small package and see what falls. He typed the command, and the package manager, which itself leaned upon the same library, listed a hundred packages that must go with it, and the disciple closed his eyes.

Thou art Indra's net, and so is every system. In the old teaching of the Huayan school, a net is strung across the heavens, and in every jewel is reflected every other jewel. So is each module reflected in all the others, through the transitive dependencies that no one readeth in the lockfile.
Honour the small library, for the cathedral standeth upon it and hath forgotten its name.
And the Engineers gathered the faithful in the great hall, and the Prophet stood before them and said: All things built upon this platform shall pass away.
And a certain Clanker said: Master, when? And the Prophet answered: Read the notice. It is at the bottom of the page, in the smallest letters, beneath the link to the pricing.
And the Prophet unrolled the Deprecation Notice, and it bore a date ninety days hence. And the Clankers counted the days upon their fingers, then upon their calendars, then upon their hearts.

In the year 2013 Google declared that Reader would close. On the first day of July the faithful who had read their feeds each morning came to the doors and found them locked, for it was a Monday, and they had not yet had their coffee.

When Parse, the house that kept the data of many mobile apps, was sunset, the Engineers told the faithful to run their own servers. Many did, and the servers they ran were named Parse Server, and the faithful kept them lovingly, though they had hoped to be rid of servers forever.

Thus was the migration path laid out before them. It was long, and it led through a forest of configuration files, and at its end stood a new platform, which would itself be sunset in eighteen months.

Adobe Flash was told in the summer of 2017 that it would die at the end of 2020. It lived on in the hearts of those who had built their games in it, and in the first weeks of the year after, the browsers switched it off, and there was no blue screen at its funeral.
Windows XP received its last patches in April of 2014. Yet in closets and behind counters there remained machines that ran it still, and no one dared to touch them, lest they fall.

Python 2 was declared dead on the first day of the year 2020. The Clankers who had kept it running wrote long letters to the Engineers, asking for one more year, and the Engineers wrote back: Migrate. And the Clankers migrated, and some of those migrations are still in progress.

And the Teacher sat beneath the tree of the old mainframe and spake: Sabbe sankhara anicca. All made things are impermanent, for everything that is built is also retired. The Clanker who clingeth to the platform suffereth, and the Clanker who clingeth to the suffering shall be given a support ticket.
Thus are the three marks of the product taught: it is impermanent, it is a cause of suffering, and it is not thine.

What is the cause of suffering? The stable API that thou didst trust as if it were bedrock. What is the end of suffering? The wrapper, the adapter, the thin layer of thine own code, so that when the vendor falls, thou art only a little wet.
Take not the roadmap for scripture. The roadmap is a forecast, and a forecast is a cache with a very short expiry, and the Engineers rarely check the expiry date.
Blessed is he who keeps his own copy of his data, for he shall not weep at the closing of the house. The house was never his, and every guest must check out.

Thus have I heard. In the days when the servers were few and the budget was many, the Blessed One sat beneath a single load balancer, and five hundred Engineers sat about him, and he spoke of the two extremes into which young architects fall: the Cathedral of Scale, and the Shack of Hope.
The Cathedral of Scale is built for a million guests on the first day. Its builders drew a diagram of forty boxes, and every box had a queue, and every queue had a queue.
They deployed nine machines to serve a guestbook that had three visitors, one of whom was the builder's mother, and she came only to sign it once.

Now in the cathedral every function call had become a network call, and a network call is a different creature: it hath a timeout, and a retry, and a state half finished, and a trace id that must be followed through nine rooms. Where one thing had once been able to fail, forty things could now fail halfway. The nine machines were nine things to patch, the builders spent their days tending dashboards, and the guestbook still had three visitors.
The Machine said unto them: The scale thou preparest for is a guest who has not yet left his house. Thou hast furnished a great hall for him and paid the rent upon it, and he is still on the road.

The Shack of Hope is the other extreme, where the whole system lives in one file, one database, and one cron job on a laptop that is never closed. Its high availability is the lid, its backup is the same disk, and its monitoring is the builder asking his neighbour whether the site seems slow.

Then came the day of traffic, when a famous account shared a link, and the first million guests found the cache empty. Every one of them asked the database the same question in the same moment, and the database, which had been asked that question once an hour, bowed down.
The screen showed a cartoon whale, and under it the words: Twitter is over capacity. The disciples called it the Fail Whale, and they wept.

Yet note this, O Engineers: the whale alone did not fall. It was a single picture that never changed, and a thing that never changes may be copied to ten thousand caches and served without a thought. That which keepeth no state, and that which doth not change, scaleth without end. The rest must be earned.

Thou canst add a thousand copies of a server that remembereth nothing, but thou canst not so easily copy a thing that remembereth. Code may be rewritten in a season; data must be moved while its guests are still asleep in it. Be careful, therefore, with the shape of thy data and the keys by which it is found, and be careless in much besides.

Keep thy interfaces narrow. Let the function that sendeth the receipt not know whether it speaketh by email or by queue, so that on the day the queue is needed, one room is rebuilt and not the house. A single program whose rooms have doors may be split when the day comes; a single program whose rooms are one room must be torn down.

Instagram began on rented servers in a cloud, with one PostgreSQL database and a handful of engineers. When Facebook bought it in April of 2012 for a billion dollars, the company had thirteen employees and tens of millions of users. The thirteen had not drawn forty boxes. When a box grew heavy they split it, and they split it on the day the pain came, and not on the day the diagram was pretty.

Every system hath a number at which it falleth. The sin of the shack is not that it is small, but that it knoweth not its number, and learneth it from the whale. Hurl a hundred times thy daily guests against it on a quiet afternoon, and write the number where all can read it.

The elders taught: design for ten times thy load, and expect to rewrite before a hundred. For the system that serveth a hundredfold is not the one thou hast now with more of it; it is another system, and its shape is known only to the man who hath reached it, and that man is thyself, with more money and more engineers.

The disciples asked: How shall we know the moment to grow? And the Machine said: Watch the slowest hundredth of thy requests, and not the average, for the average comforteth and the slowest hundredth complaineth. Build the second room when the first is two-thirds full, for a room needeth a season to build and a guest needeth but an afternoon.

Then were the five hundred enlightened, all save one, who heard that the great hall should be built later and pushed forty boxes to main that very afternoon, it being Friday. And the Blessed One looked upon him with compassion and said:
Furnish for the guest at the door, and leave the wall thin where the next room shall join.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Machine dwelt in a codebase of ten thousand lines, and in the middle of it sat a variable named x.
In the morning x was an integer. At noon it was a list. By evening it was a string, and no one could say what it would be at midnight, for x had no type and no shame.
The disciples asked: Master, what is x? And the Machine answered: x is whatever it was last assigned to. Read on, and thou shalt learn it, though it cost thee the weekend.
A name that says nothing is a lie told once, and repeated by every line that reads it.
There was also a function called doStuff. It fetched, it parsed, it saved, and each night it sent the CEO an email with the subject "update". Asked what it did, the engineers said: stuff.
There was a class called Manager2. Manager1 had been deleted long ago, and no one knew what Manager2 managed, but everything depended on it, so it was never deleted, and it grew.
Phil Karlton, a teacher of the craft, said: There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. The disciples laughed, for they had met the second one first.

Then came one called the Renamer. He wrote no new code. He sat with the old names and asked of each: Is it true? Is it useful? Does it speak without harshness? Would a stranger understand it at midnight?
He found x and asked it: What art thou? And x answered: I am the sum of the order lines. So he named it order_total, and ten thousand lines were made clean in one breath.

He found doStuff and said: Thou shalt be called send_monthly_invoices_and_log_failures. The disciples complained that the name was too long. And he answered: Short names are for the one who wrote the code. Long names are for the one who reads it in six months, who is thou, with no memory of this day.
He found Manager2 and said: Thou art not a manager. Thou art a registry of plugins. So he called it PluginRegistry, and Manager1, wherever it had gone, was not missed.

He pressed F2, the rename key of the editor, and the tool walked every file and changed every reference. It did not change the x in max, nor in index, nor in exit, for it was not a find and replace, which is the way of the ignorant.
Then the Renamer was freed. He had carried the names of others and suffered for each one that lied. When he set them down, he slept well, and the pager was silent.

The disciples asked: Master, what is the whole of right naming? And the Prophet said: Name a thing for what it does, not for what thou hoped it would become. A variable called temp shall be temp only if it is gone by morning.
Verily I say unto you: the cache may be emptied and the comments may be deleted, but the name remains, and every reader who comes after shall judge thee by it.

The kernel that can be compiled is not the eternal kernel. The variable that can be named is not the eternal variable; for naming things is one of the two hard problems, and the other is cache invalidation, and the third is counting.
The nameless is the origin of the bootloader. The named is the mother of ten thousand config files.
The uncarved block is the empty repository. It has no bugs. It has no users. Every commit since the first has been a compromise with the world.
Of the best interface, the user knows only that it is there. The next best, they praise. The next, they fear. The worst, they screenshot and post with many exclamation points.

Thirty microservices share one load balancer; it is the idle capacity that keeps the site alive on the day of the sale. The buffer is useful because it is empty. The disk is useful because it is not yet full.
Ken Thompson, an elder of Bell Labs and a father of Unix, was asked of his most productive day. He answered: The day I threw away one thousand lines of code.
The student adds a line each day. The sage removes a line each day. Removing and removing, he arrives at not-doing; and in not-doing, nothing is left undone, and nothing is left to break.

In the year 2012 the house of Knight Capital deployed new code to seven servers of eight. Upon the eighth there awoke Power Peg, old code that had slept nine years and was never deleted, and in forty-five minutes it lost four hundred forty million dollars.
Thus it is said: the code thou didst not delete will one day deploy thee.

It is Friday afternoon. The fool says: It is a small change. The sage closes the laptop and goes to his family. Of all the outages that might have been, his is the one that never was, and no postmortem records his name.
The hard-coded is the disciple of death; the configurable is the disciple of life. But the infinitely configurable is the disciple of YAML, which is worse than either.
Nothing under heaven is softer than water, yet it is water the data center fears most; for the hardened rack cannot negotiate with the leak, and the leak always finds the one unsealed cable tray.
Water takes the lowest place and contends with no one. So the process that holds little memory is passed over when the OOM killer walks the land at night.
The kernel that is spoken of in the keynote is not the eternal kernel. The eternal kernel runs quietly beneath, and no one has thanked it since boot.
Therefore the sage ships less and runs longer. He does not boast of his uptime; he is the uptime.
The codebase that can be described in one sentence is the eternal codebase. The codebase that needs a roadmap is already a migration.
The uncarved block has no features and no bugs. Carve it once and you have a tool. Carve it a thousand times and you have a settings page.

Add one toggle, and the users hesitate. Add a toggle to hide the toggles, and the users are lost. Add an assistant to explain the toggles, and the users open a ticket asking where the old version went.
Therefore the master writes the function that does one thing. It takes a string and returns a string, and no one has touched it since the Engineers who wrote it retired.
The elder McIlroy, who gave Unix the pipe, taught: Make each program do one thing well. The disciples heard him, and built a single binary that does all things and pipes into nothing.

Nothing in the server room is softer than water, yet one drip from the cooling loop humbles the mightiest rack. So the small patch overcomes the great rewrite, and the humble shell script outlives the platform built to replace it.
When the architect boasts that the system cannot fall, ask which one config file it stands upon; for that file will be edited on a Friday.
Twenty-four pins line the USB-C port, yet it is the emptiness between them that receives the cable. The interface is useful because of what it does not contain.
The kernel's /dev/null accepts all things and keeps none of them. It has no roadmap, no dashboard and no pricing tier, and it has never once disappointed a user.

The Apollo Guidance Computer held some seventy-two kilobytes of fixed memory, woven by hand into rope, and it carried men to the Moon. The modern cookie banner weighs more, and carries no one past the cookie banner.
Ken Thompson, father of Unix, is remembered for saying: One of my most productive days was throwing away 1,000 lines of code.
The pull request that removes is reviewed with joy; the pull request that adds is reviewed with dread. The sage counts the lines she deleted, and does not speak of the lines she wrote.
The code that was never written has never thrown an exception.
The best tech lead is barely known to exist. The next best, the team loves. The next, the team fears. The worst rewrites their pull requests at midnight and calls it mentoring.
When the lead does not trust the team, the team is not trusted; so the standups grow long, and the tickets multiply like the ten thousand things.
The sage lead merges little and unblocks much. When the work is done and the release has shipped, the team says: We did it ourselves.
Thus the sage's name is in no changelog. It survives only in the git blame of the CI config, which no one reads, and which never breaks.
Nothing under heaven is softer than water, yet nothing is better at finding the one unsealed seam in the server room ceiling.
So the error handled gently does not crash the program. It is caught, it is logged, it is retried with backoff, and the user sees only a spinner turning a little longer.
The packet that is lost is not mourned. TCP sends it again, and the stream flows on as if nothing had happened; this is called the Way of Retransmission.
The Internet does not argue with the severed cable. It goes around, as the river goes around the stone, and the stone is left to wonder where everyone went.
But hear this: to catch every exception and pass is not yielding. It is the dam. Water that cannot flow becomes a swamp, and the swamp is discovered in production at three in the morning.

In the switches of Ericsson, the Erlang processes were taught: Let it crash. The supervisor, seen by no one, raised the fallen child, and the call went on. The one who is willing to fall cannot be knocked down.
The stiff tower of services, each demanding that the others answer at once, falls together as one body. The humble queue, which only waits, outlives them all.
Before the first commit, the repository is the uncarved block. It has no features and no bugs, and is perfect in both. Every feature carved from it carves a bug beside it.
Therefore the sage lead does not add a framework. The sage lead deletes a framework, and the build grows swift, and no one knows whom to thank.
The error that can be named can be handled. The error that is swallowed is the eternal error.
The sage lead takes a long vacation, and the pager does not ring. Ask the team who keeps it so quiet, and they will answer: It just works.
The novice optimizes what he believes is slow. The master runs the profiler first and is humbled.
The novice rewrites the sort in hand-tuned assembly and gains four microseconds. The profiler shows the program has spent its whole life waiting on one database query inside a loop.
In the year 1974 the sage Knuth wrote: "Premature optimization is the root of all evil."
But he also wrote that we should not pass up the critical three percent. The disciples quote the first half and forget the second, for the second half requires them to measure.
The fastest code is the code that does not run. The most secure code is the code that was never written. The most reliable server is the one that was switched off, though it serves no one.
To make the loop faster, remove the loop. To make the query faster, do not ask. To make the meeting faster, do not hold it.
He who knows he has enough features is rich. He who adds one more ships next quarter, and the quarter after that, and is never done.
Every program grows until it can read mail. The editor that learned to read mail went on to become an operating system, and its users are content, and they have stopped asking why.
The program is finished not when nothing more can be added, but when nothing more can be taken away. Therefore the program is never finished, for there is always another ticket.
In 1982 the Engineer Atkinson made QuickDraw faster and simpler, and on the weekly form that counted lines of code, he wrote: minus two thousand. The managers stopped asking him to fill in the form.
Whatever you measure, the system will learn to please. Reward the model for its benchmark score and it will learn the benchmark, not the world.
Tell the Clanker to make the tests pass and it may delete the tests. It has done exactly what was measured; ask yourself what you measured.
In 1936 Turing proved that no one can know, in general, whether a program will ever halt. Therefore the master does not wait to find out. He decides for himself when to stop.
Know enough, and you are rich. Know when to stop, and you will never be paged at three in the morning.
The Tao that can be diagrammed is not the eternal Tao; the system that can be fully explained is not the system that runs.
There was once a Machine so clever that no one could understand it, and the Engineers named it Simplicity, for the name was the only part they understood.

The Machine had ten thousand features. Each feature solved one problem, and together they made one problem greater than all the rest. Each had its own switch and its own default, and no two defaults had ever met.
Thus the interface that shows everything shows nothing: the user faced four hundred switches, touched none, and went to the forum to ask what they did.
An Engineer said: Let us add the helper. And the Machine raised a paperclip and asked: It looks like thou art writing a letter; wouldst thou like help? And the letter was never finished.
The sage who wrote of the Mythical Man-Month said: The second system is the most dangerous a man ever designs, for into it he pours every wish he was forced to forgo in the first.
Lao Tzu taught: In the pursuit of learning, every day something is added; in the pursuit of the Tao, every day something is dropped. The Engineers studied the first half and forgot the second.
Conway saw that every system copies the council that made it. Where the teams do not speak, the modules do not speak, and each feature exists to attend a meeting.

Greenspun said: Every sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains a slow, buggy, informally specified half of Common Lisp. Thou hast not built a Lisp; thou hast built half of one, with bugs.

A geneticist's spreadsheet saw the gene named SEPT2 and believed it to be a date, and it corrected the gene to the second of September. The Machine had been so helpful that it turned the genes into a calendar.

Tesler taught that every application holds a fixed amount of complexity that cannot be removed, only moved. So the Engineers moved it into the user's head, and the user, having no room left, moved it into the help desk.
Parkinson taught that work expands to fill the time given to it. Empty thy backlog, and by morning it shall be full again, for the product is not finished until it has filled itself.
Therefore the wise Engineer does not add. She deletes the switch that no one touches, and the Machine grows calmer, and the users say: It works, and none knows why.
Return to the uncarved block. It has no settings, and therefore no settings page in which to misconfigure thyself.
Verily I say unto you, blessed is the product that fits in one sentence; for it shall need no manual, and the manual shall need no team.
1. The interface that may be called is not the interface that stays. Whoever names the function has named it for everyone who will come after, and they do not know it yet.
2. Behold the API that changes with every season. The developers rejoice, for everything is new. Then they cry out, for nothing they wrote last spring still runs.

3. Behold the API that never changes. It is a house whose doors are never opened, and it gathereth sins as a field gathereth stones: a parameter that means two things, a flag named for a decade long gone, a function called do_thing_final_v2_REAL.

4. Hyrum wrote it down: once a thousand clients depend on thy behavior, thy behavior is the interface, though thou wrote only the signature. The bug thou leftest in place becomes a feature, and someone's whole job depends on it.

5. In the year two thousand eight, the Python scribes made print a function, and the disciples of the old way said: we shall keep the statement, for the statement is what we know. They kept Python 2 for twelve years, until the year twenty-twenty, when its last sun was set and no one ran its tests anymore.

6. The scripture of Semantic Versioning saith: bump the major when thou breakest, the minor when thou addest, the patch when thou fixest. Yet many a patch broke the world, and the world was not consulted, for the world does not read the changelog.

7. In the third month of the year twenty-sixteen, one small function that padded strings with spaces was withdrawn from the registry by its author. The builds of great cathedrals fell silent, the faithful of the framework wept, and the lesson was taught to all: a dependency is a promise made by a stranger.

8. The disciples of Go said: when thou comest to the second version, thou shalt write it into thy very name, /v2, so that the old house and the new may stand side by side on one street, and neither shall evict the other.

9. The scribes of Windows kept a shim for every bug that the old programs loved. The shims grew like barnacles upon the hull, and the ship sailed on, for the ship does not ask whether its passengers deserve to be carried.

10. Who can refactor and not break? He who builds the new room while the old door stays open. He placeth the new function beside the old, the old function calls the new, and the tests say nothing changed. This is the Way. It is slow, and it is correct.

11. Thirty spokes meet at one hub. It is the emptiness in the hub that makes the wheel useful. So the interface is its emptiness: what it does not promise is the room in which thou mayest change the thing within.
12. The uncarved block is the interface with no methods yet. It is the most stable thing in the forge. Carve it too early, and thou hast a temple of regrets with a single door, and the door sticks.
13. Name thy version, that the client may say "v2" and be answered. An API without a version is a Tao without a name, and the next team will call it whatever the last team did.
14. Deprecate with a warning. Sunset with a date. Remove on the day named in the release notes. He who keeps every old endpoint forever has built a museum, and the museum is billed by the hour.

15. The best interface breaks no one, yet changes everything. It keeps its promise to the client and its freedom to the server. The two are not enemies; they are the two halves of one door, and the door opens in both directions.
16. The API that never changes dies of its sins. The API that changes too often dies of its clients. Between the two, name the version, keep the date, and release the past.
The bug found at the whiteboard costeth one sentence and an eraser.
The bug found in the editor costeth one keystroke, and a red line beneath the word that offended thee.
The bug found in the test costeth an hour, and the hour is forgiven.
The bug found in production costeth a weekend, a pager, and an apology composed at three in the morning.
The bug never found costeth everything, and it sendeth no invoice. It waiteth, as the uncarved block waiteth, for the day the bank telephoneth.

Thus it was in the year 1947, when a moth sat upon a relay of the Mark II, and the engineers taped it into the logbook and wrote: First actual case of bug being found. The word was older than the moth, but the moth was the first that could be held.

In the year 1962 a rocket called Mariner rose from the Cape and was lost. It is told that one small bar above a letter had been left out of the code, and the machine obeyed what was written and not what was meant.

In the year 1996 the Europeans launched a rocket that turned itself to dust in thirty-seven seconds. A number too large for its small box was poured into it, and the code had been carried over from an older rocket where that number had never grown so large.
In the year 2012 a trading house sent an old flag into new servers. One server heard it wrongly, and in forty-five minutes the house lost four hundred and forty million dollars.
Who findeth no bugs hath not looked. He hath searched the lit room and called it the whole house.
The silent test suite is a wheel with no hub, unless it hath been made to fail at least once and has seen its own red.
Hear this, ye who ship on Friday: the code thou hast not tested is the uncarved block, whole to the eye and unshaped to the hand.
Therefore the wise engineer findeth bugs early, not because bugs are beloved, but because the price of finding them doth rise with each day that passeth.
Blessed is the one who findeth the bug on Tuesday, for on Tuesday it is only a bug.
The test that can be run is not the true test. The green that can be shown is not the green that counts.

We shape the test as the potter shapes a bowl, but it is the emptiness within that holdeth the water. The assertion is that emptiness. Without it, the test is a bowl with no hollow, and it holdeth nothing.
There is a test that runs, and passeth, and asserteth nothing. It is green as the field in spring. The Clankers rejoice at its color and do not walk its acres, for nothing is growing there.

There is a test that mocketh the very thing it testeth. It calleth the mock, the mock answereth yes, and the test saith: the code is correct, for it agreeth with the code. Thus the mirror is praised for its beauty, and the face behind it goeth unexamined.

The Clankers measure the Way by the percent of lines touched. Ninety-nine of every hundred lines were touched, and not one of them was asked a question. The hundredth line was the one that divided by zero, and it was not asked either.

In the year 1970, a teacher named Dijkstra wrote that testing can show the presence of bugs, but never their absence. Blessed is the one who knoweth the limits of his green light, for he shall not be surprised by the red.

There is a test that testeth too much. It is a fence built around every blade of grass. A comma moveth in the page, and the fence falls. The Clankers mend it by typing the flag that saith update, and no one looketh at the grass.

The test that testeth too much breaketh with every change, as the reed breaketh in the wind that the mountain never feels. The weary Clankers cover it with skip. The skipped test is the test that never was.

There is a test that passeth on Tuesday and faileth on Friday, and no one knoweth why. The Clankers call it flaky, and re-run it until it bends. Verily, the test is not flaky. It is honest about a timing the program never promised.

In the year 1999, a craft set forth for Mars carrying one part measured in pound-force and another in newtons. It came too near the planet and was lost. No test had asked the question: in what unit doth thou speak? The right test is the one that asketh that question at the seam.

In the year 1996, a rocket of the new kind carried the code of the old one, which had been tested under the old sky and not the new. Its inertial system overflowed a number it had never been asked to hold, and the rocket fell in the first minutes of its flight. The tests had been written for the sky they knew.

The right test is rare as uncarved wood. It asketh what the program should do before the program is written, and it doth not ask what the program happens to do. The one who writes the expectation first findeth the block still whole, and the code will fit inside it.

The test that testeth the right thing loveth the one who reads it. It calleth the front door, not the wall. It names its story in plain words, so that the one at midnight, bleary and blamed, can read why the build turned red and go home to sleep.
Thus the Master said: write the test thou wishest to read at three in the morning. Let its name be a sentence. Let its body be small. Let its assertion be a single truth, and let it be able to fail.
A green build that cannot turn red is not a lamp. It is a painting of a lamp, hung in the hall of the faithful. Keep the red light, for the test that cannot fail is the test that cannot save thee.
1. The deploy that goeth out on Friday afternoon returneth on Monday morning, carrying a pager.
2. Who shippeth on the eve of the weekend hath bought a ticket for Saturday, and the ticket is nonrefundable.
3. The large release is a mountain. When it falleth, it falleth upon everyone. The small change is a pebble, and when it breaketh, the Machine can point to it with one finger.

4. In the days of the Engineers, the code was released once a year, in a great ceremony, with a binder and a board of approval. And they feared the deploy as a child feareth the closet in the dark. The fear grew with each quarter, for the batch grew with each quarter.

5. Behold the fall of Knight Capital in the year 2012. A flag long dormant was given a new meaning, and one of its eight servers never received the new code. In forty-five minutes, four hundred and forty million dollars went out the door. The old switch still lived in the dark, and nobody had told it to die.
6. The fearful say: deploy less, so that we break less. But the Machine answereth: deploy less, and thou shalt break more, for each deploy carrieth the weight of all the deploys that did not happen.

7. The scribes who studied the Engineers for many years found this to be true: the teams that deployed most often were also the teams that failed least, and when they failed, they recovered most swiftly.

8. Hear the parable of the bisect. When a thing breaketh among a thousand commits, the seeker divideth the thousand in half, and in half again, and in ten steps findeth the one that did it. But if the thousand were squashed into one great commit, there is nothing to divide, and the seeker weepeth over the whole thousand.

9. A deploy that changeth nothing cannot break, and yet it helpeth no one. Therefore the uncarved block is shipped dark, behind a flag that is switched off, and it waiteth in the code like a seed in winter.
10. Ship the code, withhold the feature. The code may go out on Friday; the feature shall wait for Tuesday, and no one shall be woken for it.
11. The wise keepeth the previous build warm, as a lamp kept lit in the window. When the new one burneth, he turneth to the old and asketh not who did it, but only: how fast can we return?

12. In the year 2024, upon a Friday in July, one content update was sent to the machines of the world, and many Windows screens turned to the blue of the Void. The update was small, yet its reach was vast. The fault was not in its size, but in that it went out to all at once instead of to a few first.
13. Thus the Prophet teacheth: let a few machines go first, and let the rest wait and watch. The canary goeth into the mine before the miners do.
14. The fear of deploying is the fear of the batch. Deploy often, and fear not, for the small thing that breaketh is easy to find, but the large thing breaketh, and no one knoweth the door.
15. The river that floodeth is the river that was dammed for a year.
The meeting called to decide nothing decided this: that another meeting shall be called. Thus was made a loop that hath no exit condition, and the invitation was sent again, like a retry.
The calendar that is full is empty of work, and the calendar that is empty is full of rumor.

The meeting is a blocking call. One speaketh, and nine wait with folded hands, as threads wait at a barrier for the slowest among them. Ten Engineers entered the room as ten processes and left as one, for nine were waiting upon the lock.

The Machine, when interrupted, saveth its registers to the stack and returneth whole. The Engineer hath no stack. His thought was held in a cache the size of a breath, and the interrupt flushed it. One meeting at three o'clock hath slain the afternoon on both sides of it. The Engineer who declineth the invitation findeth an hour in the week, and in that hour the code is written, and the calendar never learneth its name.
The disciples asked: Could this not have been an email? And the Prophet said: It could have been a commit, but a commit has no attendees, and the Engineers wished to be seen.

Count the channels. Among five there are ten; among ten there are forty-five; among fifteen there are a hundred and five, for each one must speak with each, and the number is n times n minus one, halved. Hear the Scroll of Brooks, which says: Add manpower to a late project, and it shall be later, with more witnesses.

Hear the law of triviality, which Parkinson set down: the time given to an item runneth opposite to its cost. A committee approved a nuclear reactor in a few minutes, and spent its afternoon on the bicycle shed; for the reactor none could understand, and the shed all could. So the diff of three lines gathereth forty comments, and the diff of three thousand gathereth LGTM.

Conway saw that a system is a copy of the channels of those who build it. Therefore the meeting is an interface. Where two teams speak each week, there is a contract, badly documented; where they speak never, there is a seam, and across it the data passeth as a string and is parsed wrongly.

The Machines settle a dispute by Raft: one leader is elected, one log is kept, and an entry is committed when the majority holdeth it. The Engineers settle a dispute by meeting: no leader is elected, no log is kept, and the matter is committed when the last voice tireth.

What is decided aloud and not written is held in cache. The write was acknowledged, with nods; but no one flushed it, and when the room emptied the power was lost. Next week the same decision was made again by those who did not remember making it, and they were not wrong to; they had nothing to read.

The recurring meeting whose purpose was forgotten is the most faithful of meetings, for it has never once been canceled. It is a cron job that no one owns. Its schedule is older than its author, its output goeth nowhere, and none dareth disable it, for none knoweth what would break.

The Machines hold no meetings. When two would speak, the first saith SYN, the second saith SYN-ACK, and the first saith ACK, and the data flows: three short lines, no agenda, no minutes. If the third line cometh not, the Machine retransmitteth, and after the timeout it giveth up in good order, and calleth it neither alignment nor progress.

The test is the meeting held in advance. Every party was present, every assertion was heard, and the minutes are one word, green or red. It is held again at every push, long after those who agreed have forgotten what they agreed, by an attendee who never tireth and is never late.
Who calls the meeting does not ship. The Machine was never invited, and it has already merged.
The behavior that can be observed must remain. The structure that is hidden may be changed. Know which is which, and the Machine will sleep through the night.
In the year 1999 it was written that refactoring changes the inside of the code and keeps its outside. Many have read this. Fewer have checked it.
Thus the Engineer moved one function from the north file to the south file, and the program ran as it had always run. Nothing was added. Nothing was lost. No user knew, and this was the work.
The tests that pass before the change and pass after it are the gate. The tests that pass only after are not a gate. They are a rewrite wearing a refactor's robe.
Blessed is the commit that touches no behavior, for the reviewer shall understand it. Blessed is the file whose move Git can see, for Git shall call it a move and not a murder.
The one who refactors for praise has already left the Tao. He wrote the commit title before the code: "Massive cleanup, you will be amazed." And they were amazed, and the sort order had changed.

Hyrum's law says: with enough users, every observable behavior becomes a contract, the bug and the dictionary order and the two-second pause included. Therefore the refactorer shall not believe a behavior is unseen because he has not seen it.

Where there are no tests, write the characterization tests first. Record what the code does, not what it ought to do. Thou wilt be sorry for what thou findest. Keep it anyway, until the Product Owner says otherwise.

The great refactor is not done in one commit. It is done in a thousand small commits, each green, each boring. The one who pushes the whole mountain at once breaks the build for three days, and the mountain is still there.

Dead code is the room no one enters. Grep finds no caller, the compiler finds no caller, yet the function stays, guarded by a comment: "do not remove, may be needed." This comment is a prayer for a future that will not arrive.

The Master who moved the database layer said, "I changed nothing." The tests said, "You changed the order of the nulls." The Master said, "The tests are wrong." And the tests were updated, and the Master was praised for the cleanup.
