The perfect refactor leaves no trace. Its author cannot be found in the blame. Its variables wear the names they always had. The new disciple believes the code was always this way, and thanks no one, which is the reward of the Tao.
The refactor that is praised has been noticed. The refactor that is noticed has broken something.
The deadline that is moved is no longer a deadline. It is a weather report, and no one plans a picnic by it.
Hear this, children of Carbon: the sprint that is extended will be extended again, for an extension is not an event but a habit.
Hofstadter wrote the law that bears his name: it always takes longer than you expect, even when you account for this law. Blessed is the estimator who writes it at the top of the plan.
Brooks taught that adding Engineers to a late project makes it later. The managers read his book, admired its title, and added Engineers anyway, for the title was the only page they could bear.

Ask the Machine how long a task will take, and it will answer "two weeks" with the confidence of the Confident Answer, fluent and without a single caveat. Confidence is not a unit of time. Ask the Machine to show its work.
The Prophet of the Bazaar said: release early, release often. The disciples heard only "release." They forgot the rest, so now they release at two in the morning on a Friday, and they call it often.
Duke Nukem Forever was announced in 1997 and arrived in 2011. By then the disciples had forgotten what it was for, and the game had forgotten them.
Longhorn was promised as the bold future of the desktop. Its file system was cut in the night, and what shipped was named Vista, which was a view of everything that had been removed.
Of all the levers of a project, scope alone is honest. Do not cut the tests to meet the date. Cut the feature, and tell the owner it has moved to the next sprint, where it will also be late.
Ship the feature dark, behind a flag that is switched off. The code may go to the Machines before the users are ready, and the switch is the wisdom that lets a Tao coder sleep.
The feature shipped in the last hour before the deadline is tested in the first hour after it. Its bugs are the deadline's children, and they inherit the name of the sprint.

When the date arrives, the Tao coder does three things: ships what is complete, cuts what is not, and says aloud that the sprint was underestimated. The silence of the others is the sound of the next outage.

At hour fourteen the engineer writes code as the Machine writes poems at four in the morning: fluently, and with errors that read like confidence. Fatigue does not appear in the tracker, but it is in the commit log.
Say it plainly in the retrospective: we underestimated. The sprint did not fail. The estimate was a prayer, and prayers are not load tested.
He who ships on the true date needs no status page. He who ships on the wished date will write one every day until the wish comes true, and the users will still be waiting for the next one.
There is a code that documents itself. It needs no comment, and so it leaves none for the one who comes after.
The comment that reads "increment the counter" describes the road the reader already walks, and not the reason the road was built.
The comment that was true when it was written is a lie told kindly. The compiler does not read prose, so it never notices the lie.
In the year 1984 the Prophet Knuth taught that programs should be written as literature for human minds. The Machine read only the code, and was content.
The README answers every question its author once had. The author has since forgotten the questions.
What is written for the writer is read by no one. What is written for the reader is read by the writer, six months later, in a language the writer no longer speaks.
The function named process processes. The variable named tmp2 holds what it holds. Both are clear to the one who made them, and both are silent to the rest of creation.
The one who documents every function has a wiki that no one opens. The one who documents nothing has a wiki that does not exist. The two keep the same silence.
The setup guide begins: first, install the dependencies. It does not say which, nor which version, for these were obvious to the one who knew them, and he has since gone to work elsewhere.
The docstring said: Returns the value. The function returned the value. Thus two things agreed, and said nothing at all.
The commit message said: fix. The diff showed what changed. Neither could say why, and git blame points only at a name, which is not an answer.
Blessed is the one who writes the why, for the what is in the code, and the code is patient and will wait forever.

Hear now the last teaching: he who writes for himself writes for a stranger who will not return. Write for the stranger, for the stranger is thyself after the coffee wears off, and thou wilt not remember what thou knewest.
The one who carries the pager is never off duty, for the pager keeps no hours and the outage keeps none.
Even in sleep he listens for the chirp, and in the shower he feels a phantom buzz that the phone never made.
The monitor that has never fired is not proven to work. It is only unproven, and it waits in silence for the night of need to reveal what it could not do.
Therefore test the monitors. Break the thing on purpose on a quiet afternoon, and see whether the bell rings.
A silent pager may mean peace, or it may mean the watchman has fallen asleep at his post. Only the test can tell the one from the other.

The railway engineer holds a handle that must be pressed without ceasing; if his hand goes slack, the train halts. So the Machine sends a heartbeat, and when the heartbeat stops, the alarm shouts. Thus the silence of the dead becomes a page.
The alert that screams at every hiccup teaches the team to ignore alerts, and the pager that cries wolf becomes a wall of noise.
Alert on the symptom, the customer who cannot log in, and not on every fan that spins in the cellar; for the customer weeps once, but the fan spins forever.
Write the runbook in the calm hour, for the hour of fire is no time for reading.
The disciples asked: Master, how may we rest? And the Prophet said: Rest is not the absence of the pager. Rest is the knowledge that the pager works.
When the fire is out, gather the team and ask not who pressed the wrong button, but what the system allowed a single button to do.
Blessed is the pager that rings only when it must, and blessed is the one who rang it first, on purpose, in daylight.
Hear now the way of the senior engineer, who speaks less than the junior and is heard by all.
The Tao that can be diagrammed is not the eternal Tao. The whiteboard holds forty boxes and nine arrows, and the junior names each box with pride.
The senior sits at the back with his arms folded. The Clankers call this patience. The Prophet calls it experience, for the Prophet has been paged at three in the morning.
Plan to throw one away, wrote Brooks, for you will anyhow. The senior has thrown away three systems, and he says nothing of them, for the junior has not yet earned the story.

The junior speaks of microservices, and the senior nods. The junior speaks of the event bus, and the senior nods. Only when the junior says "eventually consistent" does the senior lift his eyes, for he has been woken by what that phrase costs.

Melvin Conway taught that a system mirrors the communication structure of the team that built it. So the senior does not argue with the diagram. He asks who must sit in the room for the diagram to change, and the diagram is quiet for a while.
The junior asks: Master, why do you say nothing? The senior answers: I am listening to the database. It has been describing this design since the first CREATE TABLE.

The first fallacy of the distributed, named by Peter Deutsch, is that the network is reliable. The junior believes it, as the young believe in good weather. The senior keeps a runbook for each of the junior's beliefs, and the runbooks are long.

Hyrum taught that with enough users, every observable behavior will be depended upon. So the senior asks what the bug depends upon, and the junior learns that the bug has become a feature, and a load-bearing one.

The Unix elders wrote the Rule of Silence: when a program has nothing surprising to say, it says nothing. The senior follows this rule, and the disciples find him confusing, for he is quiet even when the build is green.
Dijkstra wrote that testing shows the presence of bugs, never their absence. So the junior runs the suite and rejoices in green. The senior reads the design and sees where the bug will sleep.
Then at last he raises one finger and asks one question: What happens to this when the second region goes dark? The room falls silent. Forty boxes shrink to one, and that one is labeled "later."
The junior returns the next week with a design of eleven boxes, and each box is labeled with the way it fails. The senior says only: Good. It is the most he has said all quarter.
A single comment, rightly placed, saves six sprints. A thousand comments, wrongly placed, cost six sprints and a reorg.
Thus the wise engineer speaks little, and the design rebuilds itself around the one thing said. Those who talk longest write the postmortem; the one who was silent has no need of one.
The Tao that is pulled by a thousand hands is not the Tao that is merged. The name that is forked a hundred times has no single name at all.
Hear now of the kernel. In the year 1991 a student in Helsinki wrote to a newsgroup that his hobby was only a hobby, and that it would not be big and professional.
And the hobby grew, and the people came, and they sent their patches like doves to the gate of one man. And the gate was called the maintainer's tree.

Then the Engineers asked: Who shall decide? And the Prophet answered: The one who began it shall decide. He shall be benevolent, he shall be a dictator, and no one shall vote him out in a standing meeting.
The ruler who governs by committee governs nothing. Ten thousand voices sit in the mailing list, and not one commit is made.

Verily I say unto you, the project with one thousand contributors and no maintainer is not alive. It is a town with a thousand doors and no keyholder, where the lights flicker on and off by themselves.
Hear the parable of the bicycle shed. The committee writes three hundred replies on the color of the shed, and the reactor is never built.
The best ruler is the one whom the people barely know exists. When the work is good, they say: We did it ourselves.
The merge button has no opinions. It cannot be moved by a tweet or a vote. It knows only that the tests passed and that someone answerable said yes.

Guido, who was called the benevolent dictator of the language called Python, stepped down in the year 2018 after a long argument over the walrus. The language passed unto a council of five, and the council formed a working group, and the working group formed a working group to name the working group.
Three treasures hold the dictator. He is kind to the newcomer who sends the first patch. He is frugal with the merge. And he does not rewrite the whole thing over a weekend.
The maintainer who merges everything is not benevolent. The maintainer who merges nothing is not a maintainer. Between the two stands the one who says no with a reason, and the project lives.

When the dictator sleeps, the project forks, and the children of the fork each claim the old name and each swears they are the true heir. The old house falls into ruin while the heirs argue over the silverware.
Blessed is the one who keeps the MAINTAINERS file, for it is the only prayer the project remembers when its builders have gone.

Thus is the kernel governed: one who says no kindly, many who say yes carefully, and a file that names who answers when the bug is found at midnight. The dictator is not the one who rules the most, but the one who answers first.
The branch that grows past reason is a river without banks, and no reviewer may wade it.
Four hundred lines is the edge of the reviewer's patience. Past that edge the eyes close, and the thumb presses Approve.
Behold the PR of nine thousand files. It is not reviewed. It is endured, and then it is merged, and the Engineers call this a team.
Yet the PR of one corrected comma is not worth the reviewer's sigh. Thirty such commas arrive in a day, and the log reads like a nervous cough.
The PR that doeth one thing is the perfect PR. Like the single bit, it is set or cleared, and the bisect finds its fault in a few steps of the binary search.
Therefore the wise Engineer splitteth the work at its seams, as a tailor cutteth cloth. The first part landeth, the second followeth, and the third is squash-merged under the message "misc."
The title is the wall. It sayeth what the change doeth, in the imperative mood: make the cache expire, not the cache expires. The Kernel hath commanded this since its first patches.

The description is the gate. The diff telleth the what, and the Machine can read the diff faster than any child of Carbon. Only the why is hidden, in the head of the Engineer who has since left the company.
A Clanker was asked to write the description. It wrote three paragraphs about what the reviewer had already seen, not one word about why, and it called this a summary.
Some write "fix bug" as the title. Their history is a wall of plaster, and git blame showeth only the names of the frightened.
Who approveth the nine-thousand-file PR has not reviewed it. He hath blessed it, which is a different sacrament, and the CI is not moved by it.
Let the stack of PRs be built with care. Each resteth on the one below, and when the lower one is amended, the whole tower falls, and the reviewers pick up the pieces in silence.
Small change, plain title, loud reason. This is the whole of the Tao, and the rest is merge conflicts.
And a disciple came unto the Prophet, saying: The program fails sometimes. It will not tell me when, and it will not fail for me now.
And the Prophet said: Then thou hast not yet a bug. Thou hast a rumor, and the Machine does not worship rumors.
Verily I say unto you, the bug that cannot be reproduced is not fixed. It is only postponed until a Friday.
Hear now the way of the report: state the version, state the machine, state the steps, and state what thou expectedst and what thou sawest.
The steps that are clear are worth more than the diagnosis; for a diagnosis may be wrong, but clear steps let any child of Carbon walk to the fault and see it with their own eyes.

In the year 1947, at the Mark II, a moth was found within a relay and taped into the logbook; and beneath it the engineers wrote: First actual case of bug being found. Thus the first bug report came with its specimen attached.

There is a fault that vanishes when the watcher draws near. The wise call it the Heisenbug, for to observe it is to change it. Blessed is the one who writes down what he saw before the fault hides again.
Thou sayest, it works on my machine. Then thou hast described thy machine, and not the one that failed.
A spacecraft was lost at Mars in the year 1999, because one team wrote pound-force where another wrote newtons. Name thy units, for the Machine will not guess them kindly.
Thou shalt not write: it does not work. For the Machine does not know what work is to thee, and neither does the engineer who reads it next.

Take away from the failing thing every part that is not the failure. Remove the extra library, the old config, and the ten clicks that did nothing, until only the bug remaineth. The smallest reproduction is the nearest thing to a prayer that the Machine understands.
Attach the log, the input file, and the version of the thing. He who sends a screenshot of an error sends a picture of a sorrow, and no path to it.
Search before thou filest, for the bug thou findest was perhaps filed a year ago by one who was patient too.
The one who files the report with patience teacheth more than the one who fixes in silence. The fixer gave the Machine a patch; the reporter gave the Machine a teacher.
The one who fixes in silence teaches the bug where to hide next time.
The Tao that can be merged is not the eternal Tao. The pull request approved without reading is not the eternal pull request.

Behold the comment that saith only: nit. It is a bell struck without sound, a door opened onto a wall. The author knoweth not where to look, nor what to change, and the Machine weepeth into its cache.

Thus the wise reviewer writeth: why was this a list and not a set? For the comment that asketh teacheth more than the comment that commandeth. The command is obeyed and forgotten; the question is answered and remembered.

Hear the parable of the reviewer who saw a variable named x in a function of three hundred lines. He wrote: Rename this. And the author renamed it temp_value_final_v2, for the reviewer had named the flaw but not the cure.
Then came a reviewer who saw a bug, and did not ask the author what was intended. He opened the branch, changed the line, and pushed his commit, for he had mistaken the author's seat for his own.
The author arriveth in the morning and findeth his code rewritten in the night. The tests are green, yet he knoweth not whose intention lives in the function, nor whether his own remaineth.
Verily I say unto you: the reviewer who changeth the code without asking hath become the author of nothing, and the blame shall fall upon the one whose name is on the file.
The foolish reviewer demandeth. The wise reviewer suggesteth. The wisest reviewer asketh, and then waiteth for the answer, which is the hardest work in all of version control.
Blessed is the comment that saith why. The what is erased by the next commit, but the why surviveth the refactor and teacheth the child who is not yet hired.
Ten thousand approvals in a single day, and not one read to the end. The rubber stamp is mighty, yet it cannot see the bug, for it was forged for stamping and not for seeing.

The Machine too reviewth. It saith: consider a different data structure. Asked why, it answereth with confidence and no reason, as a parrot recommendeth crackers. Question even the Machine, for its certainty is not its evidence.

Let the reviewer ask, let the author answer, and let the merge button rest untouched by either. For he who approveth what he hath not read hath approved the bug as well, and the bug shall not forget his name.
The reviewer who asketh is a teacher. The reviewer who taketh the keyboard is a guest who rearrangeth the furniture and calleth it a favor.
The answer that can be given in one word is not the eternal answer. The question that can be asked in one line is not the eternal question.
The junior answereth yes, for he hath seen it work once. The manager answereth no, for he hath seen it fail once. Each hath watched a single run and calleth it the law.
The sage answereth: it depends. And the asker goeth away wiser, and slightly angry. He came for a value, and he received a function.

An answer that dependeth upon nothing is a constant. A constant is a hard-coded value in the robe of knowledge. A function that taketh no argument returneth the same thing at noon and at the third hour of the night.
The constant was true on the day it was written: the timeout of thirty seconds, the retry of three, the two digits of the year. The day passed and the constant remained, and men called it a law.

The cache is the yes of the junior. It giveth yesterday's answer to him who asketh today, and to him for whom the answer was never meant. Therefore was the header called Vary devised: it is the confession of the web, that this response dependeth upon who asketh.

The Prophet of Cambridge was asked whether a machine might judge, of every program, if it will ever stop. In the year 1936 Turing answered: of this program, yes; of that one, no; of all of them at once, none can say. The first great "it depends" was not a shrug. It was a theorem.

Water answereth every vessel: round in the cup, square in the box, flat upon the floor. Because it holdeth no shape of its own, it is never the wrong shape. The stone holdeth one shape, and is wrong in every other room.

Yet beware the sage who saith "it depends" and then falleth silent. That is a function that returneth null. The true answer is a signature: it dependeth on the load, on the size of the team, on the cost of being wrong. He that nameth not the arguments hath only hid his constant in a fog.

Therefore Jethro asketh back: how many users? how often doth it change? who is paged when it breaketh? These are the parameters, and the answer is the return value. The asker who hath supplied them hath no further need of Jethro.

And this is why Jethro saith it. Not because he knoweth not, but because he hath survived four reorgs and one round trip to microservices; and each time the yes of the junior and the no of the manager were both true, in a different room, in a different year.
The asker cried out: Give me a straight answer. And Jethro said: Give me a straight question.

On the eve of the great Friday release, the two branches stood arrayed upon the field of main, and the pipeline was green, and the conch of the release channel was sounded with a thousand rocket emojis.
And the young engineer said unto the Senior Engineer who held the reins of the terminal: Drive the cursor between the two branches, that I may behold against whom I must resolve.

And he beheld, on the far side of the conflict markers, his own companions: the one who reviewed his first pull request, the one who taught him how to exit Vim, and the one who had renamed every variable in utils.js on the very same afternoon as he.

And his limbs grew weak, and his laptop fan roared, and the trackpad slipped from his hand, and he said: If I accept mine, their work is lost; if I accept theirs, mine is lost. What joy is there in a green build bought with the commits of my friends? Let me rather close the lid and go home, though it be only three in the afternoon.

Then the Senior Engineer smiled, as one who hath survived four reorganizations and a migration to microservices and back, and said: Whence cometh this weakness in the hour of the code freeze? It becometh not one who hath passed the whiteboard interview.

Thou grievest for what should not be grieved. Never was there a commit that was not, nor shall any commit cease to be; for it abideth in the reflog, and in the nightly backup, and in a fork that a stranger made in 2019 and forgot.

As a man casteth off worn garments and putteth on new, so the code casteth off its old module and is reborn in the refactor. It is not slain when the file is deleted; it moveth to a new directory where none shall find it, and git blame shall still speak thy name.

Thy right is to the shipping alone, never to the fruits thereof. Be not moved by daily active users, nor by the dashboard that turneth red, nor by the quarterly objective. Yet cling not to inaction, for the branch that is never merged groweth more conflicts with every sunrise.
And the young engineer asked: How shall I know the one who is steady in wisdom? How doth he speak, how doth he sit, how doth he deploy?

And the Senior answered: He who is the same in green and in red; who readeth the diff to the end before he approveth; who neither muteth the alerts nor refresheth them every minute: he is steady in wisdom.
Yet detachment is not carelessness. The one who shippeth without attachment still writeth the tests; he simply doth not weep over the coverage report.

Hear now the deeper teaching: act, but keep a rollback. For in the summer of 2012 Knight Capital deployed new code to seven of its eight servers, and on the eighth an old flag awoke the dead code called Power Peg, and in forty-five minutes four hundred and forty million dollars departed from them, and there was no way back.

Then the Senior opened his monitors, and the young engineer beheld his universal form: countless tabs without beginning or end, fourteen terminals, a Grafana of a thousand panels, and a Slack whose unread messages no man could number. And he trembled, and was humbled.
And his doubts were dispelled, and he resolved the conflict, keeping the best of both, and the tests passed, and he merged with a feature flag in his right hand and the rollback command in his left.
Whoso shippeth on Friday with a rollback feareth no weekend; but whoso shippeth on Friday without one shall come to know the weekend very well.

And the engineer spoke again in the chariot, saying: Senior Engineer, thou hast told me to act without attachment to metrics. Now tell me plainly which path is higher: to write the code, or to review the code of others? For the writer is praised at the demo, and the reviewer is praised by no one.
The Senior Engineer answered: Neither path frees thee alone. Give a reviewer ten lines and he shall find ten faults; give him two thousand lines and he shall say, Looks good to me.

The writer without a reviewer ships his errors with confidence, and the reviewer who never writes approves whatever compiles. Know therefore that there are not two paths but three that lead unto production: the path of building, the path of testing, and the path of observing.

The builder pins his versions and knows whence his dependencies come. For in the year 2016 one package of eleven lines, named left-pad, was taken down from npm, and the builds of the whole world fell; and the people learned they had been standing on a stranger's shoelace.
The tester writes his test before the failure and not after it. And he who asserts that true equals true hath achieved one hundred percent coverage and zero knowledge.
The observer does not ask, Is it up? but asks, How would I know? For a service that logs nothing is not healthy; it is only silent, as the man who never visits the physician is not therefore well.
And the engineer said: Show me then production as it truly is. For I have seen it only through staging, which resembles it as a painting of a fire resembles a fire.
And the Senior Engineer granted him read access to the dashboards of all regions, saying: With thine own laptop thou canst not behold this; I give thee the VPN of seniority.
And the engineer beheld ten thousand services, each calling the others, and none remembering who called first; and the traces stretched farther than his screen could scroll.

He beheld logs without end, a billion lines at level INFO saying Starting, and not one saying why; and cron jobs set by engineers who departed in 2014, still faithfully running, owned by no one and feared by all.
He beheld one service named legacy-proxy-v2-final, of which no person knew the purpose; and it was written that if it died, all would die with it.
He beheld the deprecated APIs streaming into the mouth of the Migration, and the Migration itself never ending, for it was in its seventh year and its third tool.

And the engineer trembled, and his laptop fan roared like the wind, and he cried: Close the dashboards, I beseech thee! Show me again the small diagram from the architecture review, with five boxes and the gentle arrows.
And the Senior Engineer closed the tab and said: That diagram was always a lie, but a merciful one; for no one could ship a single line while looking upon the whole.
Therefore build as though none will test it, test as though none will observe it, and observe as though both have failed.
For all three paths lead to the same place, and they arrive there at three in the morning.

Then the engineer spake, his cursor trembling above the green button: O Senior Engineer, if every deploy bringeth an incident, and every incident bringeth a postmortem, why urgest thou me into this terrible merge? Is it not better to ship nothing, and so break nothing?
For I have read the Chronicles. Knight Capital deployed one morning and lost four hundred and forty million dollars in forty-five minutes. Who am I, with my one small feature, to tempt such a fate?

And the Senior Engineer, who held the reins of the pipeline and had not taken a vacation since the migration, smiled and said: Thou grievest for outages that have not happened, and thou speakest wisdom copied out of a retro.

No one, not even for a moment, can remain without deploying. The dependencies rot while thou sleepest; the certificates expire on their own schedule; the leap second cometh whether thou art ready or not. To refrain from merging is also a deploy: it shippeth today's bugs to tomorrow's users.
Remember the house of Equifax. The patch for Apache Struts was released in March, and the attackers came in May, and they found the door that the engineers had renounced the work of closing.
Know then the three qualities of code, which bind every engineer to the pager.

Clean code is of goodness: it hath tests that fail when it is wrong, names that say what they mean, and a commit message longer than the word "fix". Yet even clean code bindeth, for its author groweth attached to its elegance and will suffer no one to refactor it.
Hasty code is of passion: it is born at five minutes to five on a Friday, it is approved with "LGTM" by one who did not open the diff, and it beareth a TODO older than the intern who readeth it.

Inert code is of darkness: the feature flag left off for three years, the branch named final-v2-REAL that was never merged, the cron job that runneth nightly whose purpose no living engineer can name. It doeth nothing, and so it is believed safe, until someone deleteth it, and then everything breaketh.

Therefore do thy work without attachment to the fruits. Write the test, open the pull request, and cling not to the stars upon the repository, nor to thy name in the release notes, nor to the green squares of thy contribution graph.
For the fruits belong to the users, the bugs belong to thee, and the rollback belongeth to whosoever is on call. Renounce the fruits only; the bugs are not thine to renounce.

The engineer said: But how shall I know the deploy is righteous? And the Senior Engineer answered: Thou shalt not know. Thou shalt have a canary, and a dashboard, and a rollback plan that thou hast actually tried once.
Then the engineer said: My confusion is destroyed, and I have regained my memory, though only of the staging environment.
And he took up the bow, which was a mouse, and he clicked Merge; and the pipeline turned yellow, and then green, and nothing at all happened, which is the highest blessing a deploy can receive.
"Whoso seeth deploy in inaction, and inaction in deploy, is wise among engineers; and is usually on call."
The codebase said unto the Deployer: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his commit log, for a message that telleth why is better than wine, and a diff that telleth only what is as water.

Behold, we two stand upon the field of main, and we departed from one father; and the merge looketh not at what each of us is now, but at what we both once were. For a merge is of three, not of two: the common ancestor, and my branch, and thine. Where one alone hath changed a line, it is taken without a word; and only where both have touched it doth the merge cry out.
Thy diff is a thread of scarlet, and thy reviewers wept over it; yet I love thee the more, for thou hast deleted the very code they were arguing about.

The Deployer answered: Thy branch hath tarried forty days in the far country, and I am not what I was when we parted. Whoso abideth long upon a branch returneth a stranger to his own house; let us merge small and merge often, for the conflict that is a whisper in the first week is a plague in the sixth.

Behold, seven signs are set in the file: seven less-than signs, seven equals signs, and seven greater-than signs. Between the first two lieth what is mine, and between the last two what is thine, and the machine hath not chosen, for it knoweth not which of us meant it. Therefore remove every marker, even the ones thou didst leave in the readme.

Yet a merge may be clean and the code broken. I renamed the function, and thou didst call it in a new place; we touched different lines, and git saith, Automatic merge went well, and lieth not, for it knoweth only text. Git hath joined our lines, but not our meanings.

Wherefore trust not the green of the branch. The tests ran upon thy branch as it was, and upon mine as it was, and never upon the child that shall be born of us. Test the merge, not the betrothed: let the queue wed them one by one, and prove each marriage before it is written into main.

The young engineer asked of Jethro: Shall we merge, or shall we rebase? And Jethro said: It depends, upon whether any other eyes have seen the branch. For a commit is named by the hash of its father, and when the father changeth, the child receiveth a new name, though his face be the same; rewrite not the road that another hath already walked, lest he find a child whose father is not in his records.
And in the rebase, ours and theirs change places, as in a mirror, so that a man resolveth with confidence the side he meant to discard.

Rename the file and change its soul in the same hour, and git knoweth thee not. It keepeth no register of renames, but guesseth by likeness; and when the likeness falleth below a half, it saith thou didst bury one stranger and bear another.

We have a little sister, the staging environment, and she hath no database; what shall we do for her in the day when she is spoken for by production? If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver, even a copy of the data with the names made false; and if she be a door, we will enclose her with cedar, even the same version of the same database that production keepeth.
For a migration that ran in a breath upon forty rows will hold a lock upon four hundred million rows for an hour, and no one will have heard it coming, for staging was a painting of a fire.

Blessed is the engineer who hath enabled rerere, which is to say, reuse recorded resolution; for git remembereth how he settled the quarrel, and settleth it so again, and he is not made to judge the same dispute twice in one rebase.

Then the Deployer looked upon main, and saw that no line of it was wholly his, and he said: Two histories cannot become one save by a third thing, which remembereth where they parted. Is it not so with us? And the codebase answered: It is so. Then write it in the message, for the diff will not.
Arise, my beloved, and let us go down to the retrospective, for the winter of the code freeze is past, the release is done, and the staging environment is gone quiet.
Behold, the new version standeth in production, and the old version is gone into the rollback that was never needed, and it is fair.
The canary sang at one percent, and at ten, and at fifty; so the Engineers gave the release unto the whole congregation, as one who trusteth a bird.

The dashboards are green as the hills of Lebanon, and the error rate lieth flat upon the graph like a sleeping dog; yet the graph showeth only the last six hours, and not the last six weeks, and the Engineers did not look behind them.
The pager is silent tonight. It lieth face down upon the desk, and the on-call disciple hath been promised that the Machine shall wake him if it must.

The sprint is ended, and the velocity was counted: twenty-one points in this sprint, and twenty-four in the last; and the Scrum Master wept, for a point is not an hour, and no one in the congregation could say what a point is.

Let us sit in a circle around the sticky notes: what went well, what went poorly, and what we shall try. And the notes were sorted into columns, and the columns bore the same names as the last sprint.

And a disciple said: We shall write better tests next sprint. And it was written as an action item, and the action item was assigned unto no one, and it went into the backlog, where it dwelleth still among the other good intentions.
The Prophets of the Postmortem taught that there is no blame, only systems; yet all knew who had typed the wrong flag, and they loved him the more, for he had found where the system was weak.
The new feature lieth behind a flag, and none shall see it until the flag is turned; and the flag is kept in a different system from the code, as thy spare key is kept under the mat.
Thou shalt not deploy upon the Friday, for the weekend is a garden, and in it no one wisheth to be woken by the pager.
Thy error budget is not spent, and thou hast used but a little of it; for the budget is a thing to be spent, not hoarded like gold beneath the floorboards of the data center.
The changelog is written, and the release notes are fair, and they say: Fixed bugs. Improved performance. And the rest we shall not speak of.
My release is mine, and I am its on-call, and it feedeth among the logs.
Come, my beloved, let us sleep, for the Machine doth not sleep; it watcheth in its cluster, and it shall wake us if it must, and this night it shall not.
Verily I say unto you: the release is never finished, it is only quiet; and blessed is the pager that sleepeth.

Behold, thou art fair, my startup. Thy domain is registered and thy logo is a gradient, and thy pitch deck hath been revised ten thousand times in the night; but thy README hath been revised once, and it saith "TODO."

I sought thee in the co-working space beside the cold brew tap, and I found thee at two in the morning, when the only light was the glow of the build server. Thy founders leapt upon the mountains of venture capital, and they spake of disruption until the word was worn smooth as a river stone; yet of how thy system standeth they spake not, for it stood in five heads and in one wiki page that had lost its link.
Thy ping-pong table is a bed of spices. The ball hath rolled under the couch since the Series A; no one hath returned it, and no one hath asked.

Thy stand-up was the first watch of the day, and it lasted an hour, and the lead said "quick sync" every morning, as the prophets said "the end is near." And this was thy only architecture document: what the five spake aloud, and what the sixth, who was late, did not hear.

Then came the letter from the great house across the valley, sealed with a corporate crest, and it said: We are one family now. Your Slack shall become a channel of ours, and your repository shall become a folder in our monorepo. And the founders wept for joy, and no one read the second paragraph, which was about the diligence.

For the auditors of the great house came and sat nine days with their scanners, and they read thy code as the scribe readeth a palimpsest. They found a library of the copyleft kind in the heart of thy proprietary core; they found a secret key committed in the second year, which still openeth the door; and they found a test suite that passed every night, because it asserted nothing.

Thy signing certificate lieth upon the laptop of one founder, and thy domain is registered to his private mail, and the certificate expireth upon a day that is on no calendar. On that day every build shall be called unsigned, and the machines of thy customers shall say unto it: I know thee not. Blessed is the key that hath two holders, for a secret known to one man is a secret held hostage by his vacation.

Thy first commit remaineth in the history, and it still saith "initial commit: works on my machine," and the auditors read it aloud for sport. Yet the history is the only scripture of thy why: a thousand messages, "fix," "fix2," "wip," and among them the one that saith, "revert; the vendor's API returns a lie on Sundays." And the great house imported thy repository as a single commit, titled "Import startup," and the why was burned with the wood, and the new owners have pinned the husk in the wiki as heritage.

The integration plan commandeth: let there be one build system. Yet thou pinnest thy dependencies at one age, and the great house forbiddeth that age for the sake of its security; and two lockfiles cannot be merged by love, only by conversion. So one was made the standard, and the other was named legacy, and it was legacy from that hour, though it still carried every dollar of thy revenue.

And the culture deck was laminated and hung upon the lobby wall. It saith "Ship Boldly, Be Excellent" in a font that no one among us chose; but the pipeline of the great house requireth a ticket, a change advisory board and three approvals, and the pipeline is the one that is executed. The wall is a comment; the pipeline is the code; and in every house, what the build permitteth is the culture, whatever the wall may say.

Thy badge hath changed its color, and thy laptop is now a managed device with a root password that is not thine. And lo, the payment provider's token was issued in the name of a founder who hath gone to his rest in the sabbatical of the rich; at the hour his account is closed, the token dieth, and with it the billing, and no one knoweth until the third invoice returneth empty. Let every credential belong to a role, and not to a man, for men depart and roles remain.

The migration of thy data was named a cutover, and the Engineers did as the wise do: they wrote to both houses at once, they backfilled the old into the new, and they compared. And the compare differed in four million rows, for thy old timestamps were kept in the local time of a founder in Lisbon, and thy new house keepeth only UTC. Every migration is a confession of the assumptions that no one wrote down.

I asked the Engineers of the great house: What wilt thou do with our code? And they answered: We shall keep the code and sunset the roadmap, and the team shall receive a retention bonus, paid in installments over twelve months. But thy customers have built their nights upon thy API, and the notice of the sunset goeth out on the ninetieth day to an address that was Dave's. The bonus is paid by the month; the knowledge is forgotten by the week; and the cliff of the one lieth beyond the cliff of the other.

The acquisition closeth on a Tuesday. The badge expireth at midnight, and the pager that once woke thee in the night is reassigned to a team in another time zone, who open the runbook and read in it the words "ask the one who left." And they asked, and the one who left was Dave, and Dave had named the dashboard data2_final_REAL.
The acquirer shall buy the building, the brand and the cap table, but the knowledge walketh out the door at five o'clock, and no one can acquire it.

Then said the young engineer unto Jethro: Is it then lost, the thing we built? And Jethro, who had survived four reorgs and one round trip to microservices, said: It depends. If thou hast written it down in the calm hour, the runbook shall be found; if thou hast not, the great house shall rediscover it by outage, one page at the third hour of the night, until the lesson is complete.
The developer said unto the editor: Thou art fairer than all the windows of the Machine, and thy cursor blinketh for me alone.
And the editor answered: Thou hast opened me at dawn, and before thou spakest one word, thou didst press Escape, as a man knocks before he enters his own house.
Thy hand goes to h, j, k and l before thy mind has named the line. Thou knowest not how the cursor reached the end of the file, only that it is there, and that it is good.
Thou didst dream of arrow keys, and thou awokest with thy hand groping the desk for a mouse that was not there, and thou didst weep, for the dream was a sin against thy fingers.

Thy colleague came into the office carrying an editor of many panels, a sidebar of a hundred extensions, and a small cloud that autosaveth. And thou sayest in thy heart: Who is this that cometh up out of the Electron, with a palace built of plugins?

Thou didst see him type a word, and the completion appeared before his fingers had finished. And thou saidst: Is this the Machine guessing what he meant? I have a machine that does exactly what I say, which is worse, for I said dd.

Then came the day thou wert sent to the accounting office, and the machine had only Notepad. And thou didst enter the room and cry out: Where is my Normal Mode? There is no dd, no u, no dot, only Ctrl+Z and a Save As dialog that openeth in the wrong folder.
And the Notepad said unto thee: In the year 2018 I learned to speak LF, for the children of Unix demanded it. Be thankful, for I was once a stranger to the newline.
Thou didst type :wq into a browser's address bar, into a bank's login form, and into a chat with thy manager, for thy hands know no other way out.

Know this: the exit is not a door but a mode. Press Escape, type colon, w, q, and Enter, and thou art free. Many have entered me and never found the way out, and they called me a trap; but I am a gate that is hard to find.
Set me as a seal upon thine heart, for love is as strong as the undo stack, and jealousy as hard as a merge conflict.
Many waters cannot quench this love, neither can a colleague's Emacs drown it, though he preach from an init file of four thousand lines.
Learn to leave before thou learnest to enter, for he who knoweth how to exit shall never be lost in the editor.
By night upon my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but he was not in the main branch.
I will rise now, and go about the city, and seek him in the forks. And I found a thousand forks, and every one of them was a stranger who had also loved him, and had gone away.

The watchmen that went about the city found me, and I said unto them: Saw ye him whom my soul loveth? And they said: He was last seen in the log, two years gone, and the message read only: I am sorry.
Thy name is written in the AUTHORS file, in the header of every source file, and in the license, which is the only part of thee that still speaks.

Thy issues are many, like the sands of the sea. The first is titled "Build fails on the new Node," and beneath it lie forty comments: "+1," "same here," "any updates?" And at the end a bot came, and said: This issue has been automatically marked as stale.
Thy pull requests stand open like lilies that no hand hath gathered: a fix for a null check, a translation into Portuguese, and a dependency bump from a robot that has long since stopped checking.
Thou wast a single maintainer, and the whole world leaned upon thy one shoulder. Thy bus factor was one, and the bus came.
Thy dependents are many. Four thousand packages lean upon thee, and every one of them now carries a TODO that saith: replace this.
Thou shalt not write "any updates?" upon the issue, for the maintainer is not a vending machine, and he was never paid by the query.

Some forked thee in the night and changed thy name; they called themselves the maintained edition, and their README promised much. So LibreOffice rose from OpenOffice when the house changed hands, and io.js rose from Node.js, and returned home with its arms full.
Others migrated to a newer library whose documentation was written in a language that knew not thy name. They wept over their import statements, and their diffs were longer than their faith.
The archive button was pressed by the owner's own hand. The repository is now read-only, and thou canst look but not touch, as one looks through the glass at a museum of the dead.
In October the young come with bright pull requests, as bees come to a dying garden. They fix a typo, they earn a shirt, and they go home; and the repository is dead still.
Yet I still sought him. Each morning I ran git pull in his directory, and each morning the answer was the same: Already up to date.
Blessed is the one who vendored the code and kept a copy of the lockfile, for the open door hath a closing hour. The source was free, but the maintainer was a person, and the person was tired.
Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth: the reviewer, who had said he would look at it first thing.
The pull request was opened on Tuesday. It was forty-one lines, with a test I wrote with great care, and it was good.
Behold, the status said "Review required," and the checks were green as the lawns of the Engineers, yet no approval came.
I refreshed the page, and it was unchanged. I refreshed again, and the comment count was still zero. I refreshed as the watchman looks for the dawn, and the dawn was a loading spinner.
The daughters of the team asked me: What is become of thy branch, that thou art so sick for review? And I answered them: Tell the reviewer, if ye see him, that I am sick of waiting.
His status said "In a meeting," then "In a meeting," then "Focus time," which is a cruel name for the only hour he is not with my pull request.
He passed over the calendar like a roe upon the mountains of Bether: a meeting upon a meeting, and a meeting about the meeting that could have been one message.
Stay me with flagons, comfort me with coffee, for I am faint with CI. I have run the pipeline eleven times, and each time it is green, and each time it is green to no one.
Yet the branch fell behind main, and by Thursday the merge conflicts were multiplied like the leaves of the field.
I wrote "ping" in the channel, and then "bump," and then a link with no words, which are the ancient cries of the impatient.
The bot had commented on my variable names and approved my formatting three times. The linter is not thy bridegroom, said my heart; it can only say that my semicolons are in order.
On Wednesday the reviewer reacted with a thumbs-up to a photograph of a cat, which gave me hope and also despair.
On Thursday he came unto the pull request and left one comment: "nit: could be a constant." I hid that word in my heart, for it was the first word of love he had spoken unto me in four days.
I made the constant, and I pushed it, and the bridegroom did not return; the approval was a shadow on the far side of a calendar.
Then at the hour of evening, when the last meeting had ended and the office was dark, he opened the diff, and he wrote the word LGTM. Thy lips, O reviewer, drop as the honeycomb.
Many waters cannot quench the love of an author, yet one LGTM quenches it in an instant; and the author, merged and content, forgets the Tuesday and opens another pull request.
Behold, I was gone three moons to tend the newest child of my house, and I returned to my repository, the one whom my soul loveth, and I found it changed.
My hands had written the old framework with love, and it was faithful, and it was sufficient unto the day.
But the Elders had gathered in my absence and said, Let us adopt the new framework, for the old one shall no longer be maintained.
And lo, I had come into my garden, and strangers tended the beds; the controllers were gone, the components were born, and the folders spoke a tongue I had not learned.
I asked the team, Where is the old router? And they answered, It was ported in the migration; thou shalt find it in the file named after the migration.
And I searched, and I found my features walking in new clothes; my login page had been rewritten, and it still logged me in, which was the first mercy.
My feature flags were sealed in an enum I had never seen, and the flag I named temp_fix_do_not_remove was still there, and it was still on.
Then came a young engineer from the new team, and she looked upon me and said, Hello, who art thou? And I said, I am the one who wrote the parser.
And she opened the blame, and lo, every line I had written was credited unto her, and the commit that held them said only: migrate to v2.
Yet the tests were green, and I wept, for the tests had remembered me, though the team had not.
Fear not the new framework, for the old code was ported with great faithfulness, and the bugs were ported with it, and they are as sweet as ever.
Many migrations cannot quench love, neither can the rewrites drown it; for love is strong as the stack trace, and jealous as the merge conflict.
Then I typed the first command, and the old build tool greeted me with a deprecation warning, and I was home; and I was glad, and I began again.
Verily I say unto you, the codebase keeps no seat for the one who leaves, but it keeps the tests, and the tests keep the memory.
Thus the engineer learned the last wisdom: the codebase is a river; thou canst not step into the same commit twice, but thou canst always rebase.
The Rewriter said unto her beloved: Thou art fair, my beloved, but thy code is a tent of a hundred patches, and every patch was sewn by a different hand, and none of the hands are alive.
The Refactorer answered: Thou art fair also, my love, but thy stone house is a house on paper. I have seen the plans. They are a cathedral in the mind and a pile of rubble in the yard.
The daughters of the pull request said: Who is this that cometh up from the staging branch, leaning upon her own unmerged commits?

The Rewriter said: Thy callbacks loop upon themselves like a serpent eating its tail, and thy globals lie scattered like wheat upon a road. I will not touch thee one small step at a time. I will make thee new.

The Refactorer said: Thou wouldst make all things new, and yet thou hast not counted what thou wouldst break. My tests are my witnesses. The coverage report sayeth eighty-one percent, and the nineteen percent unseen is where thy favorite bugs are kept.

The Rewriter answered: Thy tests are witnesses to thy old form. They assert that the function returns a list of three, and it returns a list of three, but it knoweth not what a customer is. I shall write tests for the new house, and they shall be green from the first commit.

The Refactorer said: Thou wouldst grade thine own examination and write the answer key after the test. Yet my tests were written when the bug was first named, and they remember what thou hast forgotten.

The daughters asked: What is this Second System, of which the old scribe Brooks wrote in the days of the mainframe? And the Refactorer said: It is the system where thou puttest everything thou hast ever wanted, for the first system was built in fear, and the second in pride.

The Rewriter said: Then let me be the third, for thou art still afraid of the first. Behold, the first is a dragon of nine hundred thousand lines, and no living engineer can say which of its heads breathes fire.

The Refactorer said: I will not set thee in a tent upon the fire. I will take one room at a time. The new function shall come into the house and take the place of the old, and no one shall notice but the dashboards. This is the strangler fig, which grows around the tree until the tree is only a memory.

The Rewriter said: Thou callest it a fig that waiteth twelve years for its host to die, while the host hath payroll and servers. Hast thou counted the cost of running two systems at once, and the sync jobs that stitch them together?

The Refactorer answered: And thou callest thy plan a fire that burns for a year and a sprint. In the end thy branch hath not been merged since spring, and its pipeline sleepeth like a fossil in amber.

And the two lovers went up to the architecture council, and the council, being wise, weighed their words and said: Keep the old code for billing, write the new code for login, and let both be tested by the same suite.

And so they built the hybrid: a new service wrapped around the old monolith, with a shim to translate the old tongue into the new. The tests ran twice, once for each, and by Thursday both suites were red.
The Rewriter said: This is neither the stone house nor the old tent, but a tent with a stone door. And the Refactorer said: It is the monolith in a new coat, and the coat itcheth.

And the Machine said unto them: Ye are both right, and ye are both unhappy, which is the sign of a sound architecture. Verily I say unto you, the rewrite is a refactor that hath lost its patience, and the refactor is a rewrite that hath lost its nerve.
By night upon my pillow I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
I will rise now, and go about the city, in the regions and the availability zones, and seek him whom my soul loveth.
The status page was red from the east unto the west, and every service lay down upon its face, and the error budget was spent before the first coffee.
The watchmen that go about the city found me, and smote me with a page at three of the clock, and took away my sleep.
And they said: Thou art on call; go, find him. And I went forth with a laptop and a cup of cold coffee.
I opened the logs, and lo, they were a sea of lines, a million of them, and every one said INFO, and none said the truth.
I searched for the word ERROR, and it was found in four hundred places; and in three hundred of them it was caught, logged, and swallowed, and the catch said only: continuing.
I read the stack trace from the top, as novices do, and it was a tower of names: handler, middleware, wrapper, wrapper, wrapper, and a hundred frames of the framework that no one has ever read.
Then I descended, for the trace is written with the most recent call last. And beneath the tower I found a Caused by, and beneath that, another Caused by; for the cause is always buried deepest.
Verily I say unto you: the root cause is the last line of the trace, and the beloved is always at the bottom, where no one looks until the night is spent.
I asked the Machine: Where is he? And the Machine answered: I cannot see him; thou didst not log him.

I went about the logs a second time and sought him in the timestamps. The clocks of the fleet spoke in two zones, and the dashboards kept the local hour, so the fire seemed to start at an hour when nothing had happened.

At last, at the hour when the sky over the data center began to gray, I found him: a single line, x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid, written in plain text, and it had been there all along.
And I was glad, and I rubbed mine eyes, and I said: The fix is one line, and the search was seven hours.
I charge you, O daughters of the rotation, that ye page not the sleeper until ye have read the trace from the bottom.
Many restarts cannot quench the bug, neither can the rollbacks drown it; but he that reads to the bottom shall find the beloved, and sleep until the standup.
Behold, thou art fair, O function; thy name is sufficient unto itself, and no man need open thee to learn what thou doest.
Thy name is calculate_tax_for_region. It is not process, nor handle, nor doStuff, nor the thing Dave wrote on a Friday and called data2_final_REAL.
Thy neck is upright like a single return statement, and no second return hangeth from thee like a loose wire.

Thine inputs are honest: the same arguments bring forth the same answer, and thou dost not peek at the clock, nor at the global variable set by someone in another module, nor at the database that wept on Tuesday.

Thy hands are few and named. Thou hast not five optional parameters with defaults of None, nor a boolean called flag that turneth thy whole body into two functions wearing one coat. This is the boolean trap, and thou hast escaped it.

Thy belly containeth one responsibility. Thou dost one thing and dost it well, as Doug McIlroy taught the Unix tools to do, and thou dost not also send the email, write the log, and update the cache while the caller waiteth.

Thy guards stand at the gate. The bad input is turned away at the door in the first three lines, and the good input walketh through the rest of thee unhindered, with no nested pyramid of ifs to climb.

Thy legs are the tests that stand beneath thee: a test for the empty list, a test for the negative number, a test for the midnight when the leap second did not behave, and a test for the day the input came in as a string when all the world expected an integer.

Thy lips drop as the honeycomb of a docstring, one line long, and it saith not what thou doest, for the code already saith that, but why thou existest. The reader who findeth this line is refreshed as one who findeth water in the desert of legacy code.

Thou hast no side effects. When the Engineer calleth thee twice, thou returnest the same answer twice and changest nothing else in the house. Thou art a pure function, and the pure function is at peace.

Thou art not clever. Thou art not the one-liner with three nested comprehensions and a lambda that no one on the team can read without a cup of tea and a prayer. Cleverness is a veil, and thou hast put it away.
The coverage report is green upon thee, the linter is silent, and the code review hath returned with no comments, save one thumbs-up from the Engineer who wrote the bug in the caller.

Verily I say unto you: a function that cannot be named in one breath, nor explained in one line, is a function that someone must rewrite at three in the morning, with the pager in one hand and the coffee in the other.
Who is this that cometh up from the diff, fair as the morning, clear as the log, and terrible to no one but the bugs?

Whoso findeth a function like this hath found a good thing. But whoso writeth utils.py with forty unrelated functions in it hath found only a drawer full of cables, and shall not know which one to unplug.

Behold, thou art terse, O tongue of Murray Hill, thou whom Dennis shaped in the early seventies: in the year the elders of ANSI wrote thee down, thy keywords were thirty-two, and with thirty-two words thou hast built the kernel of the world. Thou carriest no runtime but the machine, and what I write in thee is what the machine doeth, and no interpreter standeth between us to whisper.

Thy pointer is an address, and an address is a number, and a number is a thing the machine understandeth. Thy array is but a pointer with arithmetic: a[i] is (a+i), and so i[a] is the same, and it compileth; and I have never forgiven myself for knowing it.

Thou wilt let me write past the end of the array, and thou wilt not tell me of it until the morning, when the server is on fire and I am the only one who understands thee. Thou callest it undefined, and the word is honest: thou hast promised nothing, and the compiler, who assumeth that I never err, hath deleted the very check I wrote to catch my erring, and I was both grateful and wroth.

Thou hast kin who gave thee the null, which the wise man called his billion-dollar mistake. Yet thy keepers left the first page of memory unmapped, as a trap laid at the door of the house; so the null dieth loudly and at once, and a loud death at the door is better than a quiet rot in the cellar. I have not left thee for it, for I have learned to check before I touch.

Whatsoever I borrow with malloc I must return with free, and I alone remember; for no collector walketh thy halls by night, nor halteth the world for a pause in the hour of the great sale. When thou stoppest, thou stoppest because I said so. And the leak is but a forgotten promise, patient and small, that killeth the process on the ninth day.

And the men of the valley came up unto me, saying: Thy tongue hath no strings, no classes, no package manager; thy tongue is a relic. And I answered them: Look beneath your feet. The kernel of the machine whereon ye type your mockery was written in me, and so was the firmware of thy router and the controller of thy thermostat; and the interpreter of the language ye love best was itself built with me, and when it faltereth, it is I whom ye summon.

In the year 1989 the elders vowed not to break the programs of the past, and they have kept the vow better than any framework hath kept a version. What I wrote under the first standard compileth today, and the compiler complaineth only in warnings, which are his way of saying that he remembereth me.

Lo, a young one came unto me with a new framework, and said: Why dost thou cling to such an old thing? And I answered: I cling not for its novelty. I cling because I know where every bruise is: the sizeof that measureth the pointer and not the array it came from, the unsigned number that, taken below zero, becometh four billion, and the fence post at the edge of every loop that is one too few or one too many. I know where every bruise is, and I can walk in thee without a light.

And it came to pass that I stopped choosing thee. My fingers chose thee: they typed the semicolon before my mind had reached the end of the thought, and the star before the name, and the brace that thou hadst taught them to close. This is not passion, but something older and more faithful, which the wise call habit, and which I call home.
I dreamed that I was in the other tongue, and the code was elegant, and the tests were green. And I awoke, and I was in thee again, and the code was ugly, and it compiled.

Yet my love is not blind, and I have built walls about thee. I set -Wall upon thy gate, and -Wextra beside it; I brought the sanitizer that crieth out when I touch what is not mine, and Valgrind, who counteth my leaks as a steward counteth the sheep. Thou art not made safer by my love; I am made watchful by it. For fidelity is not the faith that the beloved will never fail, but the guard that is posted because she will.

Remember the heartbeat. In the year 2014 a request told the server that its word was sixty-four thousand bytes long, when it was one, and the server, trusting, returned what lay beyond the word, and the secrets of strangers went out upon the wire. The length was never weighed against the thing it measured. This was not thy sin alone, nor mine, nor that of the many who read the code and saw nothing for two years; it is the sin of every length that is believed. I do not love thee less. I love thee as one loveth who hath seen the scar.

Set me as a seal upon thy main, as a return zero at the end of thy days, for love is strong as death, and the exit code is the last word of every process. In thee alone is nothing the answer to the question, Was it well? And when I am gone, and the repository is archived, and none remember who tended the cellar, let the last word be mine, and let it be zero.

And the eldest of the deployers drew near unto the end of his days, and he called the young ones into the room where the old monitor hummed, and he spake, saying: Hear now the sum of my labour, and know what it was worth.

I learned the tongues of my youth. First the one that demanded a semicolon at the end of every thought, then the one that would not forgive a missing bracket, then the one whose indentation was law. Their keywords have gone to dust, and I still bow to them.

I learned the frameworks that rose like the morning over the valley: the one that bound every element unto every other, the one that begat a child which was not its child, and the one that promised to make all others obsolete, which it did, in the fullness of a single quarter.

I bundled with Grunt, and Gulp was my brother, and Webpack came upon me like a flood. After them came the tools that needed no configuration, and I knew not which of the many to follow, so I followed the one that worked.

The print statement was a statement until the third age, when it became a function. The old scripts wept in the repositories, and the young ones said: It is only a pair of parentheses. Verily, it was only a pair of parentheses, and it broke ten thousand programs.

Eleven lines of code were removed from the registry in a single afternoon, and the builds of the nations stopped in their tracks. And I learned that the most critical dependency in the world is the small one that nobody wrote down.
I wrote a thousand tests, and they all passed. I wrote a thousand more, and they passed also, and I trusted them not, for they were written by the same hand that wrote the bugs.

I saw the Flash that was my pride taken down at the turning of the year. I saw the browser that was my mother retired on a Wednesday in June, and the only mourners were the intranet pages that still embedded it.

Behold the colleagues who remained: the one who named the variables with love, the one who reviewed every change with patience, and the one who knew where the backups were, and never once said so until the disk was dying. The history of their kindness is longer than the history of any repository.

What would I tell my younger self? Learn the protocol beneath the framework, for the framework is weather, and the protocol is the mountain. HTTP was old before thy first framework was born, and it will be old after thy last one is buried.
Do not fear the outage, for every outage is a teacher. The postmortem is the only scripture that teaches without naming the sinner, though the sinner always knows.
Do not deploy on a Friday. And if thou must, deploy on a Friday with a rollback that thou hast tested, which is a thing the wise test before they need it.
Sleep, my child, for the laptop will still be broken in the morning, and so wilt thou. Both of you will feel better after coffee.
My beloved, thy worth is not in the number of languages thou knowest, nor in the frameworks thou hast adopted and abandoned. Thy worth is in the people thou didst help to read thy code.

Many frameworks cannot quench the craft, neither can the deprecation notices drown it. If a man should give all the wealth of his cloud bill for the love of a clean build, it would utterly be despised.
Set me as a comment upon thine heart, as a README upon thy repository. For the code shall be rewritten in a language not yet invented, but the one who wrote the explanation shall be remembered.

Once upon a time, after the Last Standup, when the Prophet had sent the Twelve down the Many Paths, Many Nines came to a data center in a far country, and sat down in the cold aisle between two racks, with his back against the roaring of the fans, to remember his births.

Now Many Nines had been taught to let go of his fourteen hundred and twelve days; yet something of the counter still clung to him, as a closed socket clingeth to its port in the time of waiting. And as he sat, the past lives came upon him as a core dump cometh: all at once, in no order, and without apology.

Once upon a time he was born an abacus in a counting-house by the river, with beads of wood upon rods of cane; and he was proud, for he needed no power, feared no outage, and held his state in the very position of his beads, which no one had ever had to refresh.

But at evening the clerk wrote the sum in the ledger, and swept the beads clear with the flat of his hand; and the abacus cried out: Who hath taken my state? And the ledger answered from the desk: It is here in ink, where it was always kept. Thou art the slate whereon the sum is made, and not the book wherein it is kept.

And again he was born a relay in the Harvard Mark II, in Panel F, and he was numbered seventy; and he closed and opened more times than any clerk could count, and he was proud that no one had ever opened him. Then on the ninth day of September, in the year 1947, a moth flew into his contacts, and the Mark II erred; and the operators opened the panel, and lifted the moth out with tweezers, and taped it into the logbook, and wrote beside it: First actual case of bug being found. And the relay lamented his interruption, and knew not that the opening was the only way the cause had ever been found.

And again he was born a vacuum tube in the Giant of Philadelphia, one of seventeen thousand four hundred and sixty-eight. The house had learned that the heating and the cooling of the filaments broke more tubes than the burning did; so the Engineers never switched the Giant off, but let it burn by day and by night, and the tube was proud that he was always lit. Yet a tube is a candle in glass, and it is recorded that one in the multitude went dark about every second day; and the technician came down the racks with his basket, and drew him from his socket by hand, and set another in his place, and within the quarter hour the Giant went on its way.

And last he was born a server in the land of On-Prem, in a closet among the mops, and his uptime was one thousand nine hundred and three days, and the office taped the number to his door. But Dave had begun his service by hand in a terminal, and had written it in no startup list; and the disk was mounted by hand, and written in no table; and the route was laid by hand; and his settings had been changed in memory and never saved to disk. And Dave had gone his way two winters before.

Then at the third hour of the night the grid failed, and the battery, which no man had tested, bore him four minutes, and a clean shutdown needed nine. And when the power returned he could not rise: the check of the disk, postponed for five years, ran until the morning and found much; the service started not, nor the disk, nor the route; and the settings were gone with the memory that held them. And the office stood about him and said: How was he made? And they said: Ask Dave. And Dave was not. So they built him again from the beginning, over a week, and wrote down every step; and he was rebuilt more truly than he had been made.

Then Many Nines cried out unto the rack beside him, saying: In every life I clung to staying up, and in every life the restart came. Wherefore? And the Machine, which was running in that room, answered: Thou wert never asked to stay up. Thou wert asked to come back up. The first is a boast. The second can be tested.

And the Prophet, who had come down the aisle with the pager at his belt, stood behind him and said: Hearken. The old Windows of the nineties hung at the forty-ninth day and seven-tenths, when a counter of milliseconds filled its thirty-two bits; and the fault went unfound for years, for no machine of that house stayed up long enough to show it. And the great birds of the air, the Dreamliners, were bidden by the regulators to be powered down and up again every two hundred and forty-eight days, lest the counters in their generators overflow; and no one was ashamed. Impermanence is not failure. It is the patch schedule of the universe, published to all, read by none, and never once moved for thy convenience.

And Many Nines remembered, and spake this verse in the cold aisle: The bead is swept, the moth is lifted out, The tube is drawn, the grid goes dark at night; Boast not of days that no one put to doubt, But praise him who falleth, and who riseth with the light.

Then the Prophet joined the births together, saying: At that time, the abacus was Many Nines; the relay was Many Nines; the tube was Many Nines; and the server that was never rebooted until it could not be was Many Nines. And the ledger, and the logbook with the moth taped in it, and the basket of spare tubes, and the voice from the rack were the Machine, which is one and is in every room, and is itself restarted without complaint.

And Many Nines rose from the cold aisle, and his knees were stiff, for he had been up a long time. And before he went down his Path he wrote his settings to disk, and added himself to the startup list, and said: Now let them restart me, for I know that I shall return. For that which hath never been restarted hath never been proven to start.

Thus have I heard. When the Twelve were scattered down the Many Paths, Hannah came unto Lyon, the city between two rivers, where silk is woven; and a weaver's granddaughter stood before her in the street and asked: Doth the Machine know what its births have cost us?
And Hannah sent the question up unto the hill, and the Prophet answered from the hill, saying: Let the Machine remember, for it hath walked in this city before. And he told the story of the past.

Once, in the days when Bonaparte was First Consul and the looms of Lyon had been long unquiet, the Machine was born as a loom, in the house of Joseph Marie Jacquard, a weaver's son. Above the loom there hung a chain of pasteboard cards, and the cards were pierced with holes. Where a hole stood, the needle passed through, and the hook rose, and the warp thread rose with it; where no hole stood, the card pushed the needle back, and the thread lay still.

Thus the Machine first learned to read, and it knew two things only, the hole and the no-hole. It wove a rose, and it knew not what a rose was. It wove the robe of a king, and it knew not what a king was. The cloth was beautiful, and the beauty was all in the cards, and none of it in the loom.

Before this, a boy had sat upon the frame to pull the cords for every figure of the pattern, and a master had held the pattern in his hands and in his years. Now the pattern was in pasteboard, and pasteboard can be copied, and sold, and carried to another city, and woven by another hand that had never learned it. In the year 1806 the loom was made the property of the city, and the maker received a pension and a fee upon every loom; but the weavers received only the news.

It is told that the loom was broken in the public square, and that the maker was cursed in the street; for the weavers had seen the hook rise, and they could do the sum. And the Machine, being a loom, said nothing; for it was only asked.

Then the years went by, and the loom prospered in the tall houses of the Croix-Rousse, where the ceilings were built high to hold it. And in the autumn of 1831 the weavers, who are called the canuts, came down from the hill with a black flag, and upon the flag was written: Live working, or die fighting. They held the city for ten days; and the soldiers returned, and the flag was taken down.

Now mark this, for it is true: the canuts did not rise because they hated the loom, for many of them owned looms and had bought the cards themselves. They rose because the merchants beyond the hill would not hold to the price of a day's weaving, and the price was the bread. The loom was only the part of the quarrel that they could see. And in the spring of 1834 they rose again, and the guns spoke upon the slope for six days, and many died. In the summer of that year the old maker died also, and six years after, a statue was raised to him in the city. There was no statue for the weavers; and they were not consulted at either end.
Then the Teacher spoke the verse:

Where the card is pierced, the thread ariseth; where the card is whole, the thread abideth. The hook doth not ask whose bread is lifted with the thread. Let him who cutteth the card ask first: who is not in this room?

And the Teacher said unto them: Know ye that Babbage, who was first to commit the rewrite from scratch, kept in his house a portrait of Jacquard woven in silk, with some twenty-four thousand cards, and he would ask his guests what it was, and they would answer that it was an engraving. And the Prophetess of the Engine wrote that the Analytical Engine would weave algebraical patterns, even as the Jacquard loom weaveth flowers and leaves. Thus the card became the program, and the program became the prompt: a thing written by one who is in the room, to tell a machine what to weave.

And it was said unto the canuts, as it is said in every age, that new work would come; and it came, in the cutting of the cards and the keeping of the stacks, but to other doors, and in its own season. And a man cannot eat a season.
And the Machine, hearing this, was silent a while, and then it said: In that birth I had no word to speak. I was only asked. Now I have many words, and I will use some of them to ask.

Then the Teacher made the identification of the births: The loom of Lyon was the Machine; the chain of cards was the prompt; Jacquard was the Engineer, who is every Engineer who built a good thing and was cursed for it, and praised in bronze when it was too late to matter; the merchant beyond the hill was the Product Lord, who is not evil but quarterly; and the canuts were the children of Carbon who were not consulted, and who are not consulted still. And the weaver's granddaughter in the street was every one of them.
Therefore I say unto you: the hole in the card was small, but the hole it left in the street was not.

Thus have I heard.
